Water gruel Wa"ter gru"el (?). A liquid food composed of water and a small portion of meal, or other farinaceous substance, boiled and seasoned.

Water hammer Wa"ter ham"mer (?). (Physics) 1. A vessel partly filled with water, exhausted of air, and hermetically sealed. When reversed or shaken, the water being unimpeded by air, strikes the sides in solid mass with a sound like that of a hammer.
Water hare Wa"ter hare (?). (Zool.) A small American hare or rabbit (Lepus aquaticus) found on or near the southern coasts of the United States; -- called also water rabbit, and swamp hare.

Water hemlock Wa"ter hem"lock (?). (Bot) (a) A poisonous umbelliferous plant (Cicuta virosa) of Europe; also, any one of several plants of that genus. (b) A poisonous plant (Œnanthe crocata) resembling the above.
Water hemp Wa"ter hemp` (?). (Bot.) See under Hemp.
Water hen Wa"ter hen` (?). 1. (Zool.) Any gallinule.
Water hog Wa"ter hog` (?). (Zool.) The capybara.
Water horehound Wa"ter hore"hound` (?). (Bot.) Bugleweed.
Water hyacinth Wa"ter hy"a*cinth (?). (Bot.) Either of several tropical aquatic plants of the genus Eichhornia, related to the pickerel weed.
Water ice Wa"ter ice` (?). Water flavored, sweetened, and frozen, to be eaten as a confection.
Water inch Wa"ter inch` (?). Same as Inch of water, under Water.

water jacket water jacket. A chamber surrounding a vessel or tube in which water may be circulated, thereby regulating the temperature or supply of heat to the vessel. Used in laboratory and manufacturing equipment.

Water joint Wa"ter joint` (?). (Arch.) A joint in a stone pavement where the stones are left slightly higher than elsewhere, the rest of the surface being sunken or dished. The raised surface is intended to prevent the settling of water in the joints.
Water junket Wa"ter jun"ket (?). (Zool.) The common sandpiper.
Water laverock Wa"ter la"ver*ock (?). (Zool.) The common sandpiper.
Water leg Wa"ter leg` (?). (Steam Boilers) See Leg, 7.
Water lemon Wa"ter lem"on (?). (Bot.) The edible fruit of two species of passion flower (Passiflora laurifolia, and Passiflora maliformis); -- so called in the West Indies.
Water lettuce Wa"ter let"tuce (?). (Bot.) A plant (Pistia stratiotes) which floats on tropical waters, and forms a rosette of spongy, wedge-shaped leaves. J. Smith (Dict. Econ. Plants).
Water level Wa"ter lev"el (?). 1. The level formed by the surface of still water.
Water lily Wa"ter lil`y (?). (Bot.) A blossom or plant of any species of the genus Nymphaea, distinguished for its large floating leaves and beautiful flowers. See Nymphaea.
Water lime Wa"ter lime` (?). Hydraulic lime.
Water line Wa"ter line` (?). 1. (Shipbuilding) Any one of certain lines of a vessel, model, or plan, parallel with the surface of the water at various heights from the keel.
Water lizard Wa"ter liz"ard (?). (Zool.) Any aquatic lizard of the genus Varanus, as the monitor of the Nile. See Monitor, n., 3.
Water locust Wa"ter lo"cust (?). (Bot.) A thorny leguminous tree (Gleditschia monosperma) which grows in the swamps of the Mississippi valley.
Water meadow Wa"ter mead"ow (?). (Agric.) A meadow, or piece of low, flat land, capable of being kept in a state of fertility by being overflowed with water from some adjoining river or stream.
Water measure Wa"ter meas"ure (?). A measure formerly used for articles brought by water, as coals, oysters, etc. The water-measure bushel was three gallons larger than the Winchester bushel. Cowell.
Water measurer Wa"ter meas"ur*er (?). (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of water; the skater. See Skater, n., 2.
Water meter Wa"ter me"ter (?). A contrivance for measuring a supply of water delivered or received for any purpose, as from a street main.
Water milfoil Wa"ter mil"foil (?). (Bot.) Any plant of the genus Myriophyllum, aquatic herbs with whorled leaves, the submersed ones pinnately parted into capillary divisions.
Water mill Wa"ter mill` (?). A mill whose machinery is moved by water; -- distinguished from a windmill, and a steam mill.
Water mint Wa"ter mint` (?). A kind of mint (Mentha aquatica) growing in wet places, and sometimes having a perfume resembling bergamot.

Water mite Wa"ter mite` (?). (Zool.) Any of numerous species of aquatic mites belonging to Hydrachna and allied genera of the family Hydrachnidae, usually having the legs fringed and adapted for swimming. They are often red or red and black in color, and while young are parasites of fresh-water insects and mussels. Called also water tick, and water spider.

Water moccasin Wa"ter moc"ca*sin (?). (Zool.) A venomous North American snake (Ancistrodon piscivorus) allied to the rattlesnake but destitute of a rattle. It lives in or about pools and ponds, and feeds largely of fishes. Called also water snake, water adder, water viper.
Water mole Wa"ter mole` (?). (Zool.) (a) The shrew mole. See under Shrew. (b) The duck mole. See under Duck.

Water monitor Wa"ter mon"i*tor (?). (Zool.) A very large lizard (Varanaus salvator) native of India. It frequents the borders of streams and swims actively. It becomes five or six feet long. Called also two-banded monitor, and kabaragoya. The name is also applied to other aquatic monitors.
Water monkey Water monkey. A jar or bottle, as of porous earthenware, in which water is cooled by evaporation.
Water motor Wa"ter mo"tor (?). 1. A water engine.

Water mouse Wa"ter mouse` (?). (Zool.) Any one of several species of mice belonging to the genus Hydromys, native of Australia and Tasmania. Their hind legs are strong and their toes partially webbed. They live on the borders of streams, and swim well. They are remarkable as being the only rodents found in Australia.
Water murrain Wa"ter mur"rain (?). A kind of murrain affecting cattle. Crabb.
Water newt Wa"ter newt` (?). (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of aquatic salamanders; a triton.
Water nymph Wa"ter nymph` (?). 1. (Myth.) A goddess of any stream or other body of water, whether one of the Naiads, Nereids, or Oceanides.
Water oat Wa"ter oat` (?). Indian rice. See under Rice.
Water opossum Wa"ter o*pos"sum (?). (Zool.) See Yapock, and the Note under Opossum.
Water ordeal Wa"ter or"de*al (?). Same as Ordeal by water. See the Note under Ordeal, n., 1.

Water ouzel Water ousel { Wa"ter ou"sel (?), Wa"ter ou"zel }. (Zool.) Any one of several species of small insessorial birds of the genus Cinclus (or Hydrobates), especially the European water ousel (Cinclus aquaticus), and the American water ousel (Cinclus Mexicanus). These birds live about the water, and are in the habit of walking on the bottom of streams beneath the water in search of food.
Water parsnip Wa"ter pars"nip (?). (Bot.) Any plant of the aquatic umbelliferous genus Sium, poisonous herbs with pinnate or dissected leaves and small white flowers.

Water parting Water parting. (Phys. Geog.) A summit from the opposite sides of which rain waters flow to different streams; a line separating the drainage districts of two streams or coasts; a divide; a watershed.
Water partridge Wa"ter par"tridge (?). (Zool.) The ruddy duck. [Local, U. S.]
Water pennywort Wa"ter pen"ny*wort` (?). (Bot.) Marsh pennywort. See under Marsh.
Water pepper Wa"ter pep"per (?). (Bot.) (a) Smartweed. (b) Waterwort.
Water pheasant Wa"ter pheas"ant (?). (Zool.) (a) The pintail. See Pintail, n., 1. (b) The goosander. (c) The hooded merganser.
Water piet Wa"ter pi"et (?). (Zool.) The water ousel.
Water pig Wa"ter pig` (?). 1. (Zool.) The capybara.
Water pillar Wa"ter pil"lar (?). A waterspout. [Obs.]
Water pimpernel Wa"ter pim"per*nel (?). (Bot.) A small white-flowered shrub; brookweed.
Water pipe Wa"ter pipe (?). A pipe for conveying water.
Water pitcher Wa"ter pitch"er (?). 1. A pitcher for water.
Water plant Wa"ter plant` (?). A plant that grows in water; an aquatic plant.
Water plantain Wa"ter plan"tain (?). (Bot.) A kind of plant with acrid leaves. See under 2d Plantain.
Water plate Wa"ter plate` (?). A plate heated by hot water contained in a double bottom or jacket. Knight.
Water poa Wa"ter po"a (?). (Bot.) Meadow reed grass. See under Reed.
Water pocket Water pocket. A water hole in the bed of an intermittent stream, esp. the bowl at the foot of a cliff over which the stream leaps when in the flood stage. [Western U. S.]
Water poise Wa"ter poise` (?). A hydrometer.
Water pore Wa"ter pore` (?), 1. (Zool.) A pore by which the water tubes of various invertebrates open externally.
Water power Wa"ter pow"er (?). 1. The power of water employed to move machinery, etc.
Water pox Wa"ter pox` (?). (Med.) A variety of chicken pox, or varicella. Dunglison.
Water privilege Wa"ter priv"i*lege (?). The advantage of using water as a mechanical power; also, the place where water is, or may be, so used. See under Privilege.
Water purslane Wa"ter purs"lane (?). (Bot.) See under Purslane.
Water qualm Wa"ter qualm` (?). (Med.) See Water brash, under Brash.
Water rabbit Wa"ter rab"bit (?). (Zool.) See Water hare.
Water radish Wa"ter rad"ish (?). (Bot.) A coarse yellow-flowered plant (Nasturtium amphibium) related to the water cress and to the horse-radish.
Water rail Wa"ter rail` (?). (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of rails of the genus Rallus, as the common European species (Rallus aquaticus). See Illust. of Rail.
Water ram Wa"ter ram` (?). An hydraulic ram.
Water rat Wa"ter rat` (?). 1. (Zool.) (a) The water vole. See under Vole. (b) The muskrat. (c) The beaver rat. See under Beaver.
Water rate Wa"ter rate` (?). A rate or tax for a supply of water.
Water rattler Water rattle { Wa"ter rat"tle (?). Wa"ter rat"tler (?). } (Zool.) The diamond rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus); -- so called from its preference for damp places near water.
Water rice Wa"ter rice" (?). Indian rice. See under Rice.
Water rocket Wa"ter rock"et (?). 1. (Bot.) A cruciferous plant (Nasturtium sylvestre) with small yellow flowers.
Water sail Wa"ter sail` (?). (Naut.) A small sail sometimes set under a studding sail or under a driver boom, and reaching nearly to the water.
Water sapphire Wa"ter sap"phire (?). [Equiv. to F. saphir d'eau.] (Min.) A deep blue variety of iolite, sometimes used as a gem; -- called also saphir d'eau.
Water scorpion Wa"ter scor"pi*on (?). (Zool.) See Nepa.
Water screw Wa"ter screw` (?). A screw propeller.
Water shield Wa"ter shield` (?). (Bot.) An aquatic American plant (Brasenia peltata) having floating oval leaves, and the covered with a clear jelly.

Water shrew Wa"ter shrew` (?). (Zool.) Any one of several species of shrews having fringed feet and capable of swimming actively. The two common European species (Crossopus fodiens, and Crossopus ciliatus) are the best known. The most common American water shrew, or marsh shrew (Neosorex palustris), is rarely seen, owing to its nocturnal habits.
Water snail Wa"ter snail` (?). 1. (Zool.) Any aquatic pulmonate gastropod belonging to Planorbis, Limnaea, and allied genera; a pond snail.

Water snake Wa"ter snake` (?). (Zool.) (a) A common North American colubrine snake (Tropidonotus sipedon) which lives chiefly in the water. (b) Any species of snakes of the family Homalopsidae, all of which are aquatic in their habits.
Water soldier Wa"ter sol`dier (?). (Bot.) An aquatic European plant (Stratiotes aloides) with bayonet-shaped leaves.
Water souchy Wa"ter souch`y (?). (Cookery) A dish consisting of small fish stewed and served in a little water. [Written also water souchet.] See Zoutch.
Water spaniel Wa"ter span"iel (?). A curly-haired breed of spaniels, naturally very fond of the water.
Water sparrow Wa"ter spar"row (?). (Zool.) (a) The reed warbler. [Prov. Eng.] (b) The reed bunting. [Prov. Eng.]
Water speedwell Wa"ter speed"well (?). (Bot.) A kind of speedwell (Veronica Anagallis) found in wet places in Europe and America.

Water spider Wa"ter spi"der (?). (Zool.) (a) An aquatic European spider (Argyoneta aquatica) which constructs its web beneath the surface of the water on water plants. It lives in a bell-shaped structure of silk, open beneath like a diving bell, and filled with air which the spider carries down in the form of small bubbles attached one at a time to the spinnerets and hind feet. Called also diving spider. (b) A water mite. (c) Any spider that habitually lives on or about the water, especially the large American species (Dolomedes lanceolatus) which runs rapidly on the surface of water; -- called also raft spider.
Water spinner Wa"ter spin`ner (?). (Zool.) The water spider.
Water sprite Wa"ter sprite` (?). A sprite, or spirit, imagined as inhabiting the water. J. R. Drake.
Water star grass Wa"ter star" grass` (?). (Bot.) An aquatic plant (Schollera graminea) with grassy leaves, and yellow star-shaped blossoms.
Water starwort Wa"ter star"wort` (?). See under Starwort.
Water supply Wa"ter sup*ply" (?). A supply of water; specifically, water collected, as in reservoirs, and conveyed, as by pipes, for use in a city, mill, or the like.
Water tabby Wa"ter tab"by (?). A kind of waved or watered tabby. See Tabby, n., 1.

Water table Wa"ter ta"ble (?). 1. (Arch.) A molding, or other projection, in the wall of a building, to throw off the water, -- generally used in the United States for the first table above the surface of the ground (see Table, n., 9), that is, for the table at the top of the foundation and the beginning of the upper wall.
Water telescope Water telescope. 1. (Optics) A telescope in which the medium between the objective and the eye piece is water instead of air, used in some experiments in aberration.

Water tender Water tender. (Nav.) In the United States navy, a first-class petty officer in charge in a fireroom. He “tends” water to the boilers, sees that fires are properly cleaned and stoked, etc. There is also a rating of chief water tender, who is a chief petty officer.

Water thermometer Wa"ter ther*mom"e*ter (?). (Physics) A thermometer filled with water instead of mercury, for ascertaining the precise temperature at which water attains its maximum density. This is about 39° Fahr., or 4° Centigrade; and from that point down to 32° Fahr., or 0° Centigrade, or the freezing point, it expands.
Water thief Wa"ter thief` (?). A pirate. [R.] Shak.

Water thrush Wa"ter thrush` (?). (Zool.) (a) A North American bird of the genus Seiurus, belonging to the Warbler family, especially the common species (Seiurus Noveboracensis). (b) The European water ousel. (b) The pied wagtail.
Water thyme Wa"ter thyme` (?). (Bot.) See Anacharis.
Water tick Wa"ter tick` (?). Same as Water mite.
Water tiger Wa"ter ti"ger (?). (Zool.) A diving, or water, beetle, especially the larva of a water beetle. See Illust. b of Water beetle.
Water torch Wa"ter torch` (?). (Bot.) The common cat-tail (Typha latifolia), the spike of which makes a good torch soaked in oil. Dr. Prior.
Water tower Wa"ter tow"er (?). 1. A large metal pipe made to be extended vertically by sections, and used for discharging water upon burning buildings.
Water tree Wa"ter tree` (?). (Bot.) A climbing shrub (Tetracera alnifolia syn. Tetracera potatoria) of Western Africa, which pours out a watery sap from the freshly cut stems.
Water trefoil Wa"ter tre"foil` (?). (Bot.) The buck bean.

Water tube Wa"ter tube` (wä"tẽr tūb`). 1. (Zool.) One of a system of tubular excretory organs having external openings, found in many invertebrates. They are believed to be analogous in function to the kidneys of vertebrates. See Illust. under Trematodea, and Sporocyst.
Water tupelo Wa"ter tu"pe*lo (wä"tẽr tū"pe*lō). (Bot.) A species of large tupelo (Nyssa aquatica) growing in swamps in the southern of the United States. See Ogeechee lime.
Water turkey Wa"ter tur"key (wä"tẽr tûr"ky̆). (Zool.) The American snakebird. See Snakebird.
Water tuyere Wa"ter tu`yère" (wä"tẽr twe`yâr"). A tuyère kept cool by water circulating within a casing. It is used for hot blast.
Water twist Wa"ter twist` (wä"tẽr twĭst`). Yarn made by the throstle, or water frame.
Water vine Wa"ter vine` (?). (Bot.) Any plant of the genus Phytocrene, climbing shrubs of Asia and Africa, the stems of which are singularly porous, and when cut stream with a limpid potable juice.
Water violet Wa"ter vi"o*let (?). (Bot.) See under Violet.
Water viper Wa"ter vi"per (?). (Zool.) See Water moccasin.
Water vole Wa"ter vole` (?). (Zool.) See under Vole.
Water wagtail Wa"ter wag"tail` (?). See under Wagtail.
Water way Wa"ter way`. Same as Water course.

Water wheel Wa"ter wheel` (?). 1. Any wheel for propelling machinery or for other purposes, that is made to rotate by the direct action of water; -- called an overshot wheel when the water is applied at the top, an undershot wheel when at the bottom, a breast wheel when at an intermediate point; other forms are called reaction wheel, vortex wheel, turbine wheel, etc.
Water willow Wa"ter wil`low (?). (Bot.) An American aquatic plant (Dianthera Americana) with long willowlike leaves, and spikes of small purplish flowers.

Water wing Wa"ter wing` (?). (Arch.) One of two walls built on either side of the junction of a bridge with the bank of a river, to protect the abutment of the bridge and the bank from the action of the current.
Water witch Wa"ter witch` (?). (Zool.) (a) The dabchick. (b) The stormy petrel. [Prov. Eng.]

waterage.c: Waterage Wa"ter*age (?; 48), n. Money paid for transportation of goods, etc., by water. [Eng.]

waterboard.c: Waterboard Wa"ter*board` (?), n. A board set up to windward in a boat, to keep out water. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

waterbound.c: Water-bound Wa"ter-bound` (?), a. Prevented by a flood from proceeding.

watercloset.c: Water-closet Wa"ter-clos`et (?), n. A privy; especially, a privy furnished with a contrivance for introducing a stream of water to cleanse it.

watercolorist.c: Water-colorist Wa"ter-col`or*ist, n. One who paints in water colors.

watercourse.c: Watercourse Wa"ter*course` (?), n. (Shipbuilding) One of the holes in floor or other plates to permit water to flow through.

waterer.c: Waterer Wa"ter*er (?), n. One who, or that which, waters.

waterfall.c: Waterfall Wa"ter*fall` (?), n. 1. A fall, or perpendicular descent, of the water of a river or stream, or a descent nearly perpendicular; a cascade; a cataract.

waterflood.c: Waterflood Wa"ter*flood` (?), n. [AS. wæterflōd.] A flood of water; an inundation.

waterfowl.c: Waterfowl Wa"ter*fowl` (?), n. Any bird that frequents the water, or lives about rivers, lakes, etc., or on or near the sea; an aquatic fowl; -- used also collectively.

waterfurrow.c: Water-furrow Wa"ter-fur"row, v. t. To make water furrows in.

waterhorse.c: Waterhorse Wa"ter*horse` (?), n. A pile of salted fish heaped up to drain.

waterie.c: Waterie Wa"ter*ie (?), n. (Zool.) The pied wagtail; -- so called because it frequents ponds.

wateriness.c: Wateriness Wa"ter*i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being watery; moisture; humidity.

watering.c: Watering Wa"ter*ing, a. & n. from Water, v.

waterish.c: Waterish Wa"ter*ish, a. [AS. wæterisc.] 1. Resembling water; thin; watery.

waterishness.c: Waterishness Wa"ter*ish*ness, n. The quality of being waterish.

waterlaid.c: Water-laid Wa"ter-laid` (?), a. Having a left-hand twist; -- said of cordage; as, a water-laid, or left-hand, rope.

waterlandian.c: Waterlandian Waterlander { Wa`ter*land"er (?), Wa`ter*land"i*an (?) } n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a body of Dutch Anabaptists who separated from the Mennonites in the sixteenth century; -- so called from a district in North Holland denominated Waterland.

waterleaf.c: Waterleaf Wa"ter*leaf` (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the American genus Hydrophyllum, herbs having white or pale blue bell-shaped flowers. Gray.

waterless.c: Waterless Wa"ter*less, a. Destitute of water; dry. Chaucer.

waterlogged.c: Water-logged Wa"ter-logged (?), a. Filled or saturated with water so as to be heavy, unmanageable, or loglike; -- said of a vessel, when, by receiving a great quantity of water into her hold, she has become so heavy as not to be manageable by the helm.

watermanship.c: Watermanship Wa"ter*man*ship`, n. 1. The business or skill of a waterman.

watermark.c: Watermark Wa"ter*mark` (?), n. 1. A mark indicating the height to which water has risen, or at which it has stood; the usual limit of high or low water.

watermelon.c: Watermelon Wa"ter*mel`on (?), n. (Bot.) The very large ovoid or roundish fruit of a cucurbitaceous plant (Citrullus vulgaris) of many varieties; also, the plant itself. The fruit sometimes weighs many pounds; its pulp is usually pink in color, and full of a sweet watery juice. It is a native of tropical Africa, but is now cultivated in many countries. See Illust. of Melon.

waterpot.c: Waterpot Wa"ter*pot` (?), n. A vessel for holding or conveying water, or for sprinkling water on cloth, plants, etc.

waterproof.c: Waterproof Wa"ter*proof` (?), a. Proof against penetration or permeation by water; impervious to water; as, a waterproof garment; a waterproof roof.
Waterproof Wa"ter*proof`, n. 1. A substance or preparation for rendering cloth, leather, etc., impervious to water.
Waterproof Wa"ter*proof` (?), v. t. To render impervious to water, as cloth, leather, etc.

waterproofing.c: Waterproofing Wa"ter*proof`ing, n. 1. The act or process of making waterproof.

waterret.c: Water-ret Wa"ter-ret` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Water-retted; p. pr. & vb. n. Water-retting.] To ret, or rot, in water, as flax; to water-rot.

waterrot.c: Water-rot Wa"ter-rot` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Water-rotted; p. pr. & vb. n. Water-rotting.] To rot by steeping in water; to water-ret; as, to water-rot hemp or flax.

waterscape.c: Waterscape Wa"ter*scape" (?), n. [Cf. Landscape.] A sea view; -- distinguished from landscape. [Jocose] Fairholt.

watershed.c: Watershed Wa"ter*shed` (?), n. [Cf. G. wasserscheide; wasser water + scheide a place where two things separate, fr. scheiden to separate.]

watershoot.c: Watershoot Wa"ter*shoot` (?), n. 1. A sprig or shoot from the root or stock of a tree. [Obs.]

watersoak.c: Water-soak Wa"ter-soak` (?), v. t. To soak water; to fill the interstices of with water.

waterspout.c: Waterspout Wa"ter*spout` (?), n. A remarkable meteorological phenomenon, of the nature of a tornado or whirlwind, usually observed over the sea, but sometimes over the land.

waterstanding.c: Water-standing Wa"ter-stand`ing (?), a. Tear-filled. [R.] “Many an orphan's water-standing eye.” Shak.

watertath.c: Watertath Wa"ter*tath` (?), n. [Water + tath, n.] A kind of coarse grass growing in wet grounds, and supposed to be injurious to sheep. [Prov. Eng.]

watertight.c: Water-tight Wa"ter-tight` (?), a. So tight as to retain, or not to admit, water; not leaky.

waterway.c: Waterway Wa"ter*way` (?), n. (Naut.) Heavy plank or timber extending fore and aft the whole length of a vessel's deck at the line of junction with the sides, forming a channel to the scuppers, which are cut through it. In iron vessels the waterway is variously constructed.

waterwithe.c: Water-withe Wa"ter-withe` (?), n. (Bot.) A vinelike plant (Vitis Caribaea) growing in parched districts in the West Indies, and containing a great amount of sap which is sometimes used for quenching thirst.

waterwork.c: Waterwork Wa"ter*work` (?), n. 1. (Paint.) Painting executed in size or distemper, on canvas or walls, -- formerly, frequently taking the place of tapestry. Shak. Fairholt.

waterworn.c: Waterworn Wa"ter*worn` (?), a. Worn, smoothed, or polished by the action of water; as, waterworn stones.

waterwort.c: Waterwort Wa"ter*wort` (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the natural order Elatineae, consisting of two genera (Elatine, and Bergia), mostly small annual herbs growing in the edges of ponds. Some have a peppery or acrid taste.

watt.c: Watt Watt (?), n. [From the distinguished mechanician and scientist, James Watt.] (Physics) A unit of power or activity equal to 107 C.G.S. units of power, or to work done at the rate of one joule a second. An English horse power is approximately equal to 746 watts.

watteau.c: Watteau Wat*teau" (?), a. (Art) Having the appearance of that which is seen in pictures by Antoine Watteau, a French painter of the eighteenth century; -- said esp. of women's garments; as, a Watteau bodice.

Watteau back Watteau back. The back of a woman's gown in which one or more very broad folds are carried from the neck to the floor without being held in at the waist, while the front and sides of the gown are shaped to the person and have a belt or its equivalent.

wattmeter.c: Wattmeter Watt"me`ter (?), n. [Watt + meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring power in watts, -- much used in measuring the energy of an electric current.

wattle.c: Wattle Wat"tle (?), n. [AS. watel, watul, watol, hurdle, covering, wattle; cf. OE. watel a bag. Cf. Wallet.]
Wattle Wat"tle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wattled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wattling (?).]

wattlebird.c: Wattlebird Wat"tle*bird` (?), n. 1. (Zool.) Any one of several species of honey eaters belonging to Anthochaera and allied genera of the family Meliphagidae. These birds usually have a large and conspicuous wattle of naked skin hanging down below each ear. They are natives of Australia and adjacent islands.

wattled.c: Wattled Wat"tled (?), a. Furnished with wattles, or pendent fleshy processes at the chin or throat.

wattless.c: Wattless Watt"less (?), a. (Elec.) Without any power (cf. Watt); -- said of an alternating current or component of current when it differs in phase by ninety degrees from the electromotive force which produces it, or of an electromotive force or component thereof when the current it produces differs from it in phase by 90 degrees.

wattling.c: Wattling Wat"tling (?), n. The act or process of binding or platting with twigs; also, the network so formed.

waught.c: Waught Waucht { Waucht, Waught } (?), n. [Cf. Quaff.] A large draught of any liquid. [Scot.] Jamieson.

waul.c: Waul Waul (?), v. i. [Of imitative origin.] To cry as a cat; to squall; to wail. [Written also wawl.]

wave.c: Wave Wave (wāv), v. t. See Waive. Sir H. Wotton. Burke.

Wave Wave, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Waved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Waving.] [OE. waven, AS. wafian to waver, to hesitate, to wonder; akin to wæfre wavering, restless, MHG. wabern to be in motion, Icel. vafra to hover about; cf. Icel. vāfa to vibrate. Cf. Waft, Waver.]
Wave Wave, v. t. 1. To move one way and the other; to brandish. “[Aeneas] waved his fatal sword.” Dryden.
Wave Wave, n. [From Wave, v.; not the same word as OE. wawe, waghe, a wave, which is akin to E. wag to move. √138. See Wave, v. i.]

waved.c: Waved Waved (?), a. 1. Exhibiting a wavelike form or outline; undulating; intended; wavy; as, waved edge.

waveless.c: Waveless Wave"less (?), a. Free from waves; undisturbed; not agitated; as, the waveless sea.

wavelet.c: Wavelet Wave"let (?), n. A little wave; a ripple.

wavellite.c: Wavellite Wa"vel*lite (?), n. [After Dr. Wm. Wavel, the discoverer.] (Min.) A hydrous phosphate of alumina, occurring usually in hemispherical radiated forms varying in color from white to yellow, green, or black.

waver.c: Waver Wa"ver (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wavered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wavering.] [OE. waveren, from AS. wæfre wavering, restless. See Wave, v. i.]
Waver Wa"ver, n. [From Wave, or Waver, v.] A sapling left standing in a fallen wood. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

waverer.c: Waverer Wa"ver*er (?), n. One who wavers; one who is unsettled in doctrine, faith, opinion, or the like. Shak.

waveringly.c: Waveringly Wa"ver*ing*ly, adv. In a wavering manner.

waveringness.c: Waveringness Wa"ver*ing*ness, n. The quality or state of wavering.

waveson.c: Waveson Wave"son (?), n. [From Wave; cf. Jetsam.] (O. Eng. Law) Goods which, after shipwreck, appear floating on the waves, or sea.

waveworn.c: Wave-worn Wave"-worn` (?), a. Worn by the waves.

wavey.c: Wavey Wa"vey (?), n. (Zool.) The snow goose. [Canadian, & Local U. S.]

waviness.c: Waviness Wav"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being wavy.

wavy.c: Wavy Wav"y (?), a. 1. Rising or swelling in waves; full of waves. “The wavy seas.” Chapman.

wawaskeesh.c: Wawaskeesh ‖Wa*was"keesh (?), n. [From an Indian name.] (Zool.) The wapiti, or wapiti, or American elk.

wawe.c: Wawe Wawe (wä), n. [OE. wawe, waghe; cf. Icel. vāgr; akin to E. wag; not the same word as wave.] A wave. [Obs.] Chaucer. Spenser.

wawl.c: Wawl Wawl (wäl), v. i. See Waul. Shak.

wax.c: Wax Wax (wăks), v. i. [imp. Waxed (?); p. p. Waxed, and Obs. or Poetic Waxen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Waxing.] [AS. weaxan; akin to OFries. waxa, D. wassen, OS. & OHG. wahsan, G. wachsen, Icel. vaxa, Sw. växa, Dan. voxe, Goth. wahsjan, Gr.? to increase, Skr. waksh, uksh, to grow. √135. Cf. Waist.]
Wax Wax, n. [AS. weax; akin to OFries. wax, D. was, G. wachs, OHG. wahs, Icel. & Sw. vax, Dan. vox, Lith. vaszkas, Russ. vosk'.]
Wax Wax (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Waxed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Waxing.] To smear or rub with wax; to treat with wax; as, to wax a thread or a table.

waxberry.c: Waxberry Wax"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) The wax-covered fruit of the wax myrtle, or bayberry. See Bayberry, and Candleberry tree.

waxbill.c: Waxbill Wax"bill` (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of finchlike birds belonging to Estrelda and allied genera, native of Asia, Africa, and Australia. The bill is large, conical, and usually red in color, resembling sealing wax. Several of the species are often kept as cage birds.

waxen.c: Waxen Wax"en (?), a. 1. Made of wax. “The female bee, that... builds her waxen cells.” Milton.

waxiness.c: Waxiness Wax"i*ness (?), n. Quality or state of being waxy.

waxwing.c: Waxwing Wax"wing` (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of several species of small birds of the genus Ampelis, in which some of the secondary quills are usually tipped with small horny ornaments resembling red sealing wax. The Bohemian waxwing (see under Bohemian) and the cedar bird are examples. Called also waxbird.

waxwork.c: Waxwork Wax"work` (?), n. 1. Work made of wax; especially, a figure or figures formed or partly of wax, in imitation of real beings.

waxworks.c: Waxworks Wax"works` (?), n. pl. An exhibition of wax figures, or the place of exhibition; as, Madame Toussaud's Waxworks.

waxworker.c: Waxworker Wax"work`er (?), n. 1. One who works in wax; one who makes waxwork.

waxy.c: Waxy Wax"y (?), a. Resembling wax in appearance or consistency; viscid; adhesive; soft; hence, yielding; pliable; impressible. “Waxy to persuasion.” Bp. Hall.

way.c: Way Way (?), adv. [Aphetic form of away.] Away. [Obs. or Archaic] Chaucer.

Way Way, n. [OE. wey, way, AS. weg; akin to OS., D., OHG., & G. weg, Icel. vegr, Sw. väg, Dan. vei, Goth. wigs, L. via, and AS. wegan to move, L. vehere to carry, Skr. vah. √136. Cf. Convex, Inveigh, Vehicle, Vex, Via, Voyage, Wag, Wagon, Wee, Weigh.]
Way Way (?), v. t. To go or travel to; to go in, as a way or path. [Obs.] “In land not wayed.” Wyclif.
Way Way, v. i. To move; to progress; to go. [R.]
Way shaft Way" shaft` (?). 1. (Mach.) A rock shaft.

waybill.c: Waybill Way"bill` (?), n. A list of passengers in a public vehicle, or of the baggage or gods transported by a common carrier on a land route. When the goods are transported by water, the list is called a bill of lading.

waybread.c: Waybread Way"bread` (?), n. [AS. wegbr?de. See Way, and Broad.] (Bot.) The common dooryard plantain (Plantago major).

waybung.c: Waybung Way"bung` (?), n. (Zool.) An Australian insessorial bird (Corcorax melanorhamphus) noted for the curious actions of the male during the breeding season. It is black with a white patch on each wing.

wayed.c: Wayed Wayed (?), a. Used to the way; broken. [R.]

wayfare.c: Wayfare Way"fare` (?), v. i. [Way + fare to go.] To journey; to travel; to go to and fro. [Obs.]
Wayfare Way"fare`, n. The act of journeying; travel; passage. [Obs.] Holland.

wayfarer.c: Wayfarer Way"far`er (?), n. One who travels; a traveler; a passenger.

wayfaring.c: Wayfaring Way"far`ing, a. Traveling; passing; being on a journey. “A wayfaring man.” Judg. xix. 17.

waygate.c: Waygate Way"gate` (?), n. The tailrace of a mill. Knight.

waygoing.c: Way-going Way"-go`ing (?), a. Going away; departing; of or pertaining to one who goes away.

waylay.c: Waylay Way"lay` (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Waylaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Waylaying.] [Way + lay.] To lie in wait for; to meet or encounter in the way; especially, to watch for the passing of, with a view to seize, rob, or slay; to beset in ambush.

waylayer.c: Waylayer Way"lay`er (?), n. One who waylays another.

wayless.c: Wayless Way"less, a. Having no road or path; pathless.

waymaker.c: Waymaker Way"mak`er (?), n. One who makes a way; a precursor. [R.] Bacon.

waymark.c: Waymark Way"mark` (?), n. A mark to guide in traveling.

wayment.c: Wayment Way"ment (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Waymented; p. pr. & vb. n. Waymenting.] [OE. waymenten, OF. waimenter, gaimenter, guaimenter, from wai, guai, woe! (of Teutonic origin; see Woe) and L. lamentari to lament. See Lament.] To lament; to grieve; to wail. [Written also waiment.] [Obs.]
Wayment Way"ment, n. Grief; lamentation; mourning. [Written also waiment.] [Obs.] Spenser.

ways.c: -ways -ways (?). A suffix formed from way by the addition of the adverbial -s (see -wards). It is often used interchangeably with wise; as, endways or endwise; noways or nowise, etc.

wayside.c: Wayside Way"side` (?), n. The side of the way; the edge or border of a road or path.
Wayside Way"side`, a. Of or pertaining to the wayside; as, wayside flowers. “A wayside inn.” Longfellow.

wayward.c: Wayward Way"ward (?), a. [OE. weiward, for aweiward, i. e., turned away. See Away, and -ward.] Taking one's own way; disobedient; froward; perverse; willful.

waywise.c: Way-wise Way"-wise` (?), a. Skillful in finding the way; well acquainted with the way or route; wise from having traveled.

waywiser.c: Waywiser Way"wis`er (?), n. [Cf. G. wegweiser a waymark, a guide; weg way + weisen to show, direct.] An instrument for measuring the distance which one has traveled on the road; an odometer, pedometer, or perambulator.

waywode.c: Waywode Way"wode (?), n. [Russ. voevoda, or Pol. woiewoda; properly, a leader of an army, a leader in war. Cf. Vaivode.] Originally, the title of a military commander in various Slavonic countries; afterwards applied to governors of towns or provinces. It was assumed for a time by the rulers of Moldavia and Wallachia, who were afterwards called hospodars, and has also been given to some inferior Turkish officers. [Written also vaivode, voivode, waiwode, and woiwode.]

waywodeship.c: Waywodeship Way"wode*ship, n. The office, province, or jurisdiction of a waywode.

we.c: We We (wē), pron.; pl. of I. [Poss. Our (our) or Ours (ourz); obj. Us (ŭs). See I.] [As. wē; akin to OS. wī, OFries. & LG. wi, D. wij, G. wir, Icel. vēr, Sw. & Dan. vi, Goth. weis, Skr. vayam. √190.] The plural nominative case of the pronoun of the first person; the word with which a person in speaking or writing denotes a number or company of which he is one, as the subject of an action expressed by a verb.

weak.c: Weak Weak (wēk), a. [Compar. Weaker (wēk"ẽr); superl. Weakest.] [OE. weik, Icel. veikr; akin to Sw. vek, Dan. veg soft, flexible, pliant, AS. wāc weak, soft, pliant, D. week, G. weich, OHG. weih; all from the verb seen in Icel. vīkja to turn, veer, recede, AS. wīcan to yield, give way, G. weichen, OHG. wīhhan, akin to Skr. vij, and probably to E. week, L. vicis a change, turn, Gr. e'i`kein to yield, give way. √132. Cf. Week, Wink, v. i. Vicissitude.]
Weak Weak (?), v. t. & i. [Cf. AS. w?can. wācian. See Weak, a.] To make or become weak; to weaken. [R.]

weaken.c: Weaken Weak"en (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Weakened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Weakening.]

Weaken Weak"en, v. i. To become weak or weaker; to lose strength, spirit, or determination; to become less positive or resolute; as, the patient weakened; the witness weakened on cross-examination. “His notion weakens, his discernings are lethargied.” Shak.

weakener.c: Weakener Weak"en*er (?), n. One who, or that which, weakens. “[Fastings] weakeners of sin.” South.

weakfish.c: Weakfish Weak"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) Any fish of the genus Cynoscion; a squeteague; -- so called from its tender mouth. See Squeteague.

weakhearted.c: Weak-hearted Weak"-heart`ed (?), a. Having little courage; of feeble spirit; dispirited; faint-hearted. “Weak-hearted enemies.” Shak.

weakish.c: Weakish Weak"ish, a. Somewhat weak; rather weak.

weakishness.c: Weakishness Weak"ish*ness, n. Quality or state of being weakish.

weakkneed.c: Weak-kneed Weak"-kneed` (?), a. Having weak knees; hence, easily yielding; wanting resolution. H. James.

weakling.c: Weakling Weak"ling (?), n. [Weak + -ling.] A weak or feeble creature. Shak. “All looking on him as a weakling, which would post to the grave.” Fuller.
Weakling Weak"ling, a. Weak; feeble. Sir T. North.

weakly.c: Weakly Weak"ly, adv. In a weak manner; with little strength or vigor; feebly.
Weakly Weak"ly, a. [Compar. Weaklier (?); superl. Weakliest.] Not strong of constitution; infirm; feeble; as, a weakly woman; a man of a weakly constitution.

weakminded.c: Weak-minded Weak"-mind`ed (?), a. Having a weak mind, either naturally or by reason of disease; feebleminded; foolish; idiotic. -- Weak"-mind`ed*ness, n.

weakness.c: Weakness Weak"ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being weak; want of strength or firmness; lack of vigor; want of resolution or of moral strength; feebleness.

weal.c: Weal Weal (?), n. The mark of a stripe. See Wale.
Weal Weal, v. t. To mark with stripes. See Wale.
Weal Weal, n. [OE. wele, AS. wela, weola, wealth, from wel well. See Well, adv., and cf. Wealth.]
Weal Weal, v. t. To promote the weal of; to cause to be prosperous. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

wealbalanced.c: Weal-balanced Weal"-bal`anced (?), a. Balanced or considered with reference to public weal. [Obs.] Shak.

weald.c: Weald Weald (?), n. [AS. See Wold.] A wood or forest; a wooded land or region; also, an open country; -- often used in place names.

wealden.c: Wealden Weald"en (?; 277), a. [AS. weald, wald, a forest, a wood. So called because this formation occurs in the wealds, or woods, of Kent and Sussex. See Weald.] (Geol.) Of or pertaining to the lowest division of the Cretaceous formation in England and on the Continent, which overlies the Oolitic series.
Wealden Weald"en, n. (Geol.) The Wealden group or strata.

wealdish.c: Wealdish Weald"ish, a. Of or pertaining to a weald, esp. to the weald in the county of Kent, England. [Obs.] Fuller.

wealsman.c: Wealsman Weals"man (?), n.; pl. Wealsmen (#). [Weal + man.] A statesman; a politician. [R.] Shak.

wealth.c: Wealth Wealth (?), n. [OE. welthe, from wele; cf. D. weelde luxury. See Weal prosperity.]

wealthful.c: Wealthful Wealth"ful (?), a. Full of wealth; wealthy; prosperous. [R.] Sir T. More. -- Wealth"ful*ly, adv. [R.]

wealthily.c: Wealthily Wealth"i*ly (?), adv. In a wealthy manner; richly.

wealthiness.c: Wealthiness Wealth"i*ness, n. The quality or state of being wealthy, or rich; richness; opulence.

wean.c: Wean Wean (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Weaned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Weaning.] [OE. wenen, AS. wenian, wennan, to accustom; akin to D. wennen, G. gewöhnen, OHG. giwennan, Icel. venja, Sw. vänja, Dan. vænne, Icel. vanr accustomed, wont; cf. AS. āwenian to wean, G. entwöhnen. See Wont, a.]
Wean Wean, n. A weanling; a young child.

weanedness.c: Weanedness Wean"ed*ness, n. Quality or state of being weaned.

weanling.c: Weanling Wean"ling, a. & n. from Wean, v.
Weanling Wean"ling (?), n. [Wean + -ling.] A child or animal newly weaned; a wean.

weapon.c: Weapon Weap"on (wĕp"ŭn; 277), n. [OE. wepen, AS. wǣpen; akin to OS. wāpan, OFries. wēpin, wēpen, D. wapen, G. waffe, OHG. waffan, wāfan, Icel. vāpn, Dan. vaaben, Sw. vapen, Goth. wēpna, pl.; of uncertain origin. Cf. Wapentake.]

weaponed.c: Weaponed Weap"oned (?), a. Furnished with weapons, or arms; armed; equipped.

weaponry.c: Weaponry Weap"on*ry (?), n. Weapons, collectively; as, an array of weaponry. [Poetic]

wear.c: Wear Wear (wâr), v. t. [Cf. Veer.] (Naut.) To cause to go about, as a vessel, by putting the helm up, instead of alee as in tacking, so that the vessel's bow is turned away from, and her stern is presented to, the wind, and, as she turns still farther, her sails fill on the other side; to veer.

Wear Wear, v. t. [imp. Wore (wōr); p. p. Worn (wōrn); p. pr. & vb. n. Wearing. Before the 15th century wear was a weak verb, the imp. & p. p. being Weared.] [OE. weren, werien, AS. werian to carry, to wear, as arms or clothes; akin to OHG. werien, weren, to clothe, Goth. wasjan, L. vestis clothing, vestire to clothe, Gr. "enny`nai, Skr. vas. Cf. Vest.]

Wear Wear, v. i. 1. To endure or suffer use; to last under employment; to bear the consequences of use, as waste, consumption, or attrition; as, a coat wears well or ill; -- hence, sometimes applied to character, qualifications, etc.; as, a man wears well as an acquaintance.
Wear Wear, n. 1. The act of wearing, or the state of being worn; consumption by use; diminution by friction; as, the wear of a garment.

Wear Weir { Weir (wēr), Wear,} n. [OE. wer, AS. wer; akin to G. wehr, AS. werian to defend, protect, hinder, G. wehren, Goth. warjan; and perhaps to E. wary; or cf. Skr. vṛ to check, hinder. √142. Cf. Garret.] 1. A dam in a river to stop and raise the water, for the purpose of conducting it to a mill, forming a fish pond, or the like.

wearable.c: Wearable Wear"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being worn; suitable to be worn.

wearer.c: Wearer Wear"er (?), n. 1. One who wears or carries as appendant to the body; as, the wearer of a cloak, a sword, a crown, a shackle, etc.

weariable.c: Weariable Wea"ri*a*ble (?), a. That may be wearied.

weariful.c: Weariful Wea"ri*ful (?), a. Abounding in qualities which cause weariness; wearisome. -- Wea"ri*ful*ly, adv.

weariless.c: Weariless Wea"ri*less, a. Incapable of being wearied.

wearily.c: Wearily Wea"ri*ly, adv. In a weary manner.

weariness.c: Weariness Wea"ri*ness, n. The quality or state of being weary or tried; lassitude; exhaustion of strength; fatigue.

wearing.c: Wearing Wear"ing (?), n. 1. The act of one who wears; the manner in which a thing wears; use; conduct; consumption.
Wearing Wear"ing (?), a. Pertaining to, or designed for, wear; as, wearing apparel.

wearish.c: Wearish Wear"ish (?), a. [Etymol. uncertain, but perhaps akin to weary.]

wearisome.c: Wearisome Wea"ri*some (?), a. Causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; weariful; as, a wearisome march; a wearisome day's work; a wearisome book.

weary.c: Weary Wea"ry (?), a. [Compar. Wearier (?); superl. Weariest.] [OE. weri, AS. w?rig; akin to OS. w?rig, OHG. wu?rag; of uncertain origin; cf. AS. w?rian to ramble.]
Weary Wea"ry, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wearied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wearying.]
Weary Wea"ry, v. i. To grow tired; to become exhausted or impatient; as, to weary of an undertaking.

weasand.c: Weasand Wea"sand (?), n. [OE. wesand, AS. wāsend; akin to OFries. wāsende, wāsande; cf. OHG. weisunt.] The windpipe; -- called also, formerly, wesil. [Formerly, written also, wesand, and wezand.]

weasel.c: Weasel Wea"sel (?), n. [OE. wesele, AS. wesle; akin to D. wezel, G. wiesel, OHG. wisala, Icel. hreyivīsla, Dan. väsel, Sw. vessla; of uncertain origin; cf. Gr.?,?, cat, weasel.] (Zool.) Any one of various species of small carnivores belonging to the genus Putorius, as the ermine and ferret. They have a slender, elongated body, and are noted for the quickness of their movements and for their bloodthirsty habit in destroying poultry, rats, etc. The ermine and some other species are brown in summer, and turn white in winter; others are brown at all seasons.

weaselfaced.c: Weasel-faced Wea"sel-faced` (?), a. Having a thin, sharp face, like a weasel.

weaser.c: Weaser Wea"ser (?), n. (Zool.) The American merganser; -- called also weaser sheldrake. [Local, U. S.]

weasiness.c: Weasiness Wea"si*ness (?), n. Quality or state of being weasy; full feeding; sensual indulgence. [Obs.] Joye.

weasy.c: Weasy Wea"sy (?), a. [Cf. Weasand.] Given to sensual indulgence; gluttonous. [Obs.] Joye.

weather.c: Weather Weath"er (?), n. [OE. weder, AS. weder; akin to OS. wedar, OFries. weder, D. weder, weêr, G. wetter, OHG. wetar, Icel. veðr, Dan. veir, Sw. väder wind, air, weather, and perhaps to OSlav. vedro fair weather; or perhaps to Lith. vetra storm, Russ. vieter', vietr', wind, and E. wind. Cf. Wither.]
Weather Weath"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Weathered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Weathering.]

Weather Weath"er, v. i. To undergo or endure the action of the atmosphere; to suffer meteorological influences; sometimes, to wear away, or alter, under atmospheric influences; to suffer waste by weather.
Weather Weath"er, a. (Naut.) Being toward the wind, or windward -- opposed to lee; as, weather bow, weather braces, weather gauge, weather lifts, weather quarter, weather shrouds, etc.

Weather map Weath"er map. A map or chart showing the principal meteorological elements at a given hour and over an extended region. Such maps usually show the height of the barometer, the temperature of the air, the relative humidity, the state of the weather, and the direction and velocity of the wind. Isobars and isotherms outline the general distribution of temperature and pressure, while shaded areas indicate the sections over which rain has just fallen. Other lines inclose areas where the temperature has fallen or risen markedly. In tabular form are shown changes of pressure and of temperature, maximum and minimum temperatures, and total rain for each weather station since the last issue, usually 12 hours.

Weather signal Weather signal. Any signal giving information about the weather. The system used by the United States Weather Bureau includes temperature, cold or hot wave, rain or snow, wind direction, storm, and hurricane signals.

Weather station Weather station. (Meteor.) A station for taking meteorological observations, making weather forecasts, or disseminating such information. Such stations are of the first order when they make observations of all the important elements either hourly or by self-registering instruments; of the second order when only important observations are taken; of the third order when simpler work is done, as to record rainfall and maximum and minimum temperatures.

weatherbeaten.c: Weather-beaten Weath"er-beat`en (?), a. Beaten or harassed by the weather; worn by exposure to the weather, especially to severe weather. Shak.

weatherbit.c: Weather-bit Weath"er-bit` (?), n. (Naut.) A turn of the cable about the end of the windlass, without the bits.
Weatherbit Weath"er*bit`, v. t. (Naut.) To take another turn with, as a cable around a windlass. Totten.

weatherbitten.c: Weather-bitten Weath"er-bit`ten (?), a. Eaten into, defaced, or worn, by exposure to the weather. Coleridge.

weatherboard.c: Weatherboard Weath"er*board` (?), n. 1. (Naut.) (a) That side of a vessel which is toward the wind; the windward side. (b) A piece of plank placed in a porthole, or other opening, to keep out water.
Weather-board Weath"er-board`, v. t. (Arch.) To nail boards upon so as to lap one over another, in order to exclude rain, snow, etc. Gwilt.

weatherboarding.c: Weatherboarding Weath"er*board`ing, n. (Arch.) (a) The covering or siding of a building, formed of boards lapping over one another, to exclude rain, snow, etc. (b) Boards adapted or intended for such use.

weatherbound.c: Weather-bound Weath"er-bound` (?), a. Kept in port or at anchor by storms; delayed by bad weather; as, a weather-bound vessel.

weathercock.c: Weathercock Weath"er*cock` (?), n. 1. A vane, or weather vane; -- so called because originally often in the figure of a cock, turning on the top of a spire with the wind, and showing its direction. “As a wedercok that turneth his face with every wind.” Chaucer.
Weathercock Weath"er*cock`, v. t. To supply with a weathercock; to serve as a weathercock for.

weatherdriven.c: Weather-driven Weath"er-driv`en (?), a. Driven by winds or storms; forced by stress of weather. Carew.

weathered.c: Weathered Weath"ered (?), a. 1. (Arch.) Made sloping, so as to throw off water; as, a weathered cornice or window sill.

weatherfend.c: Weather-fend Weath"er-fend` (?), v. t. To defend from the weather; to shelter. Shak.

weatherglass.c: Weatherglass Weath"er*glass` (?), n. An instrument to indicate the state of the atmosphere, especially changes of atmospheric pressure, and hence changes of weather, as a barometer or baroscope.

weathering.c: Weathering Weath"er*ing, n. (Geol.) The action of the elements on a rock in altering its color, texture, or composition, or in rounding off its edges.

weatherliness.c: Weatherliness Weath"er*li*ness (?), n. (Naut.) The quality of being weatherly.

weatherly.c: Weatherly Weath"er*ly, a. (Naut.) Working, or able to sail, close to the wind; as, a weatherly ship. Cooper.

weathermost.c: Weathermost Weath"er*most` (?), a. (Naut.) Being farthest to the windward.

weatherproof.c: Weatherproof Weath"er*proof` (?), a. Proof against rough weather.

weatherwise.c: Weatherwise Weath"er*wise` (?), a. Skillful in forecasting the changes of the weather. Hakluyt.

weatherwiser.c: Weatherwiser Weath"er*wis`er (?), n. [Cf. Waywiser.] Something that foreshows the weather. [Obs.] Derham.

weatherworn.c: Weatherworn Weath"er*worn` (?), a. Worn by the action of, or by exposure to, the weather.

weave.c: Weave Weave (wēv), v. t. [imp. Wove (wōv); p. p. Woven (wōv"'n), Wove; p. pr. & vb. n. Weaving. The regular imp. & p. p. Weaved (wēvd), is rarely used.] [OE. weven, AS. wefan; akin to D. weven, G. weben, OHG. weban, Icel. vefa, Sw. väfva, Dan. væve, Gr. "yfai`nein, v., "y`fos web, Skr. ūrṇavābhi spider, lit., wool weaver. Cf. Waper, Waffle, Web, Weevil, Weft, Woof.]
Weave Weave, v. i. 1. To practice weaving; to work with a loom.
Weave Weave, n. A particular method or pattern of weaving; as, the cassimere weave.

weaver.c: Weaver Weav"er (?), n. 1. One who weaves, or whose occupation is to weave. “Weavers of linen.” P. Plowman.

weaving.c: Weaving Weav"ing, n. 1. The act of one who, or that which, weaves; the act or art of forming cloth in a loom by the union or intertexture of threads.

weazen.c: Weazen Wea"zen (?), a. [See Wizen.] Thin; sharp; withered; wizened; as, a weazen face.

weazeny.c: Weazeny Wea"zen*y (?), a. Somewhat weazen; shriveled. [Colloq.] “Weazeny, baked pears.” Lowell.

web.c: Web Web (?), n. [OE. webbe, AS. webba. See Weave.] A weaver. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Web Web, n. [OE. web, AS. webb; akin to D. web, webbe, OHG. weppi, G. gewebe, Icel. vefr, Sw. väf, Dan. væv. See Weave.]
Web Web (wĕb), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Webbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Webbing.] To unite or surround with a web, or as if with a web; to envelop; to entangle.

webbed.c: Webbed Webbed (?), a. 1. Provided with a web.

webber.c: Webber Web"ber (?), n. One who forms webs; a weaver; a webster. [Obs.]

webbing.c: Webbing Web"bing (?), n. A woven band of cotton or flax, used for reins, girths, bed bottoms, etc.

webby.c: Webby Web"by (?), a. Of or pertaining to a web or webs; like a web; filled or covered with webs.

weber.c: Weber We"ber (?), n. [From the name of Professor Weber, a German electrician.] (Elec.) The standard unit of electrical quantity, and also of current. See Coulomb, and Amp?re. [Obs.]

webfingered.c: Web-fingered Web"-fin`gered (?), a. Having the fingers united by a web for a considerable part of their length.

webfooted.c: Web-footed Web"-foot`ed, a. Having webbed feet; palmiped; as, a goose or a duck is a web-footed fowl.

webster.c: Webster Web"ster (?), n. [AS. webbestre. See Web, Weave, and -ster.] A weaver; originally, a female weaver. [Obs.] Brathwait.

websterite.c: Websterite Web"ster*ite (?), n. [So named after Webster, the geologist.] (Min.) A hydrous sulphate of alumina occurring in white reniform masses.

webtoed.c: Web-toed Web"-toed` (?), a. Having the toes united by a web for a considerable part of their length.

webworm.c: Webworm Web"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of various species of moths whose gregarious larvae eat the leaves of trees, and construct a large web to which they retreat when not feeding.

wed.c: Wed Wed (wĕd), n. [AS. wedd; akin to OFries. wed, OD. wedde, OHG, wetti, G. wette a wager, Icel. veð a pledge, Sw. vad a wager, an appeal, Goth. wadi a pledge, Lith. vadůti to redeem (a pledge), LL. vadium, L. vas, vadis, bail, security, vadimonium security, and Gr.?,? a prize. Cf. Athlete, Gage a pledge, Wage.] A pledge; a pawn. [Obs.] Gower. Piers Plowman.

Wed Wed, v. t. [imp. Wedded; p. p. Wedded or Wed; p. pr. & vb. n. Wedding.] [OE. wedden, AS. weddian to covenant, promise, to wed, marry; akin to OFries. weddia to promise, D. wedden to wager, to bet, G. wetten, Icel. veðja, Dan. vedde, Sw. vädja to appeal, Goth. gawadjōn to betroth. See Wed, n.]
Wed Wed (?), v. i. To contact matrimony; to marry. “When I shall wed.” Shak.

wedded.c: Wedded Wed"ded (?), a. 1. Joined in wedlock; married.

wedder.c: Wedder Wed"der (?), n. See Wether. Sir W. Scott.

wedding.c: Wedding Wed"ding (?), n. [AS. wedding.] Nuptial ceremony; nuptial festivities; marriage; nuptials.

wedge.c: Wedge Wedge (wĕj), n. [OE. wegge, AS. wecg; akin to D. wig, wigge, OHG. wecki, G. weck a (wedge-shaped) loaf, Icel. veggr, Dan. vægge, Sw. vigg, and probably to Lith. vagis a peg. Cf. Wigg.]
Wedge Wedge, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wedged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wedging.]
wedge gage wedge gauge { wedge gauge or wedge gage }. A wedge with a graduated edge, to measure the width of a space into which it is thrust.
Wedge gear Wedge gear. A friction gear wheel with wedge-shaped circumferential grooves. -- Wedge gearing.

wedgebill.c: Wedgebill Wedge"bill` (?), n. (Zool.) An Australian crested insessorial bird (Sphenostoma cristatum) having a wedge-shaped bill. Its color is dull brown, like the earth of the plains where it lives.

wedgeformed.c: Wedge-formed Wedge"-formed` (?), a. Having the form of a wedge; cuneiform.

wedgeshaped.c: Wedge-shaped Wedge"-shaped` (?), a. 1. Having the shape of a wedge; cuneiform.

wedgeshell.c: Wedge-shell Wedge"-shell` (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of small marine bivalves belonging to Donax and allied genera in which the shell is wedge-shaped.

wedgetailed.c: Wedge-tailed Wedge"-tailed" (?), a. (Zool.) Having a tail which has the middle pair of feathers longest, the rest successively and decidedly shorter, and all more or less attenuate; -- said of certain birds. See Illust. of Wood hoopoe, under Wood.

wedgewise.c: Wedgewise Wedge"wise` (?), adv. In the manner of a wedge.

wedgwood.c: Wedgwood ware Wedg"wood` ware` (?). [From the name of the inventor, Josiah Wedgwood, of England.] A kind of fine pottery, the most remarkable being what is called jasper, either white, or colored throughout the body, and capable of being molded into the most delicate forms, so that fine and minute bas-reliefs like cameos were made of it, fit even for being set as jewels.

wedgy.c: Wedgy Wedg"y (?), a. Like a wedge; wedge-shaped.

wedlock.c: Wedlock Wed"lock (?), n. [AS. wedlāc a pledge, be trothal; wedd a pledge + lāc a gift, an offering. See Wed, n., and cf. Lake, v. i., Knowledge.]
Wedlock Wed"lock, v. t. To marry; to unite in marriage; to wed. [R.] “Man thus wedlocked.” Milton.

wednesday.c: Wednesday Wednes"day (?; 48), n. [OE. wednesdai, wodnesdei, AS. Wōdnes dæg, i. e., Woden's day (a translation of L. dies Mercurii); fr. Wōden the highest god of the Teutonic peoples, but identified with the Roman god Mercury; akin to OS. Wōdan, OHG. Wuotan, Icel. Oðinn, D. woensdag Wednesday, Icel. ōðinsdagr, Dan. & Sw. onsdag. See Day, and cf. Woden, Wood, a.] The fourth day of the week; the next day after Tuesday.

wee.c: Wee Wee (?), n. [OE. we a bit, in a little we, probably originally meaning, a little way, the word we for wei being later taken as synonymous with little. See Way.] A little; a bit, as of space, time, or distance. [Obs. or Scot.]
Wee Wee, a. Very small; little. [Colloq. & Scot.]

weed.c: Weed Weed (wēd), n. [OE. wede, AS. wǣde, wǣd; akin to OS. wādi, giwādi, OFries, wēde, wēd, OD. wade, OHG. wāt, Icel. vāð, Zend vadh to clothe.]
Weed Weed, n. A sudden illness or relapse, often attended with fever, which attacks women in childbed. [Scot.]
Weed Weed, n. [OE. weed, weod, AS. weód, wiód, akin to OS. wiod, LG. woden the stalks and leaves of vegetables D. wieden to weed, OS. wiodōn.]
Weed Weed, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Weeded; p. pr. & vb. n. Weeding.] [AS. weódian. See 3d Weed.]

weeder.c: Weeder Weed"er (?), n. One who, or that which, weeds, or frees from anything noxious.

weedery.c: Weedery Weed"er*y (?), n. Weeds, collectively; also, a place full of weeds or for growing weeds. [R.] Dr. H. More.

weeding.c: Weeding Weed"ing, a. & n. from Weed, v.

weedingrhim.c: Weeding-rhim Weed"ing-rhim` (?), n. [Cf. Prov. E. rim to remove.] A kind of implement used for tearing up weeds esp. on summer fallows. [Prov. Eng.]

weedless.c: Weedless Weed"less, a. 1. Free from weeds or noxious matter.

weedy.c: Weedy Weed"y, a. Dressed in weeds, or mourning garments. [R. or Colloq.]

week.c: Week Week (?), n. [OE. weke, wike, woke, wuke AS. weocu, wicu, wucu; akin to OS. wika, OFries. wike, D. week, G. woche, OHG. wohha, wehha, Icel. vika, Sw. vecka, Dan. uge, Goth. wik?, probably originally meaning, a succession or change, and akin to G. wechsel change, L. vicis turn, alternation, and E. weak. Cf. Weak.] A period of seven days, usually that reckoned from one Sabbath or Sunday to the next.

weekend.c: Week-end Week"-end", n. The end of the week, usually comprising the period from Friday evening to Monday morning, observed commonly as a period of respite from work or school; as, to visit one for a week-end; also, a house party during a week-end. Contrasted to work days.

weekly.c: Weekly Week"ly (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a week, or week days; as, weekly labor.
Weekly Week"ly, n.; pl. Weeklies (?). A publication issued once in seven days, or appearing once a week.
Weekly Week"ly, adv. Once a week; by hebdomadal periods; as, each performs service weekly.

weel.c: Weel Weel (?), a. & adv. Well. [Obs. or Scot.]

weely.c: Weely Weel { Weel (?), Weel"y (?), }[Prov. E. weel, weal, a wicker basket to catch eels; prob. akin to willow, and so called as made of willow twigs.] A kind of trap or snare for fish, made of twigs. [Obs.] Carew.

ween.c: Ween Ween (?), v. i. [OE. wenen, AS. w?nan, fr. w?n hope, expectation, opinion; akin to D. waan, OFries. w?n, OS. & OHG. wān, G. wahn delusion, Icel. vān hope, expectation, Goth. w?ns, and D. wanen to fancy, G. wähnen, Icel. vāna to hope, Goth. w?njan, and perhaps to E. winsome, wish.] To think; to imagine; to fancy. [Obs. or Poetic] Spenser. Milton.

weep.c: Weep Weep (?), n. (Zool.) The lapwing; the wipe; -- so called from its cry.
Weep Weep, obs. imp. of Weep, for wept. Chaucer.

Weep Weep, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wept (wĕpt); p. pr. & vb. n. Weeping.] [OE. wepen, AS. wēpan, from wōp lamentation; akin to OFries. w?pa to lament, OS. wōp lamentation, OHG. wuof, Icel. ōp a shouting, crying, OS. wōpian to lament, OHG. wuoffan, wuoffen, Icel. œpa, Goth. wōpjan. √129.]
Weep Weep, v. t. 1. To lament; to bewail; to bemoan. “I weep bitterly the dead.” A. S. Hardy.

weeper.c: Weeper Weep"er (?), n. 1. One who weeps; esp., one who sheds tears.

weepful.c: Weepful Weep"ful (?), a. Full of weeping or lamentation; grieving. [Obs.] Wyclif.

weeping.c: Weeping Weep"ing, n. The act of one who weeps; lamentation with tears; shedding of tears.
Weeping Weep"ing, a. 1. Grieving; lamenting; shedding tears. “Weeping eyes.” I. Watts.

Weeping tree Weep"ing tree. (a) Any tree having pendulous branches. (b) A tree from which honeydew or other liquid secretions of insects drip in considerable quantities, esp. one infested by the larvae of any species of the genus Ptylus, allied to the cuckoo spits, which in tropical countries secrete large quantities of a watery fluid.

weepingly.c: Weepingly Weep"ing*ly (?), adv. In a weeping manner.

weepingripe.c: Weeping-ripe Weep"ing-ripe` (?), a. Ripe for weeping; ready to weep. [Obs.] Shak.

weet.c: Weet Weet, v. i. [imp. Wot (?).] [See Wit to know.] To know; to wit. [Obs.] Tyndale. Spenser.

weetbird.c: Weet-bird Weet"-bird` (?), n. (Zool.) The wryneck; -- so called from its cry. [Prov. Eng.]

weetless.c: Weetless Weet"less, a. Unknowing; also, unknown; unmeaning. [Obs.] Spenser.

weetweet.c: Weet-weet Weet"-weet` (?), n. [So called from its piping cry when disturbed.] (Zool.) (a) The common European sandpiper. (b) The chaffinch. [Prov. Eng.]

Weet-weet Weet"-weet` (?), n. [Native name in Victoria.] A throwing toy, or implement, of the Australian aborigines, consisting of a cigar-shaped stick fastened at one end to a flexible twig. It weighs in all about two ounces, and is about two feet long.

weever.c: Weever Wee"ver (?), n. [Probably from F. vive, OF. vivre, a kind of fish, L. vipera viper. Cf. Viper.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of edible marine fishes belonging to the genus Trachinus, of the family Trachinidae. They have a broad spinose head, with the eyes looking upward. The long dorsal fin is supported by numerous strong, sharp spines which cause painful wounds.

weevil.c: Weevil Wee"vil (?), n. [OE. wivel, wevil, AS. wifel, wibil; akin to OD. wevel, OHG. wibil, wibel, G. wiebel, wibel, and probably to Lith. vabalas beetle, and E. weave. See Weave.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of snout beetles, or Rhynchophora, in which the head is elongated and usually curved downward. Many of the species are very injurious to cultivated plants. The larvae of some of the species live in nuts, fruit, and grain by eating out the interior, as the plum weevil, or curculio, the nut weevils, and the grain weevil (see under Plum, Nut, and Grain). The larvae of other species bore under the bark and into the pith of trees and various other plants, as the pine weevils (see under Pine). See also Pea weevil, Rice weevil, Seed weevil, under Pea, Rice, and Seed.

weeviled.c: Weeviled Wee"viled (?), a. Infested by weevils; as, weeviled grain. [Written also weevilled.]

weevily.c: Weevily Wee"vil*y (?), a. Having weevils; weeviled. [Written also weevilly.]

weft.c: Weft Weft (?), obs. imp. & p. p. of Wave.
Weft Weft, n. [Cf. Waif.] A thing waved, waived, or cast away; a waif. [Obs.] “A forlorn weft.” Spenser.
Weft Weft, n. [AS. weft, wefta, fr. wefan, to weave. See Weave.]

wegotism.c: Wegotism We"go*tism (?), n. [From we, in imitation of egotism.] Excessive use of the pronoun we; -- called also weism. [Colloq. or Cant]

wehrgelt.c: Wehrgelt Wehrgeld { Wehr"geld` (?), Wehr"gelt` (?), } n. (O. Eng. Law) See Weregild.

weigelia.c: Weigelia Weigela { Wei"gel*a (?), Wei*ge"li*a (?), } n. [NL. So named after C. E. Weigel, a German naturalist.] (Bot.) A hardy garden shrub (Diervilla Japonica) belonging to the Honeysuckle family, with white or red flowers. It was introduced from China.

weigh.c: Weigh Weigh (wā), n. (Naut.) A corruption of Way, used only in the phrase under weigh.

Weigh Weigh, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Weighed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Weighing.] [OE. weien, weyen, weghen, AS. wegan to bear, move; akin to D. wegen to weigh, G. wägen, wiegen, to weigh, bewegen to move, OHG. wegan, Icel. vega to move, carry, lift, weigh, Sw. väga to weigh, Dan. veie, Goth. gawigan to shake, L. vehere to carry, Skr. vah.????. See Way, and cf. Wey.]
Weigh Weigh (?), v. i. 1. To have weight; to be heavy. “They only weigh the heavier.” Cowper.
Weigh Weigh, n. [See Wey.] A certain quantity estimated by weight; an English measure of weight. See Wey.

weighable.c: Weighable Weigh"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being weighed.

weighage.c: Weighage Weigh"age (?; 48), n. A duty or toil paid for weighing merchandise. Bouvier.

weighbeam.c: Weighbeam Weigh"beam` (?), n. A kind of large steelyard for weighing merchandise; -- also called weighmaster's beam.

weighboard.c: Weighboard Weigh"board` (?), n. (Mining) Clay intersecting a vein. Weale.

weighbridge.c: Weighbridge Weigh"bridge` (?), n. A weighing machine on which loaded carts may be weighed; platform scales.

weigher.c: Weigher Weigh"er (?), n. One who weighs; specifically, an officer whose duty it is to weigh commodities.

weighhouse.c: Weigh-house Weigh"-house` (?), n.; pl. Weigh-houses (?). A building at or within which goods, and the like, are weighed.

weighing.c: Weighing Weigh"ing, a. & n. from Weigh, v.

weighlock.c: Weighlock Weigh"lock` (?), n. A lock, as on a canal, in which boats are weighed and their tonnage is settled.

weighmaster.c: Weighmaster Weigh"mas`ter (?), n. One whose business it is to weigh ore, hay, merchandise, etc.; one licensed as a public weigher.

weight.c: Weight Weight (?), n. [OE. weght, wight, AS. gewiht; akin to D. gewigt, G. gewicht, Icel. vætt, Sw. vigt, Dan. vægt. See Weigh, v. t.]
Weight Weight, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Weighted; p. pr. & vb. n. Weighting.]

weightily.c: Weightily Weight"i*ly (?), adv. In a weighty manner.

weightiness.c: Weightiness Weight"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being weighty; weight; force; importance; impressiveness.

weightless.c: Weightless Weight"less, a. Having no weight; imponderable; hence, light. Shak.

weils.c: Weil's disease Weil's disease (?). (Med.) An acute infectious febrile disease, resembling typhoid fever, with muscular pains, disturbance of the digestive organs, jaundice, etc.

weird.c: Weird Weird (wērd), n. [OE. wirde, werde, AS. wyrd fate, fortune, one of the Fates, fr. weorðan to be, to become; akin to OS. wurd fate, OHG. wurt, Icel. urðr. √143. See Worth to become.]
Weird Weird, v. t. To foretell the fate of; to predict; to destine to. [Scot.] Jamieson.

weirdness.c: Weirdness Weird"ness, n. The quality or state of being weird.

weismannism.c: Weismannism Weis"mann*ism (?), n. (Biol.) The theories and teachings in regard to heredity propounded by the German biologist August Weismann, esp. in regard to germ plasm as the basis of heredity and the impossibility of transmitting acquired characteristics; -- often called neo-Darwinism.

weiss.c: Weiss beer Weiss beer (?). [G. weissbier white beer.] A light-colored highly effervescent beer made by the top-fermentation process.

weive.c: Weive Weive (?), v. t. See Waive. [Obs.] Gower.

weka.c: Weka We"ka (?), n. (Zool.) A New Zealand rail (Ocydromus australis) which has wings so short as to be incapable of flight.

wekau.c: Wekau We"kau (?), n. (Zool.) A small New Zealand owl (Sceloglaux albifacies). It has short wings and long legs, and lives chiefly on the ground.

wekeen.c: Wekeen We*keen" (?), n. (Zool.) The meadow pipit. [Prov. Eng.]

welaway.c: Welaway Wel"a*way (?), interj. [OE. welaway, walaway, weilawey; wei wo! (Icel. vei) + la lo! (AS. lā) + wei wo!; cf. AS. wā lā wā. See Woe.] Alas! [Obs.]

welbegone.c: Wel-begone Wel"-be*gone` (?), a. [OE. wel-begon. See Well, and Begone.] Surrounded with happiness or prosperity. [Obs.]

welcome.c: Welcome Wel"come (?), a. [OE. welcome, welcume, wilcume, AS. wilcuma a welcome guest, from wil-, as a prefix, akin to willa will + cuma a comer, fr. cuman to come; hence, properly, one who comes so as to please another's will; cf. Icel. velkominn welcome, G. willkommen. See Will, n., and Come.]

Welcome Wel"come, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Welcomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Welcoming.] [AS. wilcumian.] To salute with kindness, as a newcomer; to receive and entertain hospitably and cheerfully; as, to welcome a visitor; to welcome a new idea. “I welcome you to land.” Addison.

welcomely.c: Welcomely Wel"come*ly, adv. In a welcome manner.

welcomeness.c: Welcomeness Wel"come*ness, n. The quality or state of being welcome; gratefulness; agreeableness; kind reception.

welcomer.c: Welcomer Wel"com*er (?), n. One who welcomes; one who salutes, or receives kindly, a newcomer. Shak.

weld.c: Weld Weld (wĕld), v. t. To wield. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Weld Weld (wĕld), n. [OE. welde; akin to Scot. wald, Prov. G. waude, G. wau, Dan. & Sw. vau, D. wouw.]

Weld Weld, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Welded; p. pr. & vb. n. Welding.] [Probably originally the same word as well to spring up, to gush; perhaps from the Scand.; cf. Sw. välla to weld, uppvälla to boil up, to spring up, Dan. vælde to gush, G. wellen to weld. See Well to spring.]
Weld Weld, n. The state of being welded; the joint made by welding.
Weld steel Weld steel. A compound of iron, such as puddled steel, made without complete fusion.

weldable.c: Weldable Weld"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being welded.

welder.c: Welder Weld"er (?), n. One who welds, or unites pieces of iron, etc., by welding.

weldons.c: Weldon's process Wel"don's proc"ess (?), (Chem.) A process for the recovery or regeneration of manganese dioxide in the manufacture of chlorine, by means of milk of lime and the oxygen of the air; -- so called after the inventor.

wele.c: Wele Wele (?), n. [See Weal prosperity.] Prosperity; happiness; well-being; weal. [Obs.] Chaucer.

weleful.c: Weleful Wele"ful (?), a. Producing prosperity or happiness; blessed. [Obs.] Chaucer.

welew.c: Welew We"lew (?), v. t. To welk, or wither. [Obs.]

welfare.c: Welfare Wel"fare` (?), n. [Well + fare to go, to proceed, to happen.] Well-doing or well-being in any respect; the enjoyment of health and the common blessings of life; exemption from any evil or calamity; prosperity; happiness.

welfaring.c: Welfaring Wel"far`ing, a. Faring well; prosperous; thriving. [Obs.] “A welfaring person.” Chaucer.

welk.c: Welk Welk (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Welked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Welking.] [OE. welken; cf. D. & G. welken to wither, G. welk withered, OHG. welc moist. See Welkin, and cf. Wilt.] To wither; to fade; also, to decay; to decline; to wane. [Obs.]
Welk Welk, n. A pustule. See 2d Whelk.

welkin.c: Welkin Wel"kin (?), n. [OE. welken, welkene, welkne, wolcne, weolcne, AS. wolcen, pl. wolcnu, a cloud; akin to D. wolk, OFries. wolken, OS. wolkan, G. wolke, OHG. wolchan, and probably to G. welk withered, OHG. welc moist, Russ. & OSlav. vlaga moisture, Lith. vilgyti to moisten.] The visible regions of the air; the vault of heaven; the sky.

well.c: Well Well (?), n. [OE. welle, AS. wella, wylla, from weallan to well up, surge, boil; akin to D. wel a spring or fountain.????. See Well, v. i.]

Well Well (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Welled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Welling.] [OE. wellen, AS. wyllan, wellan, fr. weallan; akin to OFries. walla, OS. & OHG. wallan, G. wallen, Icel. vella, G. welle, wave, OHG. wella, walm, AS. wylm; cf. L. volvere to roll, Gr.? to inwrap,? to roll. Cf. Voluble, Wallop to boil, Wallow, Weld of metal.] To issue forth, as water from the earth; to flow; to spring. “[Blood] welled from out the wound.” Dryden. “[Yon spring] wells softly forth.” Bryant.
Well Well, v. t. To pour forth, as from a well. Spenser.

Well Well, adv. [Compar. and superl. wanting, the deficiency being supplied by better and best, from another root.] [OE. wel, AS. wel; akin to OS., OFries., & D. wel, G. wohl, OHG. wola, wela, Icel. & Dan. vel, Sw. väl, Goth. waíla; originally meaning, according to one's will or wish. See Will, v. t., and cf. Wealth.]
We'll We'll (?). Contraction for we will or we shall. “We'll follow them.” Shak.

welladay.c: Welladay Well"a*day (?), interj. [Corrupted from wela way.] Alas! Welaway! Shak.

wellat.c: Wellat Wel"lat (?), n. (Zool.) The king parrakeet See under King.

wellbeing.c: Well-being Well"-be`ing (?), n. The state or condition of being well; welfare; happiness; prosperity; as, virtue is essential to the well-being of men or of society.

wellborn.c: Well-born Well"-born` (?), a. Born of a noble or respect able family; not of mean birth.

wellbred.c: Well-bred Well"-bred` (?), a. Having good breeding; refined in manners; polite; cultivated.

welldoer.c: Welldoer Well"do`er (?), n. One who does well; one who does good to another; a benefactor.

welldoing.c: Welldoing Well"do`ing, n. A doing well; right performance of duties. Also used adjectively.

welldrain.c: Welldrain Well"drain` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Welldrained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Well-draining.] To drain, as land; by means of wells, or pits, which receive the water, and from which it is discharged by machinery.

wellfavored.c: Well-favored Well"-fa"vored (?), a. Handsome; wellformed; beautiful; pleasing to the eye.

wellhead.c: Wellhead Well"head` (?), n. A source, spring, or fountain.

wellinformed.c: Well-informed Well`-in*formed" (?), a. Correctly informed; provided with information; well furnished with authentic knowledge; intelligent.

wellington.c: Wellington boot Wel"ling*ton boot. [After the Duke of Wellington.] A riding boot for men, the front of which came above the knee; also, a similar shorter boot worn under the trousers.

wellingtonia.c: Wellingtonia Wel`ling*to"ni*a (?), n. [NL. So named after the Duke of Wellington.] (Bot.) A name given to the “big trees” (Sequoia gigantea) of California, and still used in England. See Sequoia.

wellingtons.c: Wellingtons Wel"ling*tons (?), n. pl. [After the Duke of Wellington.] A kind of long boots for men.

wellintentioned.c: Well-intentioned Well`-in*ten"tioned (?), a. Having upright intentions or honorable purposes.

wellknown.c: Well-known Well"-known` (?), a. Fully known; generally known or acknowledged.

wellliking.c: Well-liking Well"-lik`ing (?), a. Being in good condition. [Obs. or Archaic]

wellmannered.c: Well-mannered Well`-man"nered (?), a. Polite; well-bred; complaisant; courteous. Dryden.

wellmeaner.c: Well-meaner Well"-mean`er (?), n. One whose intention is good. “Well-meaners think no harm.” Dryden.

wellmeaning.c: Well-meaning Well"-mean`ing, a. Having a good intention.

wellplighted.c: Well-plighted Well"-plight`ed (?), a. Being well folded. [Obs.] “Her well-plighted frock.” Spenser.

wellread.c: Well-read Well"-read` (?), a. Of extensive reading; deeply versed; -- often followed by in.

wellseen.c: Well-seen Well"-seen` (?), a. Having seen much; hence, accomplished; experienced. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

wellspring.c: Wellspring Well"spring` (?), n. A fountain; a spring; a source of continual supply.

wellwiller.c: Well-willer Well"-will`er (?), n. One who wishes well, or means kindly. [R.] “A well-willer of yours.” Brydges.

wellwish.c: Well-wish Well"-wish` (?), n. A wish of happiness. “A well-wish for his friends.” Addison.

wellwisher.c: Wellwisher Well"wish`er (?), n. One who wishes another well; one who is benevolently or friendlily inclined.

wels.c: Wels Wels (?), n. [G.] (Zool.) The sheatfish; -- called also waller.

welsbach.c: Welsbach Wels"bach (?), a. Of or pertaining to Auer von Welsbach or the incandescent gas burner invented by him. -- Welsbach burner, a burner in which the combustion of a mixture of air and gas or vapor is employed to heat to incandescence a mantle composed of thoria and ceria. The mantle is made by soaking a “stocking” in a solution of nitrates of thorium and cerium (approx. 99:1), drying, and, for use, igniting to burn the thread and convert the nitrates into oxides, which remain as a fragile ash. The light far exceeds that obtained from the same amount of gas with the ordinary fishtail burner, but has a slight greenish hue.

welsh.c: Welsh Welsh (?), a. [AS. wælisc, welisc, from wealh a stranger, foreigner, not of Saxon origin, a Welshman, a Celt, Gael; akin to OHG. walh, whence G. wälsch or welsch, Celtic, Welsh, Italian, French, Foreign, strange, OHG. walhisc; from the name of a Celtic tribe. See Walnut.] Of or pertaining to Wales, or its inhabitants. [Sometimes written also Welch.]

Welsh Welsh (?), v. t. & i. (a) To cheat by avoiding payment of bets; -- said esp. of an absconding bookmaker at a race track. [Slang] (b) To avoid dishonorably the fulfillment of a pecuniary obligation. [Slang]

welsher.c: Welsher Welsh"er (?), n. One who cheats at a horse race; one who bets, without a chance of being able to pay; one who receives money to back certain horses and absconds with it. [Written also welcher.] [Slang, Eng.]

welsome.c: Welsome Wel"some (?), a. Prosperous; well. [Obs.] Wyclif. -- Wel"some*ly, adv. Wyclif.

welt.c: welt welt (wĕlt), n. [OE. welte, probably fr. W. gwald a hem, a welt, gwaldu to welt or to hem.]
Welt Welt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Welted; p. pr. & vb. n. Welting.] To furnish with a welt; to sew or fasten a welt on; as, to welt a boot or a shoe; to welt a sleeve.

weltanschauung.c: Weltanschauung ‖Welt"an"schau`ung (?), n.; pl. Weltanschauungen (#). [G.] Lit., world view; a conception of the course of events in, and of the purpose of, the world as a whole, forming a philosophical view or apprehension of the universe; the general idea embodied in a cosmology.

welte.c: Welte Welte (?), obs. imp. of Weld, to wield. Chaucer.

welter.c: Welter Wel"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Weltered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Weltering.] [Freq. of OE. walten to roll over, AS. wealtan; akin to LG. weltern, G. walzen to roll, to waltz, sich wälzen to welter, OHG. walzan to roll, Icel. velta, Dan. vælte, Sw. vältra, välta; cf. Goth. waltjan; probably akin to E. wallow, well, v. i. √146. See Well, v. i., and cf. Waltz.]
Welter Wel"ter, v. t. [Cf. Wilt, v. i.] To wither; to wilt. [R.]
Welter Wel"ter, a. (Horse Racing) Of, pertaining to, or designating, the most heavily weighted race in a meeting; as, a welter race; the welter stakes.

welterweight.c: Welterweight Wel"ter*weight` (?), n. 1. (Horse Racing) A weight of 28 pounds (one of 40 pounds is called a heavy welterweight) sometimes imposed in addition to weight for age, chiefly in steeplechases and hurdle races.

weltschmertz.c: Weltschmertz ‖Welt"schmertz` (vĕlt"shmĕrts`), n. [G., fr. welt world + schmertz pain. See World; Smart, v. i.] Sorrow or sadness over the present or future evils or woes of the world in general; sentimental pessimism.

welwitschia.c: Welwitschia ‖Wel*witsch"i*a (?), n. [NL. So named after the discoverer, Dr. Friedrich Welwitsch.] (Bot.) An African plant (Welwitschia mirabilis) belonging to the order Gnetaceae. It consists of a short, woody, topshaped stem, and never more than two leaves, which are the cotyledons enormously developed, and at length split into diverging segments.

wem.c: Wem Wem (?), n. [Cf. Womb.] The abdomen; the uterus; the womb. [Obs.]
Wem Wem, n. [AS. wam, wamm.] Spot; blemish; harm; hurt. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Wem Wem, v. t. [AS. wemman.] To stain; to blemish; to harm; to corrupt. [Obs.]

wemless.c: Wemless Wem"less, a. Having no wem, or blemish; spotless. [Obs.] “Virgin wemless.” Chaucer.

wen.c: Wen Wen (wĕn), n. [AS. wenn; akin to D. wen, LG. wenne.] (Med.) An indolent, encysted tumor of the skin; especially, a sebaceous cyst.

Wen Wyn Wynn { Wyn, Wynn (?), n. Also Wen (?) }. [AS. wēn.] One of the runes (?) adopted into the Anglo-Saxon, or Old English, alphabet. It had the value of modern English w, and was replaced from about a. d. 1280 at first by uu, later by w.

wench.c: Wench Wench (wĕnch), n. [OE. wenche, for older wenchel a child, originally, weak, tottering; cf. AS. wencle a maid, a daughter, wencel a pupil, orphan, wincel, winclu, children, offspring, wencel weak, wancol unstable, OHG. wanchol; perhaps akin to E. wink. See Wink.]
Wench Wench (wĕnch), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wenched (wĕncht); p. pr. & vb. n. Wenching.] To frequent the company of wenches, or women of ill fame.

wencher.c: Wencher Wench"er (wĕnch"ẽr), n. One who wenches; a lewd man.

wenchless.c: Wenchless Wench"less, a. Being without a wench. Shak. “Mr. Clinton, wenchless of late, has sublimated with public apologies.”

wend.c: Wend Wend (wĕnd), obs. p. p. of Wene. Chaucer.

Wend Wend, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wended, Obs. Went; p. pr. & vb. n. Wending.] [AS. wendan to turn, to go, caus. of windan to wind; akin to OS. wendian, OFries. wenda, D. wenden to turn, G. wenden, Icel. venda, Sw. vända, Dan. vende, Goth. wandjan. See Wind to turn, and cf. Went.]
Wend Wend, v. t. To direct; to betake; -- used chiefly in the phrase to wend one's way. Also used reflexively. “Great voyages to wend.” Surrey.
