wildgrave.c: Wildgrave Wild"grave` (?), n. [G. wildgraf or D. wildgraaf. See Wild, and cf. Margrave.] A waldgrave, or head forest keeper. See Waldgrave.

wilding.c: Wilding Wild"ing, n. (Bot.) A wild or uncultivated plant; especially, a wild apple tree or crab apple; also, the fruit of such a plant. Spenser.
Wilding Wild"ing, a. Not tame, domesticated, or cultivated; wild. [Poetic] “Wilding flowers.” Tennyson.

wildish.c: Wildish Wild"ish, a. Somewhat wild; rather wild. “A wildish destiny.” Wordsworth.

wildly.c: Wildly Wild"ly, adv. In a wild manner; without cultivation; with disorder; rudely; distractedly; extravagantly.

wildness.c: Wildness Wild"ness, n. The quality or state of being wild; an uncultivated or untamed state; disposition to rove or go unrestrained; rudeness; savageness; irregularity; distraction.

wildwood.c: Wildwood Wild"wood (?), n. A wild or unfrequented wood. Also used adjectively; as, wildwood flowers; wildwood echoes. Burns.

wile.c: Wile Wile (?), n. [OE. wile, AS. wīl; cf. Icel. v?l, væl. Cf. Guile.] A trick or stratagem practiced for insnaring or deception; a sly, insidious; artifice; a beguilement; an allurement.
Wile Wile, v. t. 1. To practice artifice upon; to deceive; to beguile; to allure. [R.] Spenser.

wileful.c: Wileful Wile"ful (?), a. Full of wiles; trickish; deceitful.

wilfley.c: Wilfley table Wil"fley ta`ble (?). (Ore Dressing) An inclined percussion table, usually with longitudinal grooves in its surface, agitated by side blows at right angles to the flow of the pulp; -- so called after the inventor.

wilfulness.c: Wilfulness Wilfully Wilful Wil"ful (?), a., Wil"ful*ly, adv., Wil"ful*ness, n. See Willful, Willfully, and Willfulness.

wiliness.c: Wiliness Wi"li*ness, n. The quality or state of being wily; craftiness; cunning; guile.

will.c: Will Will (?), n. [OE. wille, AS. willa; akin to OFries. willa, OS. willeo, willio, D. wil, G. wille, Icel. vili, Dan. villie, Sw. vilja, Goth wilja. See Will, v.]

Will Will (?), v. t. & auxiliary. [imp. Would (?). Indic. present, I will (Obs. I wol), thou wilt, he will (Obs. he wol); we, ye, they will.] [OE. willen, imp. wolde; akin to OS. willan, OFries. willa, D. willen, G. wollen, OHG. wollan, wellan, Icel. & Sw. vilja, Dan. ville, Goth. wiljan, OSlav. voliti, L. velle to wish, volo I wish; cf. Skr. vṛ to choose, to prefer. Cf. Voluntary, Welcome, Well, adv.]
Will Will (?), v. i. To be willing; to be inclined or disposed; to be pleased; to wish; to desire.
Will Will, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Willed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Willing. Indic. present I will, thou willeth, he wills; we, ye, they will.] [Cf. AS. willian. See Will, n.]
Will Will, v. i. To exercise an act of volition; to choose; to decide; to determine; to decree.

willemite.c: Willemite Wil"lem*ite (?), n. [From Willem I., king of the Netherlands.] (Min.) A silicate of zinc, usually occurring massive and of a greenish yellow color, also in reddish crystals (troostite) containing manganese.

willet.c: Willet Wil"let (?), n. (Zool.) A large North American snipe (Symphemia semipalmata); -- called also pill-willet, will-willet, semipalmated tattler, or snipe, duck snipe, and stone curlew.

willier.c: Willier Wil"li*er (?), n. One who works at a willying machine.

willingly.c: Willingly Will"ing*ly, adv. In a willing manner; with free will; without reluctance; cheerfully. Chaucer.

willingness.c: Willingness Will"ing*ness, n. The quality or state of being willing; free choice or consent of the will; freedom from reluctance; readiness of the mind to do or forbear.

willywaw.c: Willywaw Williwaw { Wil"li*waw, Wil"ly*waw } (?), n. (Naut.) A whirlwind, or whirlwind squall, encountered in the Straits of Magellan. W. C. Russell.

willock.c: Willock Wil"lock (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The common guillemot. (b) The puffin. [Prov. Eng.]

willothewisp.c: Will-o'-the-wisp Will"-o'-the-wisp` (?), n. See Ignis fatuus and phosphine.

willow.c: Willow Wil"low (?), n. [OE. wilowe, wilwe, AS. wilig, welig; akin to OD. wilge, D. wilg, LG. wilge. Cf. Willy.]
Willow Wil"low (?), v. t. To open and cleanse, as cotton, flax, or wool, by means of a willow. See Willow, n., 2.

willowed.c: Willowed Wil"lowed (?), a. Abounding with willows; containing willows; covered or overgrown with willows. “Willowed meads.” Collins.

willower.c: Willower Wil"low*er (?), n. A willow. See Willow, n., 2.

willowherb.c: Willow-herb Wil"low-herb` (?), n. (Bot.) A perennial herb (Epilobium spicatum) with narrow willowlike leaves and showy rose-purple flowers. The name is sometimes made to include other species of the same genus.

willowish.c: Willowish Wil"low*ish, a. Having the color of the willow; resembling the willow; willowy. Walton.

willowthorn.c: Willow-thorn Wil"low-thorn` (?), n. (Bot.) A thorny European shrub (Hippophae rhamnoides) resembling a willow.

willowweed.c: Willow-weed Wil"low-weed` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A European species of loosestrife (Lysimachia vulgaris). (b) Any kind of Polygonum with willowlike foliage.

willowwort.c: Willow-wort Wil"low-wort` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) Same as Willow-weed. (b) Any plant of the order Salicaceae, or the Willow family.

willsome.c: Willsome Will"some (?), a. [Written also wilsome.] 1. Willful; obstinate. [Obs.]

willy.c: Willy nilly Wil"ly nil"ly (?). Whether I (he, she, they) want to or not. See Will I, nill I, etc., under 3d Will.

willying.c: Willying Wil"ly*ing, n. The process of cleansing wool, cotton, or the like, with a willy, or willow.

wilne.c: Wilne Wil"ne (?), v. t. [AS. wilnian.] To wish; to desire. [Obs.] “He willneth no destruction.” Chaucer.

wilt.c: Wilt Wilt, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wilting.] [Written also welt, a modification of welk.] To begin to wither; to lose freshness and become flaccid, as a plant when exposed when exposed to drought, or to great heat in a dry day, or when separated from its root; to droop;. to wither. [Prov. Eng. & U. S.]
Wilt Wilt, v. t. 1. To cause to begin to wither; to make flaccid, as a green plant. [Prov. Eng. U. S.]

wilton.c: Wilton carpet Wil"ton car`pet (?). A kind of carpet woven with loops like the Brussels, but differing from it in having the loops cut so as to form an elastic velvet pile; -- so called because made originally at Wilton, England.

wily.c: Wily Wil"y (?), a. [Compar. Wilier (?); superl. Wiliest.] [From Wile.] Full of wiles, tricks, or stratagems; using craft or stratagem to accomplish a purpose; mischievously artful; subtle. “Wily and wise.” Chaucer. “The wily snake.” Milton.

wimble.c: Wimble Wim"ble (?), n. [OE. wimbil; akin to Dan. vimmel, OD. wemelen to bore. Cf. Gimlet.] An instrument for boring holes, turned by a handle. Specifically: (a) A gimlet. “ It is but like the little wimble, to let in the greater auger.” Selden. (b) A stonecutter's brace for boring holes in stone. (c) An auger used for boring in earth.
Wimble Wim"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wimbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wimbling (?).] To bore or pierce, as with a wimble. “A foot soldier... wimbled also a hole through said coffin.” Wood.
Wimble Wim"ble (?), a. [Cf. Sw. vimmelkantig giddy, whimsical, dial. Sw. vimmla to be giddy or skittish, and E. whim.] Active; nimble.[Obs.] Spenser.

wimple.c: Wimple Wim"ple (?), n. [OE. wimpel, AS. winpel; akin to D. & G. wimpel a pennant, streamer, OHG. wimpal a veil, Icel. vimpill, Dan. & Sw. vimpel a pennant, streamer; of uncertain origin. Cf. Gimp.]
Wimple Wim"ple, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wimpled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wimpling (?).]
Wimple Wim"ple, v. i. To lie in folds; also, to appear as if laid in folds or plaits; to ripple; to undulate. “Wimpling waves.” Longfellow.

win.c: Win Win (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Won (?), Obs. Wan (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Winning.] [OE. winnen, AS. winnan to strive, labor, fight, endure; akin to OFries. winna, OS. winnan, D. winnen to win, gain, G. gewinnen, OHG. winnan to strive, struggle, Icel. vinna to labor, suffer, win, Dan. vinde to win, Sw. vinna, Goth. winnan to suffer, Skr. van to wish, get, gain, conquer. √138. Cf. Venerate, Winsome, Wish, Wont, a.]
Win Win, v. i. To gain the victory; to be successful; to triumph; to prevail.

wince.c: Wince Wince (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Winced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wincing (?).] [OE. wincen, winchen, OF. quencir, guenchir, guenchier, giencier, guinchier, and (assumed) winchier, winchir, to give way, to turn aside, fr. OHG. wankjan, wenken, to give way, to waver, fr. winchan to turn aside, to nod, akin to E. wink. See Wink.]
Wince Wince, n. The act of one who winces.

Wince Wince, n. [See Winch.] (Dyeing & Calico Printing) A reel used in dyeing, steeping, or washing cloth; a winch. It is placed over the division wall between two wince pits so as to allow the cloth to descend into either compartment. at will.

wincer.c: Wincer Win"cer (?), n. One who, or that which, winces, shrinks, or kicks.

winch.c: Winch Winch (?), v. i. [See Wince.] To wince; to shrink; to kick with impatience or uneasiness.
Winch Winch, n. A kick, as of a beast, from impatience or uneasiness. Shelton.
Winch Winch, n. [OE. winche, AS. wince a winch, a reel to wind thread upon. Cf. Wink.]

wincing.c: Wincing Win"cing (?), n. The act of washing cloth, dipping it in dye, etc., with a wince.

wincopipe.c: Wincopipe Win"co*pipe (?), n. (Bot.) A little red flower, no doubt the pimpernel, which, when it opens in the morning, is supposed to bode a fair day. See Pimpernel.

wind.c: Wind Wind (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wound (wound) (rarely Winded); p. pr. & vb. n. Winding.] [OE. winden, AS. windan; akin to OS. windan, D. & G. winden, OHG. wintan, Icel. & Sw. vinda, Dan. vinde, Goth. windan (in comp.). Cf. Wander, Wend.]
Wind Wind (?), v. i. 1. To turn completely or repeatedly; to become coiled about anything; to assume a convolved or spiral form; as, vines wind round a pole.
Wind Wind (?), n. The act of winding or turning; a turn; a bend; a twist; a winding.

Wind Wind (wĭnd, in poetry and singing often wīnd; 277), n. [AS. wind; akin to OS., OFries., D., & G. wind, OHG. wint, Dan. & Sw. vind, Icel. vindr, Goth winds, W. gwynt, L. ventus, Skr. vāta (cf. Gr. 'ah`ths a blast, gale, 'ah^nai to breathe hard, to blow, as the wind); originally a p. pr. from the verb seen in Skr. vā to blow, akin to AS. wāwan, D. waaijen, G. wehen, OHG. wāen, wājen, Goth. waian. √131. Cf. Air, Ventail, Ventilate, Window, Winnow.]
Wind Wind (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Winded; p. pr. & vb. n. Winding.]

Wind Wind (?), v. t. [From Wind, moving air, but confused in sense and in conjugation with wind to turn.] [imp. & p. p. Wound (wound), R. Winded; p. pr. & vb. n. Winding.] To blow; to sound by blowing; esp., to sound with prolonged and mutually involved notes. “Hunters who wound their horns.” Pennant.

Wind signal Wind signal. In general, any signal announcing information concerning winds, and esp. the expected approach of winds whose direction and force are dangerous to shipping, etc. The wind-signal system of the United States Weather Bureau consists of storm, information, hurricane, hot wind, and inland storm signals.

windage.c: Windage Wind"age (?), n. [From Wind air in motion.]

windbore.c: Windbore Wind"bore` (?), n. The lower, or bottom, pipe in a lift of pumps in a mine. Ansted.

windbound.c: Windbound Wind"bound` (?), a. (Naut.) prevented from sailing, by a contrary wind. See Weatherbound.

windbreak.c: Wind-break Wind"-break` (?), v. t. To break the wind of; to cause to lose breath; to exhaust. [R.]
Wind-break Wind"-break`, n. A clump of trees serving for a protection against the force of wind. [Local, U. S.]

windbroken.c: Wind-broken Wind"-bro`ken (?), a. Having the power of breathing impaired by the rupture, dilatation, or running together of air cells of the lungs, so that while the inspiration is by one effort, the expiration is by two; affected with pulmonary emphysema or with heaves; -- said of a horse. Youatt.

winder.c: Winder Wind"er (?), v. t. & i. [Prov. E. winder a fan, and to winnow.?. Cf. Winnow.] To fan; to clean grain with a fan. [Prov. Eng.]
Winder Wind"er, n. A blow taking away the breath. [Slang]
Winder Wind"er, v. i. To wither; to fail. [Obs.] Holland.

windfall.c: Windfall Wind"fall` (?), n. 1. Anything blown down or off by the wind, as fruit from a tree, or the tree itself, or a portion of a forest prostrated by a violent wind, etc. “They became a windfall upon the sudden.” Bacon.

windfallen.c: Windfallen Wind"fall`en (?), a. Blown down by the wind.

windfertilized.c: Wind-fertilized Wind"-fer`ti*lized (?), a. (Bot.) Anemophilous; fertilized by pollen borne by the wind.

windflower.c: Windflower Wind"flow`er (?), n. (Bot.) The anemone; -- so called because formerly supposed to open only when the wind was blowing. See Anemone.

windgall.c: Windgall Wind"gall` (?), n. (Far.) A soft tumor or synovial swelling on the fetlock joint of a horse; -- so called from having formerly been supposed to contain air.

windhover.c: Windhover Wind"hov`er (?), n. [From its habit of hovering over one spot.] (Zool.) The kestrel; -- called also windbibber, windcuffer, windfanner. [Prov. Eng.]

windiness.c: Windiness Wind"i*ness (?), n. 1. The quality or state of being windy or tempestuous; as, the windiness of the weather or the season.

winding.c: Winding Wind"ing (?), n. [From Wind to blow.] (Naut.) A call by the boatswain's whistle.
Winding Wind"ing, a. [From Wind to twist.] Twisting from a direct line or an even surface; circuitous. Keble.
Winding Wind"ing, n. 1. A turn or turning; a bend; a curve; flexure; meander; as, the windings of a road or stream.

windingly.c: Windingly Wind"ing*ly, adv. In a winding manner.

windjammer.c: Windjammer Wind"jam`mer (?), n. 1. (Naut.) A sailing vessel or one of its crew; -- orig. so called contemptuously by sailors on steam vessels. [Colloq.]

windlass.c: Windlass Wind"lass (?), n.[Perhaps from wind to turn + lace.] A winding and circuitous way; a roundabout course; a shift.
Windlass Wind"lass, v. i. To take a roundabout course; to work warily or by indirect means. [Obs.] Hammond.
Windlass Wind"lass, n. [OE. windelas, windas, Icel. vindilāss, vindās, fr. vinda to wind + āss a pole; cf. Goth. ans a beam. See Wind to turn.]
Windlass Wind"lass, v. t. & i. To raise with, or as with, a windlass; to use a windlass. The Century.

windless.c: Windless Wind"less (?), a. 1. Having no wind; calm.

windlestraw.c: Windlestraw Windlestrae { Win"dle*strae` (?), Win"dle*straw` (?) }, n. (Bot.) A grass used for making ropes or for plaiting, esp. Agrostis Spica-ventis. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Shelley.

windmill.c: Windmill Wind"mill` (?), n. A mill operated by the power of the wind, usually by the action of the wind upon oblique vanes or sails which radiate from a horizontal shaft. Chaucer.

windore.c: Windore Win"dore (?), n. [A corrupt. of window; or perh. coined on the wrong assumption that window is from wind + door.] A window. [Obs.] Hudibras.

window.c: Window Win"dow (?), n. [OE. windowe, windoge, Icel. vindauga window, properly, wind eye; akin to Dan. vindue.????. See Wind, n., and Eye.]
Window Win"dow (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Windowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Windowing.]

windowed.c: Windowed Win"dowed (?), a. Having windows or openings. [R.] “Looped and windowed raggedness.” Shak.

windowless.c: Windowless Win"dow*less, a. Destitute of a window. Carlyle.

windowpane.c: Windowpane Win"dow*pane` (?), n. 1. (Arch.) See Pane, n., (3) b. [In this sense, written also window pane.]

windowy.c: Windowy Win"dow*y (?), a. Having little crossings or openings like the sashes of a window. [R.] Donne.

windpipe.c: Windpipe Wind"pipe` (?), n. (Anat.) The passage for the breath from the larynx to the lungs; the trachea; the weasand. See Illust. under Lung.

windrode.c: Wind-rode Wind"-rode` (?), a. (Naut.) Caused to ride or drive by the wind in opposition to the course of the tide; -- said of a vessel lying at anchor, with wind and tide opposed to each other. Totten.

windrow.c: Windrow Wind"row, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Windrowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Windrowing.] To arrange in lines or windrows, as hay when newly made. Forby.

windshaken.c: Wind-shaken Wind"-shak`en (?), a. Shaken by the wind; specif. (Forestry), affected by wind shake, or anemosis (which see, above).

windsor.c: Windsor Wind"sor (?), n. A town in Berkshire, England.

windstorm.c: Windstorm Wind"storm (?), n. A storm characterized by high wind with little or no rain.

windsucker.c: Wind-sucker Wind"-suck`er (?), n. 1. (Far.) A horse given to wind-sucking Law.

windsucking.c: Wind-sucking Wind"-suck`ing, n. (Far.) A vicious habit of a horse, consisting in the swallowing of air; -- usually associated with crib-biting, or cribbing. See Cribbing, 4.

windtight.c: Windtight Wind"tight` (?), a. So tight as to prevent the passing through of wind. Bp. Hall.

windup.c: Wind-up Wind"-up` (?), n. Act of winding up, or closing; a concluding act or part; the end.

windward.c: Windward Wind"ward (?), n. The point or side from which the wind blows; as, to ply to the windward; -- opposed to leeward.
Windward Wind"ward, a. Situated toward the point from which the wind blows; as, the Windward Islands.
Windward Wind"ward, adv. Toward the wind; in the direction from which the wind blows.

windy.c: Windy Wind"y (?), a. [Compar. Windier (?); superl. Windiest.] [AS. windig.]

wine.c: Wine Wine (?), n. [OE. win, AS. win, fr. L. vinum (cf. Icel. vīn; all from the Latin); akin to Gr. o'i^nos,?, and E. withy. Cf. Vine, Vineyard, Vinous, Withy.]

wineberry.c: Wineberry Wine"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) (a) The red currant. (b) The bilberry. (c) A peculiar New Zealand shrub (Coriaria ruscifolia), in which the petals ripen and afford an abundant purple juice from which a kind of wine is made. The plant also grows in Chili.

winebibber.c: Winebibber Wine"bib`ber (?), n. One who drinks much wine. Prov. xxiii. 20. -- Wine"bib`bing (#), n.

wineglass.c: Wineglass Wine"glass` (?), n. A small glass from which to drink wine.

wineglassful.c: Wineglassful Wine"glass`ful (?);, n. pl. Wineglassfuls (?). As much as a wineglass will hold; enough to fill a wineglass. It is usually reckoned at two fluid ounces, or four tablespoonfuls.

wineless.c: Wineless Wine"less, a. destitute of wine; as, wineless life.

winery.c: Winery Win"er*y (?), n. [Cf. F. vinerie.] A place where grapes are converted into wine.

winesap.c: Winesap Wine"sap` (?), n. [Wine + sap for sop.] A variety of winter apple of medium size, deep red color, and yellowish flesh of a rich, rather subacid flavor.

wing.c: Wing Wing (?), n. [OE. winge, wenge; probably of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. vinge, Icel. vængr.]
Wing Wing (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Winged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Winging.] 1. To furnish with wings; to enable to fly, or to move with celerity.
Wing it Wing it, v. i. To perform an act, such as to give a speech, without the usual preparation. To improvise or ad-lib.

winged.c: Winged Winged (?), a. 1. Furnished with wings; transported by flying; having winglike expansions.

winger.c: Winger Wing"er (?), n. (Naut.) One of the casks stowed in the wings of a vessel's hold, being smaller than such as are stowed more amidships. Totten.

wingfish.c: Wingfish Wing"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) A sea robin having large, winglike pectoral fins. See Sea robin, under Robin.

wingfooted.c: Wing-footed Wing"-foot`ed (?), a. 1. Having wings attached to the feet; as, wing-footed Mercury; hence, swift; moving with rapidity; fleet. Drayton.

winghanded.c: Wing-handed Wing"-hand`ed (?), a. (Zool.) Having the anterior limbs or hands adapted for flight, as the bats and pterodactyls.

wingleaved.c: Wing-leaved Wing"-leaved` (?), a. (Bot.) Having pinnate or pinnately divided leaves.

wingless.c: Wingless Wing"less, a. Having no wings; not able to ascend or fly.

winglet.c: Winglet Wing"let (?), n. 1. A little wing; a very small wing.

wingmanship.c: Wingmanship Wing"man*ship (?), n. [From Wing, in imitation of horsemanship.] Power or skill in flying. [R.] Duke of Argyll.

wingshell.c: Wing-shell Wing"-shell` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) Any one of various species of marine bivalve shells belonging to the genus Avicula, in which the hinge border projects like a wing. (b) Any marine gastropod shell of the genus Strombus. See Strombus. (c) Any pteropod shell.

wink.c: Wink Wink (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Winked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Winking.] [OE. winken, AS. wincian; akin to D. wenken, G. winken to wink, nod, beckon, OHG. winchan, Sw. vinka, Dan. vinke, AS. wancol wavering, OHG. wanchal wavering, wanch?n to waver, G. wanken, and perhaps to E. weak; cf. AS. wincel a corner. Cf. Wench, Wince, v. i.]
Wink Wink, v. t. To cause (the eyes) to wink.[Colloq.]
Wink Wink, n. 1. The act of closing, or closing and opening, the eyelids quickly; hence, the time necessary for such an act; a moment.

winker.c: Winker Wink"er (?), n. 1. One who winks. Pope.

winkingly.c: Winkingly Wink"ing*ly, adv. In a winking manner; with the eye almost closed. Peacham.

winkle.c: Winkle Win"kle (?), n. [AS. wincle.] (Zool.) (a) Any periwinkle. Holland. (b) Any one of various marine spiral gastropods, esp., in the United States, either of two species of Fulgar (Fulgar canaliculata, and Fulgar carica).

winklehawk.c: Winkle-hawk Win"kle-hawk` (?), n. [D. winkel-haak a carpenter's square.] A rectangular rent made in cloth; -- called also winkle-hole. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.

winnebagoes.c: Winnebagoes Win`ne*ba"goes (?), n.; sing. Winnebago (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of North American Indians who originally occupied the region about Green Bay, Lake Michigan, but were driven back from the lake and nearly exterminated in 1640 by the IIlinnois.

winner.c: Winner Win"ner (?), n. One who wins, or gains by success in competition, contest, or gaming.

winning.c: Winning Win"ning (?), a. Attracting; adapted to gain favor; charming; as, a winning address. “Each mild and winning note.” Keble.
Winning Win"ning, n. 1. The act of obtaining something, as in a contest or by competition.

winningly.c: Winningly Win"ning*ly, adv. In a winning manner.

winningness.c: Winningness Win"ning*ness, n. The quality or state of being winning. “Winningness in style.” J. Morley.

winninish.c: Winninish Win"nin*ish (?), n. (Zool.) The land-locked variety of the common salmon. [Canada]

winnow.c: Winnow Win"now (wĭn"no), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Winnowed (wĭn"nod); p. pr. & vb. n. Winnowing.] [OE. windewen, winewen, AS. windwian; akin to Goth. winpjan (in comp.), winpi-skauro a fan, L. ventilare to fan, to winnow; cf. L. wannus a fan for winnowing, G. wanne, OHG. wanna. √131. See Wind moving air, and cf. Fan., n., Ventilate.]
Winnow Win"now (?), v. i. To separate chaff from grain.

winnower.c: Winnower Win"now*er (?), n. One who, or that which, winnows; specifically, a winnowing machine.

winnowing.c: Winnowing Win"now*ing, n. The act of one who, or that which, winnows.

winsome.c: Winsome Win"some (?), a. [Compar. Winsomer (?); superl. Winsomest.] [AS. wynsum, fr. wynn joy; akin to OS. wunnia, OHG. wunna, wunni, G. wonne, Goth. wunan to rejoice (in unwunands sad), AS. wunian to dwell.????. See Win, v. t., Wont, a.]

winsomeness.c: Winsomeness Win"some*ness, n. The characteristic of being winsome; attractiveness of manner. J. R. Green.

winter.c: Winter Win"ter (?), n. [AS. winter; akin to OFries. & D. winter, OS. & OHG. wintar, G. winter, D. & Sw. vinter, Icel. vetr, Goth. wintrus; of uncertain origin; cf. Old Gallic vindo- white (in comp.), OIr. find white.????.]
Winter Win"ter, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wintered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wintering.] To pass the winter; to hibernate; as, to winter in Florida.
Winter Win"ter, v. i. To keep, feed or manage, during the winter; as, to winter young cattle on straw.

winterbeaten.c: Winter-beaten Win"ter-beat`en (?), a. Beaten or harassed by the severe weather of winter. Spenser.

wintergreen.c: Wintergreen Win"ter*green` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant which keeps its leaves green through the winter.

winterground.c: Winter-ground Win"ter-ground` (?), v. t. To coved over in the season of winter, as for protection or shelter; as, to winter-ground the roods of a plant.

winterkill.c: Winterkill Win"ter*kill` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Winterkilled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Winterkilling.] To kill by the cold, or exposure to the inclemency of winter; as, the wheat was winterkilled. [U. S.]
Winterkill Win"ter*kill`, v. i. To die as the result of exposure to the cold of winter; as, the tree winterkills easily.

winterly.c: Winterly Win"ter*ly, a. Like winter; wintry; cold; hence, disagreeable, cheerless; as, winterly news. [R.] Shak.

winterproud.c: Winter-proud Win"ter-proud` (?), a. Having too rank or forward a growth for winter.

winterrig.c: Winter-rig Win"ter-rig` (?), v. t. [See Winter and Ridge.] To fallow or till in winter. [Prov. Eng.]

winters.c: Winter's bark Win"ter's bark` (?). (Bot.) The aromatic bark of tree (Drimys Winteri syn. Drymis Winteri) of the Magnolia family, which is found in Southern Chile. It was first used as a cure for scurvy by its discoverer, Captain John Winter, vice admiral to sir Francis Drake, in 1577.

winterweed.c: Winterweed Win"ter*weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A kind of speedwell (Veronica hederifolia) which spreads chiefly in winter. Dr. Prior.

wintry.c: Wintry Win"try (?), a. [AS. wintrig.] Suitable to winter; resembling winter, or what belongs to winter; brumal; hyemal; cold; stormy; wintery.

winy.c: Winy Win"y (?), a. Having the taste or qualities of wine; vinous; as, grapes of a winy taste. Dampier.

winze.c: Winze Winze (?), n. (Mining.) A small shaft sunk from one level to another, as for the purpose of ventilation.

wipe.c: Wipe Wipe (?), n. [Cf. Sw. vipa, Dan. vibe, the lapwing.] (Zool.) The lapwing. [Prov. Eng.]

Wipe Wipe, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wiped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wiping.] [OE. vipen, AS. wīpian; cf. LG. wiep a wisp of straw, Sw. vepa to wrap up, to cuddle one's self up, vepa a blanket; perhaps akin to E. whip.]
Wipe Wipe, n. 1. Act of rubbing, esp. in order to clean.

wiper.c: Wiper Wip"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, wipes.

wirble.c: Wirble Wir"ble (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wirbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wirbling (?).] [Cf. Warble, Whirl.] To whirl; to eddy. [R.]

wirche.c: Wirche Wirche (?), v. i. & t. To work [Obs.] Chaucer.

wire.c: Wire Wire (wīr), n. [OE. wir, AS. wir; akin to Icel. vīrr, Dan. vire, LG. wir, wire; cf. OHG. wiara fine gold; perhaps akin to E. withy. √141.]
Wire Wire (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wiring.] 1. To bind with wire; to attach with wires; to apply wire to; as, to wire corks in bottling liquors.
Wire Wire, v. i. 1. To pass like a wire; to flow in a wirelike form, or in a tenuous stream. [R.] P. Fletcher.
Wire gun Wire gun. same as Wire-wound gun.

Wire tapper Wire tapper. One that taps, or cuts in on, telegraph wires and intercepts messages; hence (Slang), a swindler who pretends to tap wires or otherwise intercept advance telegraphic news for betting. -- Wire tapping.

wiredraw.c: Wiredraw Wire"draw` (?), v. t. [imp. Wiredrew (?); p. p. Wiredrawn (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wiredrawing.]

wiredrawer.c: Wire-drawer Wire"-draw`er (?), n. One who draws metal into wire.

wireheel.c: Wire-heel Wire"-heel` (?), n. (Far.) A disease in the feet of a horse or other beast.

wireless.c: Wireless Wire"less, a. Having no wire; specif. (Elec.), designating, or pertaining to, a method of telegraphy, telephony, or other information transmisssion, in which the messages, data, etc., are transmitted through space by electric waves; as, a wireless message; a wireless network; a wireless keyboard.
Wireless Wire"less, n. Short for Wireless telegraphy, Wireless telephony, etc.; as, to send a message by wireless.

wirepuller.c: Wire-puller wirepuller wirepuller, Wire"-pull`er (?), n. One who pulls the wires, as of a puppet; hence, one who uses secret influence (i.e. pulls wires or strings) for his own ends; an intriguer.

wirepulling.c: Wire-pulling Wire"-pull`ing, n. The act of pulling the wires, as of a puppet; hence, secret influence or management, especially in politics; intrigue.

wiretailed.c: Wire-tailed Wire"-tailed` (?), a. (Zool.) Having some or all of the tail quills terminated in a long, slender, pointed shaft, without a web or barbules.

wirework.c: Wirework Wire"work` (?), n. Work, especially openwork, formed of wires.

wireworker.c: Wire-worker Wire"-work`er (?), n. One who manufactures articles from wire.

wireworm.c: Wireworm Wire"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) One of the larvae of various species of snapping beetles, or elaters; -- so called from their slenderness and the uncommon hardness of the integument. Wireworms are sometimes very destructive to the roots of plants. Called also wire grub. (b) A galleyworm.

wirewound.c: Wire-wound gun Wire"-wound` gun. (Ordnance) A gun in the construction of which an inner tube (either entire or in segments) is wound with wire under tension to insure greater soundness and uniformity of resistance. In modern construction hoops and jackets are shrunk on over the wire.

wiriness.c: Wiriness Wir"i*ness (?), n. The quality of being wiry.

wiring.c: Wiring Wir"ing (?), n. 1. The act of one that wires anything.

wis.c: Wis Wis (?), adv. [Aphetic form of iwis, ywis; or fr. Icel. viss certain. See Ywis.] Certainly; really; indeed. [Obs.] “As wis God helpe me.” Chaucer.

Wis Wis, v. t. [Due to mistaking OE. iwis certain, AS. gewiss, for I wis. See Ywis.] To think; to suppose; to imagine; -- used chiefly in the first person sing. present tense, I wis. See the Note under Ywis. [Obs. or Poetic] “Howe'er you wis.” R. Browning.

wisdom.c: Wisdom Wis"dom (-dŭm), n. [AS. wīsdōm. See Wise, a., and -dom.]

Wisdom literature Wis"dom lit"er*a*ture. The class of ancient Hebrew writings which deal reflectively with general ethical and religious topics, as distinguished from the prophetic and liturgical literature, and from the law. It is comprised chiefly in the books of Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiasticus, Ecclesiastes, and Wisdom of Solomon. The “wisdom” (Hokhmah) of these writings consists in detached sage utterances on concrete issues of life, without the effort at philosophical system that appeared in the later Hellenistic reflective writing beginning with Philo Judaeus.

wise.c: Wise Wise (wīz), a. [Compar. Wiser (wīz"ẽr); superl. Wisest.] [OE. wis, AS. wīs; akin to OS. & OFries. wīs, D. wijs, G. weise, OHG. wīs, wīsi, Icel. vīss, Sw. vis, Dan. viis, Goth. weis; akin to wit, v. i. See Wit, v., and cf. Righteous, Wisdom.]

wise wise, a. [OE. wise, AS. wīse; akin to OS. wīsa, OFries. wīs, D. wijs, wijze, OHG. wīsa, G. weise, Sw. vis, Dan. viis, Icel. öðruvīs otherwise; from the root of E. wit; hence, originally, knowledge, skill. See Wit, v., and cf. Guise.] Way of being or acting; manner; mode; fashion. “All armed in complete wise.” Spenser.

wiseacre.c: Wiseacre Wise"a*cre (?), n. [OD. wijssegger or G. weissager a foreteller, prophet, from weissagen to foretell, to prophesy, OHG. wīssag?n, corrupted (as if compounded of the words for wise and say) fr. wīzzag?n, fr. wīzzag? a prophet, akin to AS. wītiga, wītga, from the root of E. wit. See Wit, v.]

wisehearted.c: Wise-hearted Wise"-heart`ed (?), a. Wise; knowing; skillful; sapient; erudite; prudent. Ex. xxviii. 3.

wiselike.c: Wise-like Wise"-like` (?), a. Resembling that which is wise or sensible; judicious.

wiseling.c: Wiseling Wise"ling (?), n. One who pretends to be wise; a wiseacre; a witling. Donne.

wisely.c: Wisely Wise"ly, adv. In a wise manner; prudently; judiciously; discreetly; with wisdom.

wish.c: Wish Wish (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wishing.] [OE. wischen, weschen, wuschen, AS. w?scan; akin to D. wenschen, G. wünschen, Icel. æeskja, Dan. önske, Sw. önska; from AS. w?sc a wish; akin to OD. & G. wunsch, OHG. wunsc, Icel.?sk, Skr. vā?chā a wish, vā?ch to wish; also to Skr. van to like, to wish.?. See Winsome, Win, v. t., and cf. Wistful.]
Wish Wish (?), v. t. 1. To desire; to long for; to hanker after; to have a mind or disposition toward.
Wish Wish, n. 1. Desire; eager desire; longing.

wishable.c: Wishable Wish"a*ble (?), a. Capable or worthy of being wished for; desirable. Udall.

wishbone.c: Wishbone Wish"bone` (?), n. The forked bone in front of the breastbone in birds; -- called also merrythought, and wishing bone. See Merrythought, and Furculum.

wishedly.c: Wishedly Wish"ed*ly, adv. According to wish; conformably to desire. [Obs.] Chapman.

wisher.c: Wisher Wish"er (?), n. One who wishes or desires; one who expresses a wish. Shak.

wishful.c: Wishful Wish"ful (?), a. [Cf. Wistful.] 1. Having desire, or ardent desire; longing.

wishing.c: Wishing Wish"ing, a. & n. from Wish, v. t.

wishly.c: Wishly Wish"ly, adv. According to desire; longingly; with wishes. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Chapman.

wishtonwish.c: Wishtonwish Wish"ton*wish (?), n. [Probably of American Indian origin.] (Zool.) The prairie dog.

wishwash.c: Wish-wash Wish"-wash` (?), n. Any weak, thin drink.

wishywashy.c: Wishy-washy Wish"y-wash`y (?), a. [See Wash.] Thin and pale; weak; without strength or substance; -- originally said of liquids. Fig., weak-minded; spiritless.
Wishy-washy Wish"y-wash`y, n. A weak or thin drink or liquor; wish-wash.

wisket.c: Wisket Wis"ket (?), n. A whisket, or basket. [Prov. Eng.] Ainsworth.

wisly.c: Wisly Wis"ly (?), adv. [See Wis, adv.] Certainly. [Obs.] “God so wisly have mercy on me.” Chaucer.

wisp.c: Wisp Wisp (?), n. [OE. wisp, wips; probably akin to D. & G. wisch, Icel. visk, and perhaps to L. virga a twig, rod. Cf. Verge a rod, Whisk, n.]
Wisp Wisp, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wisped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wisping.]

wispen.c: Wispen Wisp"en (?), a. Formed of a wisp, or of wisp; as, a wispen broom. [Obs.]

wisse.c: Wisse Wis"se (?), v. t. [AS. wīsian. See Wise, a.] To show; to teach; to inform; to guide; to direct. [Obs.]

wist.c: Wist Wist (?), archaic imp. & p. p. of Wit, v. Knew.

wistaria.c: Wistaria Wis*ta"ri*a (?), n. [NL.] [So named after Caspar Wistar, an American anatomist.] (Bot.) A genus of climbing leguminous plants bearing long, pendulous clusters of pale bluish flowers. Now commonly spelled Wisteria.

wistful.c: Wistful Wist"ful (?), a. [For wishful; perhaps influenced by wistly, which is probably corrupted from OE. wisly certainly (from Icel. viss certain, akin to E. wit). See Wish.]

wistit.c: Wistit Wis"tit, n. [Prob. from native name: cf. F. ouistiti.] (Zool.) A small South American monkey; a marmoset. [Written also wistiti, and ouistiti.]

wistly.c: Wistly Wist"ly (?), adv. [See Wistful.] Attentively; observingly. [Obs.] Shak.

wit.c: Wit Wit (wĭt), v. t. & i. [inf. (To) Wit; pres. sing. Wot; pl. Wite; imp. Wist(e); p. p. Wist; p. pr. & vb. n. Wit(t)ing. See the Note below.] [OE. witen, pres. ich wot, wat, I know (wot), imp. wiste, AS. witan, pres. wāt, imp. wiste, wisse; akin to OFries. wita, OS. witan, D. weten, G. wissen, OHG. wizzan, Icel. vita, Sw. veta, Dan. vide, Goth. witan to observe, wait I know, Russ. vidiete to see, L. videre, Gr.?, Skr. vid to know, learn; cf. Skr. vid to find.????. Cf. History, Idea, Idol, -oid, Twit, Veda, Vision, Wise, a. & n., Wot.] To know; to learn. “I wot and wist alway.” Chaucer.
Wit Wit (?), n. [AS. witt, wit; akin to OFries. wit, G. witz, OHG. wizzī, Icel. vit, Dan. vid, Sw. vett. √133. See Wit, v.]

witan.c: Witan Wit"an (?), n. pl. [AS., pl. of wita sage, councilor.] Lit., wise men; specif. (A.-S. Hist.), The members of the national, or king's, council which sat to assist the king in administrative and judicial matters; also, the council.

witch.c: Witch Witch (?), n. [Cf. Wick of a lamp.] A cone of paper which is placed in a vessel of lard or other fat, and used as a taper. [Prov. Eng.]

Witch Witch, n. [OE. wicche, AS. wicce, fem., wicca, masc.; perhaps the same word as AS. wītiga, wītga, a soothsayer (cf. Wiseacre); cf. Fries. wikke, a witch, LG. wikken to predict, Icel. vitki a wizard, vitka to bewitch.]
witch witch (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. witched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. witching.] [AS. wiccian.] To bewitch; to fascinate; to enchant.

witchery.c: Witchery Witch"er*y (?), n.; pl. Witcheries (?). 1. Sorcery; enchantment; witchcraft.

witchhazel.c: Witch-hazel Witch"-ha`zel (?), n. [See Wych-elm, and Hazel.] (Bot.) The wych-elm. (b) An American shrub or small tree (Hamamelis Virginica), which blossoms late in autumn.

witching.c: witching witch"ing, a. That witches or enchants; suited to enchantment or witchcraft; bewitching. “The very witching time of night.” Shak. -- Witch"ing*ly, adv.

witchuck.c: Witchuck Wit"chuck` (?), n. (Zool.) The sand martin, or bank swallow. [Prov. Eng.]

witcracker.c: Wit-cracker Wit"-crack`er (?), n. One who breaks jests; a joker. [Obs.] Shak.

witcraft.c: Witcraft Wit"craft` (?), n. 1. Art or skill of the mind; contrivance; invention; wit. [Obs.] Camden.

wite.c: Wite Wite (?), v. t. [AS. wītan; akin to D. wijten, G. verweisen, Icel. vīta to mulct, and E. wit; cf. AS. wītan to see, L. animadvertere to observe, to punish.????. See Wit, v.] To reproach; to blame; to censure; also, to impute as blame. [Obs. or Scot.] Spenser.
Wite Wite, n. [AS. wīte punishment.????. See Wite, v.] Blame; reproach. [Obs. or Scot.] Chaucer.

witen.c: Witen Wit"en (?), obs. pl. pres. of Wit. Chaucer.

witenagemote.c: Witenagemote Wit"e*na*ge*mote` (?; 277), n. [AS. witena gemōt an assembly of the wise; wita a wise man + gemōt assembly.] (AS. Hist.) A meeting of wise men; the national council, or legislature, of England in the days of the Anglo-Saxons, before the Norman Conquest.

with.c: With With (?), prep. [OE. with, AS. wi? with, against; akin to AS. wi?er against, OFries. with, OS. wi?, wi?ar, D. weder, weêr (in comp.), G. wider against, wieder gain, OHG. widar again, against, Icel. vi? against, with, by, at, Sw. vid at, by, Dan. ved, Goth. wipra against, Skr. vi asunder. Cf. Withdraw, Withers, Withstand.] With denotes or expresses some situation or relation of nearness, proximity, association, connection, or the like. It is used especially: --

withal.c: Withal With*al", prep. With; -- put after its object, at the end of sentence or clause in which it stands. [Obs.]

withamite.c: Withamite With"am*ite (wĭth"aim*īt), n. [From its discoverer, H. Witham.] (Min.) A variety of epidote, of a reddish color, found in Scotland.

withdraw.c: Withdraw With*draw" (wĭth*drä"), v. t. [imp. Withdrew (-drü"); p. p. Withdrawn (-drän"); p. pr. & vb. n. Withdrawing.] [With against + draw.] 1. To take back or away, as what has been bestowed or enjoyed; to draw back; to cause to move away or retire; as, to withdraw aid, favor, capital, or the like.
Withdraw With*draw", v. i. To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place; to go away; as, he withdrew from the company. “When the sea withdrew.” King Horn.

withdrawal.c: Withdrawal With*draw"al (?), n. The act of withdrawing; withdrawment; retreat; retraction. Fielding.

withdrawer.c: Withdrawer With*draw"er (?), n. One who withdraws; one who takes back, or retracts.

withdrawingroom.c: Withdrawing-room With*draw"ing-room` (?), n. [See Withdraw, and cf. Drawing-room.] A room for retirement from another room, as from a dining room; a drawing-room.

withdrawment.c: Withdrawment With*draw"ment (?), n. The act of withdrawing; withdrawal. W. Belsham.

withe.c: Withe Withe (?; 277), n. [OE. withe.????. See Withy, n.] [Written also with.]
Withe Withe, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Withed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Withing.] To bind or fasten with withes.

wither.c: Wither With"er (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Withered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Withering.] [OE. wideren; probably the same word as wederen to weather (see Weather, v. & n.); or cf. G. verwittern to decay, to be weather-beaten, Lith. vysti to wither.]
Wither With"er, v. t. 1. To cause to fade, and become dry.

witherband.c: Witherband With"er*band` (?), n. [Withers + band.] (Far.) A piece of iron in a saddle near a horse's withers, to strengthen the bow.

withered.c: Withered With"ered (?), a. Faded; dried up; shriveled; wilted; wasted; wasted away. -- With"ered*ness, n. Bp. Hall.

withering.c: Withering With"er*ing (?), a. Tending to wither; causing to shrink or fade. -- With"er*ing*ly, adv.

witherite.c: Witherite With"er*ite (?), n. [So called after Dr. W. Withering.] (Min.) Barium carbonate occurring in white or gray six-sided twin crystals, and also in columnar or granular masses.

witherling.c: Witherling With"er*ling (?), n. [Wither + -ling.] A withered person; one who is decrepit. [Obs.] Chapman.

withernam.c: Withernam With"er*nam (?), n. [AS. wiðernām; wiðer against + nām a seizure, fr. niman to take.] (Law) A second or reciprocal distress of other goods in lieu of goods which were taken by a first distress and have been eloigned; a taking by way of reprisal; -- chiefly used in the expression capias in withernam, which is the name of a writ used in connection with the action of replevin (sometimes called a writ of reprisal), which issues to a defendant in replevin when he has obtained judgment for a return of the chattels replevied, and fails to obtain them on the writ of return. Blackstone.

witherod.c: Withe-rod Withe"-rod` (?), n. (Bot.) A North American shrub (Viburnum nudum) whose tough osierlike shoots are sometimes used for binding sheaves.

withers.c: Withers With"ers (?), n. pl. [Properly, the parts which resist the pull or strain in drawing a load; fr. OE. wither resistance, AS. wiðre, fr. wiðer against; akin to G. widerrist withers. See With, prep.] The ridge between the shoulder bones of a horse, at the base of the neck. See Illust. of Horse.

witherwrung.c: Wither-wrung With"er-wrung` (?), a. Injured or hurt in the withers, as a horse.

withhold.c: Withhold With*hold" (?), v. t. [imp. Withheld (?); p. p. Withheld, Obs. or Archaic Withholden (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Withholding.] [With again, against, back + hold.]

withholdment.c: Withholdment With*hold"ment (?), n. The act of withholding.

within.c: Within With*in" (?), prep. [OE. withinne, withinnen, AS. wiðinnan; wið with, against, toward + innan in, inwardly, within, from in in. See With, prep., In, prep.]
Within With*in", adv. 1. In the inner part; inwardly; internally. “The wound festers within.” Carew.

withinforth.c: Withinforth With*in"forth` (?), adv. Within; inside; inwardly. [Obs.] Wyclif.

withinside.c: Withinside With*in"side` (?), adv. In the inner parts; inside. [Obs.] Graves.

without.c: Without With*out" (?), prep. [OE. withoute, withouten, AS. wið?tan; wið with, against, toward +?tan outside, fr.?t out. See With, prep., Out.]
Without With*out", conj. Unless; except; -- introducing a clause.
Without With*out", adv. 1. On or art the outside; not on the inside; not within; outwardly; externally.

withoutdoor.c: Without-door With*out"-door` (?), a. Outdoor; exterior. [Obs.] “Her without-door form.” Shak.

withoutforth.c: Withoutforth With*out"forth` (?), adv. Without; outside' outwardly. Cf. Withinforth. [Obs.] Chaucer.

withsay.c: Withsay With*say" (?), v. t. To contradict; to gainsay; to deny; to renounce. [Obs.] Gower.

withset.c: Withset With*set" (?), v. t. To set against; to oppose. [Obs.] “Their way he them withset.” R. of Brunne.

withstand.c: Withstand With*stand" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Withstood (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Withstanding.] [AS. wiðstandan. See With, prep., and Stand.] To stand against; to oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force; as, to withstand an attack of troops; to withstand eloquence or arguments. Piers Plowman.

withstander.c: Withstander With*stand"er (?), n. One who withstands, or opposes; an opponent; a resisting power.

withstood.c: Withstood With*stood" (?), imp. & p. p. o? Withstand.

withwind.c: Withwind With"wind` (?), n. [AS. wiðowinde.] (Bot.) A kind of bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis).

withy.c: Withy With"y (?), n.; pl. Withies (#). [OE. withe, wipi, AS. wī?ig a willow, willow twig; akin to G. weide willow, OHG. wīda, Icel. vī?ja, a withy, Sw. vide a willow twig, Dan. vidie a willow, osier, Gr.?, and probably to L. vitis a vine, viere to plait, Russ. vite. √141. Cf. Wine, Withe.]
Withy With"y, a. Made of withes; like a withe; flexible and tough; also, abounding in withes.

witing.c: Witing Wit"ing (?), n. [See Wit, v.] Knowledge. [Obs.] “Withouten witing of any other wight.” Chaucer.

witless.c: Witless Wit"less (?), a. Destitute of wit or understanding; wanting thought; hence, indiscreet; not under the guidance of judgment. “Witless bravery.” Shak.

witling.c: Witling Wit"ling (?), n. [Wit + -ling; cf. G. witzling.] A person who has little wit or understanding; a pretender to wit or smartness.

witness.c: Witness Wit"ness (?), n. [AS. witness, gewitnes, from witan to know. √133. See Wit, v. i.]
Witness Wit"ness, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Witnessed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Witnessing.]
Witness Wit"ness, v. i. To bear testimony; to give evidence; to testify. Chaucer.

witsnapper.c: Wit-snapper Wit"-snap`per (?), n. One who affects repartee; a wit-cracker. [Obs.] Shak.

witstarved.c: Wit-starved Wit"-starved` (?), a. Barren of wit; destitute of genius. Examiner.

witted.c: Witted Wit"ted (?), a. Having (such) a wit or understanding; as, a quick-witted boy.

witticaster.c: Witticaster Wit"tic*as`ter (?), n. [Formed like criticaster.] A witling. [R.] Milton.

witticism.c: Witticism Wit"ti*cism (?), n. [From Witty.] A witty saying; a sentence or phrase which is affectedly witty; an attempt at wit; a conceit. Milton.

wittified.c: Wittified Wit"ti*fied (?), a. [Witty + -fy + -ed.] Possessed of wit; witty. [R.] R. North.

wittily.c: Wittily Wit"ti*ly, adv. In a witty manner; wisely; ingeniously; artfully; with wit; with a delicate turn or phrase, or with an ingenious association of ideas.

wittiness.c: Wittiness Wit"ti*ness, n. The quality of being witty.

wittingly.c: Wittingly Wit"ting*ly (?), adv. [See Wit, v.] Knowingly; with knowledge; by design.

wittol.c: Wittol Wit"tol (?), n. [Said to be for white tail, and so called in allusion to its white tail; but cf. witwal.]

wittolly.c: Wittolly Wit"tol*ly (?), a. Like a wittol; cuckoldly. [Obs.] Shak.

witts.c: Witts Witts (?), n. (Mining) Tin ore freed from earthy matter by stamping. Knight.

witty.c: Witty Wit"ty (?), a. [Compar. Wittier (?); superl. Wittiest.] [AS. witig, wittig. See Wit, n.]

witwall.c: Witwall Witwal { Wit"wal`, Wit"wall` } (?), n. [Akin to G. wittewal, wiedewall, MHG. witewal, D. wiedewaal, wielewaal, OD. weduwael, and perhaps the same word as OE. wodewale. Cf. Wood, n., Wittol.] (Zool.) (a) The golden oriole. (b) The greater spotted woodpecker. [Prov. Eng.]

witworm.c: Witworm Wit"worm` (?), n. One who, or that which, feeds on or destroys wit. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

wive.c: Wive Wive, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wiving.] [AS. wīfian, gewīfian. See Wite.] To marry, as a man; to take a wife.
Wive Wive, v. t. 1. To match to a wife; to provide with a wife. “An I could get me but a wife... I were manned, horsed, and wived.” Shak.

wivern.c: Wivern Wiver { Wiv"er (?), Wiv"ern (?), } n. [OE. wivere a serpent, OF. wivre, guivre, F. givre, guivre, wiver, from L. vipera; probably influenced by OHG. wipera, from the Latin. See Viper, and cf. Weever.]

wizard.c: Wizard Wiz"ard (?), n. [Probably from wise + -ard.] 1. A wise man; a sage. [Obs.]

wizardly.c: Wizardly Wiz"ard*ly, a. Resembling or becoming a wizard; wizardlike; weird.

wizardry.c: Wizardry Wiz"ard*ry (?), n. The character or practices o? wizards; sorcery; magic. “He acquired a reputation bordering on wizardry.” J. A. Symonds.

wizen.c: Wizen Wiz"en (?), v. i. [OE. wisenen, AS. wisnian akin to weornian to decay, OHG. wesan?n to grow dry, G. verwesen to rot, Icel. visna to wither, Sw. vissna, Dan. visne, and probably to L. virus an offensive odor, poison. Cf. Virus.] To wither; to dry. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Wizen Wiz"en, a. Wizened; thin; weazen; withered.
Wizen Wiz"en, n. The weasand. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

wizened.c: Wizened Wiz"ened (?), a. Dried; shriveled; withered; shrunken; weazen; as, a wizened old man.

wizenfaced.c: Wizen-faced Wiz"en-faced` (?), a. Having a shriveled, thin, withered face.

wlatsome.c: Wlatsome Wlat"some (?), a. [AS. wlatian to disgust, irk, wl?tta loathing.] Loathsome; disgusting; hateful. [Obs.]

wo.c: Wo Wo (?), n. & a. See Woe. [Obs.] Chaucer.

woad.c: Woad Woad (?), n. [OE. wod, AS. wād; akin to D. weede, G. waid, OHG. weit, Dan. vaid, veid, Sw. veide, L. vitrum.] [Written also wad, and wade.]

woaded.c: Woaded Woad"ed, a. Colored or stained with woad. “Man tattoed or woaded, winter-clad in skins.” Tennyson.

woadwaxen.c: Woad-waxen Woad"-wax`en (?), n. [Cf. Wood-wax.] (Bot.) A leguminous plant (Genista tinctoria) of Europe and Russian Asia, and adventitious in America; -- called also greenwood, greenweed, dyer's greenweed, and whin, wood-wash, wood-wax, and wood-waxen.

wode.c: Wode Wode (?), a. [AS. wōd.] Mad. See Wood, a. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Chaucer.

wodegeld.c: Wodegeld Wode"geld` (?), n. [See Wood, and Geld.] (O. Eng. Law) A geld, or payment, for wood. Burrill.

woden.c: Woden Wo"den (?), n. [AS. Wōden; akin to OS. Wōdan, OHG. Wuotan, Icel. Oðinn, and probably to E. wood, a. Cf. Wednesday.] (Northern Myth.) A deity corresponding to Odin, the supreme deity of the Scandinavians. Wednesday is named for him. See Odin.

woe.c: Woe Woe (?), n. [OE. wo, wa, woo, AS. wā, interj.; akin to D. wee, OS. & OHG. wē, G. weh, Icel. vei, Dan. vee, Sw. ve, Goth. wai; cf. L. vae, Gr.?. √128. Cf. Wail.] [Formerly written also wo.]

woebegone.c: Woe-begone Woe"-be*gone` (?), a. [OE. wo begon. See Woe, and Begone, p. p.] Beset or overwhelmed with woe; immersed in grief or sorrow; woeful. Chaucer.

woful.c: Woful Woeful { Woe"ful, Wo"ful } (?), a. 1. Full of woe; sorrowful; distressed with grief or calamity; afflicted; wretched; unhappy; sad.

wofully.c: Wofully Woefully { Woe"ful*ly, Wo"ful*ly, } adv. In a woeful manner; sorrowfully; mournfully; miserably; dolefully.

wofulness.c: Wofulness Woefulness { Woe"ful*ness, Wo"ful*ness, } n. The quality or state of being woeful; misery; wretchedness.

wol.c: Wol Wol (?), v. t. & i. See 2d Will. [Obs.] Chaucer.

wold.c: Wold Wold (?), n. [OE. wold, wald, AS. weald, wald, a wood, forest; akin to OFries. & OS. wald, D. woud, G. wald, Icel. völlr, a field, and probably to Gr.? a grove, Skr. vā?a a garden, inclosure. Cf. Weald.]

wolde.c: Wolde Wolde (?), obs. imp. of Will. See Would.

wolf.c: Wolf Wolf (?), n.; pl. Wolves (#). [OE. wolf, wulf, AS. wulf; akin to OS. wulf, D. & G. wolf, Icel. ūlfr, Sw. ulf, Dan. ulv, Goth. wulfs, Lith. vilkas, Russ. volk', L. lupus, Gr. ly`kos, Skr. vṛka; also to Gr. "e`lkein to draw, drag, tear in pieces. √286. Cf. Lupine, a., Lyceum.]

wolfberry.c: Wolfberry Wolf"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) An American shrub (Symphoricarpus occidentalis) which bears soft white berries.

wolffian.c: Wolffian Wolff"i*an (?), a. (Anat.) Discovered, or first described, by Caspar Friedrich Wolff (1733-1794), the founder of modern embryology.

wolfhound.c: Wolfhound Wolf"hound` (?), n. (Zool.) Originally, a large hound used in hunting wolves; now, any one of certain breeds of large dogs, some of which are nearly identical with the great Danes.

wolfish.c: Wolfish Wolf"ish (?), a. Like a wolf; having the qualities or form of a wolf; as, a wolfish visage; wolfish designs.

wolfkin.c: Wolfkin Wolf"kin (?), n. A little or young wolf. Tennyson.

wolfling.c: Wolfling Wolf"ling (?), n. A young wolf. Carlyle.

wolfram.c: Wolfram steel Wol"fram steel. Same as Tungsten steel.

wolframate.c: Wolframate Wol"fram*ate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of wolframic acid; a tungstate.

wolframic.c: Wolframic Wol*fram"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to wolframium. See Tungstic.

wolframite.c: Wolframite Wol"fram*ite (?), n. [G., wolframit, wolfram; wolf wolf + rahm cream, soot; cf. G. wolfsruss wolfram, lit., wolf's soot.] (Min.) Tungstate of iron and manganese, generally of a brownish or grayish black color, submetallic luster, and high specific gravity. It occurs in cleavable masses, and also crystallized. Called also wolfram.

wolframium.c: Wolframium Wol*fra"mi*um (?), n. [NL. See Wolfram.] (Chem.) The technical name of the element tungsten. See Tungsten.

wolfsbane.c: Wolfsbane Wolfs"bane` (?), n. (Bot.) A poisonous plant (Aconitum Lycoctonum), a kind of monkshood; also, by extension, any plant or species of the genus Aconitum. See Aconite.

wolfsclaw.c: Wolf's-claw Wolf's"-claw` (?), n. (Bot.) A kind of club moss. See Lycopodium.

wolfsfoot.c: Wolf's-foot Wolf's"-foot` (?), n. (Bot.) Club moss. See Lycopodium.

wolfsmilk.c: Wolf's-milk Wolf's"-milk` (?), n. (Bot.) Any kind of spurge (Euphorbia); -- so called from its acrid milky juice.

woll.c: Woll Woll (?), v. t. & i. See 2d Will. [Obs.]

wollastonite.c: Wollastonite Wol"las*ton*ite (?), n. [After Dr. W. H. Wollaston, an English chemist, who died in 1828.] (Min.) A silicate of lime of a white to gray, red, or yellow color, occurring generally in cleavable masses, rarely in tabular crystals; tabular spar.

wollastons.c: Wollaston's doublet Wol"las*ton's dou"blet (?). [After W. H. Wollaston, English physicist.] (Optics) A magnifying glass consisting of two plano-convex lenses. It is designed to correct spherical aberration and chromatic dispersion.

wolverine.c: Wolverine Wolverene { Wol`ver*ene", Wol`ver*ine" } (?), n. [From Wolf, with a dim suffix; prob. so called from its supposed wolfish qualities.] 1. (Zool.) A carnivorous mammal (Gulo gulo formerly Gulo luscus), of the weasel family Mustelidae, about the size of a large badger; called also glutton and carcajou. It is a native of the northern parts of America, Europe, and Asia.
Wolverine State Wol`ver*ine" State. Michigan; -- a nickname.

woman.c: Woman Wom"an (?), n.; pl. Women (#). [OE. woman, womman, wumman, wimman, wifmon, AS. wīfmann, wīmmann; wīf woman, wife + mann a man. See Wife, and Man.]
Woman Wom"an, v. t. 1. To act the part of a woman in; -- with indefinite it. Daniel.

womanhood.c: Womanhood Wom"an*hood (?), n. 1. The state of being a woman; the distinguishing character or qualities of a woman, or of womankind.

womanish.c: Womanish Wom"an*ish (?), a. Suitable to a woman, having the qualities of a woman; effeminate; not becoming a man; -- usually in a reproachful sense. See the Note under Effeminate. “ Thy tears are womanish.” Shak. “ Womanish entreaties.” Macaulay.

womanize.c: Womanize Wom"an*ize (?), v. t. To make like a woman; to make effeminate. [Obs.] V. Knox.

womankind.c: Womankind Wom"an*kind` (?), n. The females of the human race; women, collectively.

womanless.c: Womanless Wom"an*less, a. Without a woman or women.

womanlike.c: Womanlike Wom"an*like (?), a. Like a woman; womanly.

womanliness.c: Womanliness Wom"an*li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being womanly.

womanly.c: Womanly Wom"an*ly, a. Becoming a woman; feminine; as, womanly behavior. Arbuthnot.
Womanly Wom"an*ly, adv. In the manner of a woman; with the grace, tenderness, or affection of a woman. Gascoigne.

womans.c: Woman's Christian Temperance Union Woman's Christian Temperance Union. An association of women formed in the United States in 1874, for the advancement of temperance by organizing preventive, educational, evangelistic, social, and legal work. It is also known as the Women's Christian Temperance Union and by its acronym WCTU or W.C.T.U.. It was one of the political forces leading to passage of the constitutional amendment, later repealed, which prohibited the sale of alcoholic beverages.

womb.c: Womb Womb (wōom), n. [OE. wombe, wambe, AS. wamb, womb; akin to D. wam belly, OS. & OHG. wamba, G. wamme, wampe, Icel. vömb, Sw. våmb, Dan. vom, Goth. wamba.] 1. The belly; the abdomen. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Womb Womb, v. t. To inclose in a womb, or as in a womb; to breed or hold in secret. [Obs.] Shak.

wombat.c: Wombat Wom"bat (?), n. [From the native name, womback, wombach, in Australia.] (Zool.) Any one of three species of Australian burrowing marsupials of the genus Phascolomys, especially the common species (Phascolomys ursinus). They are nocturnal in their habits, and feed mostly on roots.

won.c: Won Won (?), imp. & p. p. of Win.
Won Won, v. i. [See 1st Wone.] To dwell or abide. [Obs. or Scot.] “ Where he wans in forest wild.” Milton.

wonder.c: Wonder Won"der (?), n. [OE. wonder, wunder, AS. wundor; akin to D. wonder, OS. wundar, OHG. wuntar, G. wunder, Icel. undr, Sw. & Dan. under, and perhaps to Gr.? to gaze at.]
Wonder Won"der, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wondered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wondering.] [AS. wundrian.]

wondered.c: Wondered Won"dered (?), a. Having performed wonders; able to perform wonderful things. [Obs.] Shak.

wonderful.c: Wonderful Won"der*ful (?), a. Adapted to excite wonder or admiration; surprising; strange; astonishing.

wonderingly.c: Wonderingly Won"der*ing*ly, adv. In a wondering manner.

wonderland.c: Wonderland Won"der*land` (?), n. A land full of wonders, or marvels. M. Arnold.

wonderly.c: Wonderly Won"der*ly, adv. [AS. wundorlice.] Wonderfully; wondrously. [Obs.] Chaucer.

wonderment.c: Wonderment Won"der*ment (?), n. Surprise; astonishment; a wonderful appearance; a wonder. Bacon.

wonderstruck.c: Wonderstruck Won"der*struck` (?), a. Struck with wonder, admiration, or surprise. Dryden.

wonderwork.c: Wonderwork Won"der*work` (?), n. [AS. wundorweorc.] A wonderful work or act; a prodigy; a miracle.

wonderworker.c: Wonder-worker Won"der-work`er (?), n. One who performs wonders, or miracles.

wonderworking.c: Wonder-working Won"der-work`ing, a. Doing wonders or surprising things.

wondrous.c: Wondrous Won"drous (?), adv. [OE. wonders, adv. (later also adj.). See Wonder, n., and cf. -wards.] In a wonderful or surprising manner or degree; wonderfully.
Wondrous Won"drous, a. Wonderful; astonishing; admirable; marvelous; such as excite surprise and astonishment; strange.

wone.c: Wone Wone (?), v. i. [OE. wonen, wunen, wonien, wunien, AS. wunian.????. See Wont, a.] To dwell; to abide. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.
Wone Wone, n. [OE. See Wone, v. i., Wont, a.]

wong.c: Wong Wong (?), n. [AS. wang, wong.] A field. [Obs.] Spelman. “Woods and wonges.” Havelok the Dane.

wont.c: Won't Won't (?). A colloquial contraction of woll not. Will not. See Will.

Wont Wont (?), a. [For woned, p. p. of won, wone, to dwell, AS. wunian; akin to D. wonen, OS. wun?n, OHG, won?n, G. wohnen, and AS. wund, gewuna, custom, habit; orig. probably, to take pleasure; cf. Icel. una to dwell, to enjoy, Goth. wunan to rejoice (in unwunands sad); and akin to Skr. van to like, to wish.????. Cf. Wean, Win.] Using or doing customarily; accustomed; habituated; used. “As he was wont to go.” Chaucer.
Wont Wont, n. Custom; habit; use; usage.
Wont Wont, v. i. [imp. Wont, p. p. Wont, or Wonted; p. pr. & vb. n. Wonting.] To be accustomed or habituated; to be used.
Wont Wont, v. t. To accustom; -- used reflexively.

wontedness.c: Wontedness Wont"ed*ness, n. The quality or state of being accustomed. [R.] Eikon Basilike.

woo.c: Woo Woo (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wooed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wooing.] [OE. wowen, wo?en, AS. w?gian, fr. w?h bent, crooked, bad; akin to OS. wāh evil, Goth. unwahs blameless, Skr. va?c to waver, and perhaps to E. vaccilate.]
Woo Woo, v. i. To court; to make love. Dryden.

wood.c: Wood Wood (wŏod), a. [OE. wod, AS. wōd; akin to OHG. wuot, Icel. ōðr, Goth. wōds, D. woede madness, G. wuth, wut, also to AS. wōð song, Icel. ōðr, L. vates a seer, a poet. Cf. Wednesday.] Mad; insane; possessed; rabid; furious; frantic. [Obs.] [Written also wode.]
Wood Wood, v. i. To grow mad; to act like a madman; to mad. Chaucer.
Wood Wood, n. [OE. wode, wude, AS. wudu, wiodu; akin to OHG. witu, Icel. vi?r, Dan. & Sw. ved wood, and probably to Ir. & Gael. fiodh, W. gwydd trees, shrubs.]
Wood Wood (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wooded; p. pr. & vb. n. Wooding.] To supply with wood, or get supplies of wood for; as, to wood a steamboat or a locomotive.
Wood Wood (?), v. i. To take or get a supply of wood.
Wood hyacinth Wood hyacinth. A European squill (Scilla nonscripta) having a scape bearing a raceme of drooping blue, purple, white, or sometimes pink, bell-shaped flowers.

Wood partridge Wood partridge. (a) Any of several small partridges of Java, Sumatra, Borneo, and neighboring regions belonging to the genera Caloperdix, Rollulus, and Melanoperdix. (b) The Canada grouse. [Local, U. S.]

Wood tick Wood" tick` (?). (Zool.) Any one of several species of ticks of the genus Ixodes whose young cling to bushes, but quickly fasten themselves upon the bodies of any animal with which they come in contact. When they attach themselves to the human body they often produce troublesome sores. The common species of the Northern United States is Ixodes unipunctata.

woodbine.c: Woodbine Wood"bine` (?), n. [AS. wudubind black ivy; -- so named as binding about trees. See Wood, and Bind, v. t.] (Bot.) (a) A climbing plant having flowers of great fragrance (Lonicera Periclymenum); the honeysuckle. (b) The Virginia creeper. See Virginia creeper, under Virginia. [Local, U. S.]

woodbound.c: Wood-bound Wood"-bound` (?), a. Incumbered with tall, woody hedgerows.

woodburytype.c: Woodbury-type Wood"bur*y-type` (?), n. [After the name of the inventor, W. Woodbury.]

woodchat.c: Woodchat Wood"chat` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) Any one of several species of Asiatic singing birds belonging to the genera Ianthia and Larvivora. They are closely allied to the European robin. The males are usually bright blue above, and more or less red or rufous beneath. (b) A European shrike (Enneoctonus rufus). In the male the head and nape are rufous red; the back, wings, and tail are black, varied with white.

woodchuck.c: Woodchuck Wood"chuck` (?), n. 1. (Zool.) A common large North American marmot (Arctomys monax). It is usually reddish brown, more or less grizzled with gray. It makes extensive burrows, and is often injurious to growing crops. Called also ground hog.

woodcraft.c: Woodcraft Wood"craft` (?), n. Skill and practice in anything pertaining to the woods, especially in shooting, and other sports in the woods.

woodcut.c: Woodcut Wood"cut` (?), n. An engraving on wood; also, a print from it. Same as Wood cut, under Wood.

woodcutter.c: Woodcutter Wood"cut`ter (?), n. 1. A person who cuts wood.

woodcutting.c: Woodcutting Wood"cut`ting, n. 1. The act or employment of cutting wood or timber.

wooded.c: Wooded Wood"ed, a. Supplied or covered with wood, or trees; as, land wooded and watered.

wooden.c: Wooden Wood"en (?), a. 1. Made or consisting of wood; pertaining to, or resembling, wood; as, a wooden box; a wooden leg; a wooden wedding.

woodenly.c: Woodenly Wood"en*ly (?), adv. Clumsily; stupidly; blockishly. R. North.

woodenness.c: Woodenness Wood"en*ness, n. Quality of being wooden; clumsiness; stupidity; blockishness.

woodhacker.c: Woodhacker Woodhack { Wood"hack` (?), Wood"hack`er (?), } n. (Zool.) The yaffle. [Prov. Eng.]

woodhole.c: Woodhole Wood"hole` (?), n. A place where wood is stored.

woodhouse.c: Woodhouse Wood"house` (?), n. A house or shed in which wood is stored, and sheltered from the weather.

woodiness.c: Woodiness Wood"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being woody. Evelyn.

woodland.c: Woodland Wood"land (?), n. Land covered with wood or trees; forest; land on which trees are allowed to grow, either for fuel or timber.
Woodland Wood"land (?), a. Of or pertaining to woods or woodland; living in the forest; sylvan.

woodlander.c: Woodlander Wood"land*er (?), n. A dweller in a woodland.

woodlayer.c: Wood-layer Wood"-lay`er (?), n. (Bot.) A young oak, or other timber plant, laid down in a hedge among the whitethorn or other plants used in hedges.

woodless.c: Woodless Wood"less, a. Having no wood; destitute of wood. Mitford. -- Wood"less*ness, n.

woodly.c: Woodly Wood"ly, adv. In a wood, mad, or raving manner; madly; furiously. [Obs.] Chaucer.

woodman.c: Woodman Wood"man (?), n.; pl. Woodmen (?). [Written also woodsman.]

woodness.c: Woodness Wood"ness, n. [From Wood mad.] Anger; madness; insanity; rage. [Obs.] Spenser.

woodnote.c: Wood-note Wood"-note` (?), n. [Wood, n. + note.] A wild or natural note, as of a forest bird. [R.]

woodpecker.c: Woodpecker Wood"peck`er (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of scansorial birds belonging to Picus and many allied genera of the family Picidae.

woodrock.c: Woodrock Wood"rock` (?), n. (Min.) A compact woodlike variety of asbestus.

woodroof.c: Woodroof Woodruff { Wood"ruff` (?), Wood"roof` (?), } n. [AS. wudurofe. See Wood, n., and cf. Ruff a plaited collar.] (Bot.) A little European herb (Asperula odorata) having a pleasant taste. It is sometimes used for flavoring wine. See Illust. of Whorl.

woodsare.c: Wood-sare Wood"-sare` (?), n. [Wood + Prov. E. sare for sore.] (Bot.) A kind of froth seen on herbs. [Obs.]

woodsere.c: Wood-sere Wood"-sere` (?), n. The time when there no sap in the trees; the winter season. [Written also wood-seer.] [Obs.] Tusser.

woodsman.c: Woodsman Woods"man (?), n.; pl. Woodsmen (?). A woodman; especially, one who lives in the forest.

woods.c: Wood's metal Wood's" met"al (?). A fusible alloy consisting of one or two parts of cadmium, two parts of tin, four of lead, with seven or eight part of bismuth. It melts at from 66° to 71° C. See Fusible metal, under Fusible.

woodstone.c: Woodstone Wood"stone` (?), n. (Min.) A striped variety of hornstone, resembling wood in appearance.

woodsy.c: Woodsy Woods"y (?), a. Of or pertaining to the woods or forest. [Colloq. U. S.]

woodwall.c: Woodwall Wood"wall` (?), n. (Zool.) The yaffle. [Written also woodwale, and woodwele.]

woodward.c: Woodward Wood"ward` (?), n. (Eng. Forest Law) An officer of the forest, whose duty it was to guard the woods.

woodwardia.c: Woodwardia Wood*war"di*a (?), n. [NL. After Thomas J. Woodward, an English botanist.] (Bot.) A genus of ferns, one species of which (Woodwardia radicans) is a showy plant in California, the Azores, etc.

woodwaxen.c: Wood-waxen Wood-wax Wood-wash { Wood"-wash` (?), Wood"-wax` (?), Wood"-wax`en (?), } n. [AS. wuduweaxe.] (Bot.) Same as Woadwaxen.

woodwork.c: Woodwork Wood"work` (?), n. Work made of wood; that part of any structure which is wrought of wood.

woodworm.c: Woodworm Wood"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) See Wood worm, under Wood.

woody.c: Woody Wood"y (?), a. 1. Abounding with wood or woods; as, woody land. “The woody wilderness.” Bryant.

wooer.c: Wooer Woo"er (?), n. [AS. wōgere. See Woo, v. t.] One who wooes; one who courts or solicits in love; a suitor. “A thriving wooer.” Gibber.

woof.c: Woof Woof (wōof), n. [OE. oof, AS. ōwef, ōweb, āweb; on, an, on + wef, web, fr. wefan to weave. The initial w is due to the influence of E. weave. See On, Weave, and cf. Abb.]

woofell.c: Woofell Woo"fell (?), n. (Zool.) The European blackbird. “The woofell near at hand that hath a golden bill.” Drayton.

woofy.c: Woofy Woof"y (?), a. Having a close texture; dense; as, a woofy cloud. J. Baillie.

wooingly.c: Wooingly Woo"ing*ly (?), adv. In a wooing manner; enticingly; with persuasiveness. Shak.

wook.c: Wook Wook" (wōk), obs. imp. of Wake. Woke. Chaucer.

wool.c: Wool Wool (wŏol), n. [OE. wolle, wulle, AS. wull; akin to D. wol, OHG. wolla, G. wolle, Icel. & Sw. ull, Dan. uld, Goth, wulla, Lith. vilna, Russ. volna, L. vellus, Skr. ūrṇā wool, vṛ to cover. √146, 287. Cf. Flannel, Velvet.]

woold.c: Woold Woold (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Woolded; p. pr. & vb. n. Woolding.] [D. woelen, bewoelen; akin to G. wuhlen, bewuhlen. √146.] (Naut.) To wind, or wrap; especially, to wind a rope round, as a mast or yard made of two or more pieces, at the place where it has been fished or scarfed, in order to strengthen it.

woolder.c: Woolder Woold"er (?), n. 1. (Naut.) A stick used to tighten the rope in woolding.

woolding.c: Woolding Woold"ing, n. (Naut.) (a) The act of winding or wrapping anything with a rope, as a mast. (b) A rope used for binding masts and spars.

wooldyed.c: Wool-dyed Wool"-dyed` (?), a. Dyed before being made into cloth, in distinction from piece-dyed; ingrain.

wooled.c: Wooled Wooled (?), a. Having (such) wool; as, a fine-wooled sheep.

woolen.c: Woolen Wool"en (?), a. [OE. wollen; cf. AS. wyllen. See Wool.] [Written also woollen.]
Woolen Wool"en, n. [Written also woollen.] Cloth made of wool; woollen goods.

woolenet.c: Woolenet Wool`en*et" (?), n. A thin, light fabric of wool. [Written also woollenet, woolenette, and woollenette.]

woolert.c: Woolert Woo"lert (?), n. (Zool.) The barn owl. [Prov. Eng.] [Written also oolert, and owlerd.]

woolfell.c: Woolfell Wool"fell` (?), n. [Wool + fell a skin.] A skin with the wool; a skin from which the wool has not been sheared or pulled. [Written also woolfel.]

woolgathering.c: Woolgathering Wool"gath`er*ing (?), a. Indulging in a vagrant or idle exercise of the imagination; roaming upon a fruitless quest; idly fanciful.
Woolgathering Wool"gath`er*ing, n. Indulgence in idle imagination; a foolish or useless pursuit or design.

woolgrower.c: Woolgrower Wool"grow`er (?), n. One who raises sheep for the production of wool. -- Wool"grow`ing, n.

woolhall.c: Wool-hall Wool"-hall` (?), n. A trade market in the woolen districts. [Eng.]

woolliness.c: Woolliness Wool"li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being woolly.

woolly.c: Woolly Wool"ly, a. 1. Consisting of wool; as, a woolly covering; a woolly fleece.

woolman.c: Woolman Wool"man (?), n.; pl. Woolmen (?). One who deals in wool.

woolpack.c: Woolpack Wool"pack` (?), n. A pack or bag of wool weighing two hundred and forty pounds.

woolsack.c: Woolsack Wool"sack` (?), n. A sack or bag of wool; specifically, the seat of the lord chancellor of England in the House of Lords, being a large, square sack of wool resembling a divan in form.

woolstock.c: Woolstock Wool"stock` (?), n. A heavy wooden hammer for milling cloth.

woolward.c: Woolward Wool"ward (?), adv. [Wool + -ward.] In wool; with woolen raiment next the skin. [Obs.]

woolwardgoing.c: Woolward-going Wool"ward-go`ing (?), n. A wearing of woolen clothes next the skin as a matter of penance. [Obs.]

wootz.c: Wootz Wootz (wōots), n. [Perhaps a corruption of Canarese ukku steel.] A species of steel imported from the East Indies, valued for making edge tools; Indian steel. It has in combination a minute portion of alumina and silica.

wopen.c: Wopen Wo"pen (?), obs. p. p. of Weep. Wept. Chaucer.

word.c: Word Word (?), n. [AS. word; akin to OFries. & OS. word, D. woord, G. wort, Icel. orð, Sw. & Dan. ord, Goth. waúrd, OPruss. wirds, Lith. vardas a name, L. verbum a word; or perhaps to Gr. "rh`twr an orator. Cf. Verb.]
Word Word, v. i. To use words, as in discussion; to argue; to dispute. [R.]
Word Word, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Worded; p. pr. & vb. n. Wording.]

Word method Word method. (Education) A method of teaching reading in which words are first taken as single ideograms and later analyzed into their phonetic and alphabetic elements; -- contrasted with alphabet method and sentence method.

wordbook.c: Wordbook Word"book` (?), n. [Cf. D. woordenboek, G. wörterbuch.] A collection of words; a vocabulary; a dictionary; a lexicon.

wordcatcher.c: Word-catcher Word"-catch`er (?), n. One who cavils at words.

wordily.c: Wordily Word"i*ly (?), adv. In a wordy manner.

wordiness.c: Wordiness Word"i*ness, n. The quality or state of being wordy, or abounding with words; verboseness. Jeffrey.

wording.c: Wording Word"ing, n. The act or manner of expressing in words; style of expression; phrasing.

wordish.c: Wordish Word"ish, a. Respecting words; full of words; wordy. [R.] Sir P. Sidney. -- Word"ish*ness, n.

wordle.c: Wordle Wor"dle (?), n. One of several pivoted pieces forming the throat of an adjustable die used in drawing wire, lead pipe, etc. Knight.

wordless.c: Wordless Word"less (?), a. Not using words; not speaking; silent; speechless. Shak.

wordplay.c: Wordplay Word"play` (?), n. A more or less subtle playing upon the meaning of words.

wordsman.c: Wordsman Words"man (?), n. One who deals in words, or in mere words; a verbalist. [R.] “Some speculative wordsman.” H. Bushnell.

work.c: Work Work (wûrk), n. [OE. work, werk, weorc, AS. weorc, worc; akin to OFries. werk, wirk, OS., D., & G. werk, OHG. werc, werah, Icel. & Sw. verk, Dan. værk, Goth. gawaúrki, Gr. 'e`rgon, ϝe`rgon, work, "re`zein to do, 'o`rganon an instrument, 'o`rgia secret rites, Zend verez to work. √145. Cf. Bulwark, Energy, Erg, Georgic, Liturgy, Metallurgy, Organ, Orgy, Surgeon, Wright.]

Work Work (wûrk), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Worked (wûrkt), or Wrought (rät); p. pr. & vb. n. Working.] [AS. wyrcean (imp. worthe, wrohte, p. p. geworht, gewroht); akin to OFries. werka, wirka, OS. wirkian, D. werken, G. wirken, Icel. verka, yrkja, orka, Goth. waúrkjan. √145. See Work, n.]
Work Work (wûrk), v. t. 1. To labor or operate upon; to give exertion and effort to; to prepare for use, or to utilize, by labor.

workable.c: Workable Work"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being worked, or worth working; as, a workable mine; workable clay.

workbag.c: Workbag Work"bag` (?), n. A bag for holding implements or materials for work; especially, a reticule, or bag for holding needlework, and the like.

workbasket.c: Workbasket Work"bas`ket (?), n. A basket for holding materials for needlework, or the like.

workbench.c: Workbench Work"bench` (?), n. A bench on which work is performed, as in a carpenter's shop.

workbox.c: Workbox Work"box` (?), n. A box for holding instruments or materials for work.

workday.c: Workday Work"day` (?), n. & a. [AS. weorcdæg.] A day on which work is performed, as distinguished from Sunday, festivals, etc., a working day.

worker.c: Worker Work"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, works; a laborer; a performer; as, a worker in brass.

workfellow.c: Workfellow Work"fel`low (?), n. One engaged in the same work with another; a companion in work.

workful.c: Workful Work"ful (?), a. Full of work; diligent. [R.]

workingday.c: Working-day Work"ing-day (?), a. Pertaining to, or characteristic of, working days, or workdays; everyday; hence, plodding; hard-working.

workingman.c: Workingman Work"ing*man (?), n.; pl. Workingmen (?). A laboring man; a man who earns his daily support by manual labor.

workless.c: Workless Work"less, a. 1. Without work; not laboring; as, many people were still workless.

workmanlike.c: Workmanlike Work"man*like` (?), a. Becoming a workman, especially a skillful one; skillful; well performed.

workmanly.c: Workmanly Work"man*ly, a. Becoming a skillful workman; skillful; well performed; workmanlike.
Workmanly Work"man*ly, adv. In a skillful manner; in a manner becoming a skillful workman. Shak.

workmanship.c: Workmanship Work"man*ship, n. 1. The art or skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making anything.

workmaster.c: Workmaster Work"mas`ter (?), n. The performer of any work; a master workman. [R.] Spenser.

workmens.c: Workmen's compensation act Workmen's compensation act. (Law) A statute fixing the compensation that a workman may recover from an employer in case of accident, esp. the British act of 6 Edw. VII. c. 58 (1906) giving to a workman, except in certain cases of “serious and willful misconduct,” a right against his employer to a certain compensation on the mere occurrence of an accident where the common law gives the right only for negligence of the employer.

workroom.c: Workroom Work"room` (?), n. Any room or apartment used especially for labor.

workshop.c: Workshop Work"shop` (?), n. A shop where any manufacture or handiwork is carried on.

worktable.c: Worktable Work"ta`ble (?), n. A table for holding working materials and implements; esp., a small table with drawers and other conveniences for needlework, etc.

workwise.c: Workwise Workways { Work"ways` (?), Work"wise` (?) }, adv. In a working position or manner; as, a T rail placed workwise, i.e., resting on its base.

workwoman.c: Workwoman Work"wom`an (?), n.; pl. Workwomen (?), n. A woman who performs any work; especially, a woman skilled in needlework.

workyday.c: Workyday Work"y*day` (?), n. [See Workday, Workingday.] A week day or working day, as distinguished from Sunday or a holiday. Also used adjectively. [Written also workiday, and workaday.] [Obs. or Colloq.]

world.c: World World (?), n. [OE. world, werld, weorld, weoreld, AS. weorold, worold; akin to OS. werold, D. wereld, OHG. weralt, worolt, werolt, werlt, G. welt, Icel. veröld, Sw. verld, Dan. verden; properly, the age of man, lifetime, humanity; AS. wer a man + a word akin to E. old; cf. AS. yld lifetime, age, ylde men, humanity. Cf. Werewolf, Old.]

worldliness.c: Worldliness World"li*ness (?), n. The quality of being worldly; a predominant passion for obtaining the good things of this life; covetousness; addictedness to gain and temporal enjoyments; worldly-mindedness.

worldling.c: Worldling World"ling (?), [World + -ling.] A person whose soul is set upon gaining temporal possessions; one devoted to this world and its enjoyments.

worldly.c: Worldly World"ly, adv. With relation to this life; in a worldly manner.

worldlyminded.c: Worldly-minded World"ly-mind`ed (?), a. Devoted to worldly interests; mindful of the affairs of the present life, and forgetful of those of the future; loving and pursuing this world's goods, to the exclusion of piety and attention to spiritual concerns. -- World"ly*mind`ed*ness, n.

worldlywise.c: Worldly-wise World"ly-wise` (?), a. Wise in regard to things of this world. Bunyan.

worldwide.c: World-wide World"-wide` (?), a. Extended throughout the world; as, world-wide fame. Tennyson.

worm.c: Worm Worm (wûrm), n. [OE. worm, wurm, AS. wyrm; akin to D. worm, OS. & G. wurm, Icel. ormr, Sw. & Dan. orm, Goth. waúrms, L. vermis, Gr.? a wood worm. Cf. Vermicelli, Vermilion, Vermin.]
Worm Worm (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wormed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Worming.] To work slowly, gradually, and secretly.
Worm Worm, v. t. 1. To effect, remove, drive, draw, or the like, by slow and secret means; -- often followed by out.

wormeaten.c: Worm-eaten Worm"-eat`en (?), a. 1. Eaten, or eaten into, by a worm or by worms; as, worm-eaten timber.

wormed.c: Wormed Wormed (?), a. Penetrated by worms; injured by worms; worm-eaten; as, wormed timber.

wormhole.c: Wormhole Worm"hole` (?), n. A burrow made by a worm.

wormian.c: Wormian Wor"mi*an (?), a. (Anat.) Discovered or described by Olanus Wormius, a Danish anatomist.

wormseed.c: Wormseed Worm"seed` (?), n. (Bot.) Any one of several plants, as Artemisia santonica, and Chenopodium anthelminticum, whose seeds have the property of expelling worms from the stomach and intestines.

wormshaped.c: Worm-shaped Worm"-shaped` (?), a. Shaped like a worm;?hick and almost cylindrical, but variously curved or bent; as, a worm-shaped root.

wormshell.c: Worm-shell Worm"-shell` (?), n. (Zool.) Any species of Vermetus.

wormwood.c: Wormwood Worm"wood (?), n. [AS. werm?d, akin to OHG. wermuota, wormuota, G. wermuth, wermut; of uncertain origin.]

wornout.c: Worn-out Worn"-out` (?), a. Consumed, or rendered useless, by wearing; as, worn-out garments.

worrel.c: Worrel Worral { Wor"ral (?), Wor"rel (?), } n. (Zool.) An Egyptian fork-tongued lizard, about four feet long when full grown.

worriment.c: Worriment Wor"ri*ment (?), n. [See Worry.] Trouble; anxiety; worry. [Colloq. U. S.]

worrisome.c: Worrisome Wor"ri*some (?), a. Inclined to worry or fret; also, causing worry or annoyance.

worrit.c: Worrit Wor"rit (?), v. t. To worry; to annoy. [Illiterate]

worry.c: Worry Wor"ry (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Worried (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Worrying.] [OE. worowen, wirien, to strangle, AS. wyrgan in āwyrgan; akin to D. worgen, wurgen, to strangle, OHG. wurgen, G. würgen, Lith. verszti, and perhaps to E. wring.]
Worry Wor"ry (?), v. i. To feel or express undue care and anxiety; to manifest disquietude or pain; to be fretful; to chafe; as, the child worries; the horse worries.

Worry Wor"ry, n.; pl. Worries (?). A state of undue solicitude; a state of disturbance from care and anxiety; vexation; anxiety; fret; as, to be in a worry. “The whir and worry of spindle and of loom.” Sir T. Browne.
