worryingly.c: Worryingly Wor"ry*ing*ly, adv. In a worrying manner.

worse.c: Worse Worse (?), a., compar. of Bad. [OE. werse, worse, wurse, AS. wiersa, wyrsa, a comparative with no corresponding positive; akin to OS. wirsa, OFries. wirra, OHG. wirsiro, Icel. verri, Sw. värre, Dan. värre, Goth. waírsiza, and probably to OHG. werran to bring into confusion, E. war, and L. verrere to sweep, sweep along. As bad has no comparative and superlative, worse and worst are used in lieu of them, although etymologically they have no relation to bad.] Bad, ill, evil, or corrupt, in a greater degree; more bad or evil; less good; specifically, in poorer health; more sick; -- used both in a physical and moral sense.
Worse Worse, n. 1. Loss; disadvantage; defeat. “Judah was put to the worse before Israel.” Kings xiv. 12.

Worse Worse, adv. [AS. wiers, wyrs; akin to OS. & OHG. wirs, Icel. verr, Goth, waírs; a comparative adverb with no corresponding positive. See Worse, a.] In a worse degree; in a manner more evil or bad.
Worse Worse, v. t. [OE. wursien, AS. wyrsian to become worse.] To make worse; to put disadvantage; to discomfit; to worst. See Worst, v.

worsen.c: Worsen Wors"en (?), v. t. 1. To make worse; to deteriorate; to impair.
Worsen Wors"en, v. i. To grow or become worse. De Quincey.

worship.c: Worship Wor"ship (?), n. [OE. worshipe, wurðscipe, AS. weorðscipe; weorð worth + -scipe -ship. See Worth, a., and -ship.]
Worship Wor"ship, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Worshiped (?) Worshipped; p. pr. & vb. n. Worshiping or Worshipping.]
Worship Wor"ship (?), v. i. To perform acts of homage or adoration; esp., to perform religious service.

worshipability.c: Worshipability Wor`ship*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being worthy to be worshiped. [R.] Coleridge.

worshipable.c: Worshipable Wor"ship*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being worshiped; worthy of worship. [R.] Carlyle.

worshiper.c: Worshiper Wor"ship*er (?), n. One who worships; one who pays divine honors to any being or thing; one who adores. [Written also worshipper.]

worshipful.c: Worshipful Wor"ship*ful (?), a. Entitled to worship, reverence, or high respect; claiming respect; worthy of honor; -- often used as a term of respect, sometimes ironically. “This is worshipful society.” Shak.

worst.c: Worst Worst (?), a., superl. of Bad. [OE. werst, worste, wurste, AS. wyrst, wierst, wierrest. See Worse, a.] Bad, evil, or pernicious, in the highest degree, whether in a physical or moral sense. See Worse. “Heard so oft in worst extremes.” Milton.
Worst Worst, n. That which is most bad or evil; the most severe, pernicious, calamitous, or wicked state or degree.

Worst Worst, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Worsted; p. pr. & vb. n. Worsting.] [See Worse, v. t. & a.] To gain advantage over, in contest or competition; to get the better of; to defeat; to overthrow; to discomfit.
Worst Worst, v. i. To grow worse; to deteriorate. [R.] “Every face... worsting.” Jane Austen.

worsted.c: Worsted Worst"ed (?; 277), n. [From Worsted, now spelled Worstead, a town in Norfolk, England; for Worthstead. See Worth, n., and Stead.]

wort.c: Wort Wort (?), n. [OE. wort, wurt, AS. wyrt herb, root; akin to OS. wurt, G. wurz, Icel. jurt, urt, Dan. urt, Sw. ört, Goth. waúrts a root, L. radix, Gr.? a root,? a branch, young shoot,? a branch, and E. root, n. Cf. Licorice, Orchard, Radish, Root, n., Whortleberry, Wort an infusion of malt.]

Wort Wort (?), n. [OE. worte, wurte, AS. wyrte; akin to OD. wort, G. würze, bierwürze, Icel. virtr, Sw. vört. See Wort an herb.] An infusion of malt which is unfermented, or is in the act of fermentation; the sweet infusion of malt, which ferments and forms beer; hence, any similar liquid in a state of incipient fermentation.

worth.c: Worth Worth (?), v. i. [OE. worthen, wurþen, to become, AS. weorðan; akin to OS. werðan, D. worden, G. werden, OHG. werdan, Icel. verða, Sw. varda, Goth. waírpan, L. vertere to turn, Skr. vṛt, v. i., to turn, to roll, to become. √143. Cf. Verse, -ward, Weird.] To be; to become; to betide; -- now used only in the phrases, woe worth the day, woe worth the man, etc., in which the verb is in the imperative, and the nouns day, man, etc., are in the dative. Woe be to the day, woe be to the man, etc., are equivalent phrases.

Worth Worth, a. [OE. worth, wurþ, AS. weorð, wurE; akin to OFries. werth, OS. werð, D. waard, OHG. werd, G. wert, werth, Icel. verðr, Sw. värd, Dan. værd, Goth. waírps, and perhaps to E. wary. Cf. Stalwart, Ware an article of merchandise, Worship.]
Worth Worth, n. [OE. worth, wurþ, AS. weorð, wurð; weorð, wurð, adj. See Worth, a.]

worthful.c: Worthful Worth"ful (?), a. Full of worth; worthy; deserving. Marston.

worthily.c: Worthily Wor"thi*ly (?), adv. In a worthy manner; excellently; deservedly; according to merit; justly; suitably; becomingly.

worthiness.c: Worthiness Wor"thi*ness, n. The quality or state of being worthy; desert; merit; excellence; dignity; virtue; worth.

worthless.c: Worthless Worth"less (?), a. [AS. weorðleás.] Destitute of worth; having no value, virtue, excellence, dignity, or the like; undeserving; valueless; useless; vile; mean; as, a worthless garment; a worthless ship; a worthless man or woman; a worthless magistrate.

worthwhile.c: worthwhile worthwhile, adj. Worth the time or effort spent. See worth while.

worthy.c: Worthy Wor"thy (?), a. [Compar. Worthier (?); superl. Worthiest.] [OE. worthi, wurþi, from worth, wurþ, n.; cf. Icel. verðugr, D. waardig, G. würdig, OHG. wirdīg. See Worth, n.]

Worthy Wor"thy, n.; pl. Worthies (?). A man of eminent worth or value; one distinguished for useful and estimable qualities; a person of conspicuous desert; -- much used in the plural; as, the worthies of the church; political worthies; military worthies.
Worthy Wor"thy, v. t. To render worthy; to exalt into a hero. [Obs.] Shak.

wost.c: Wost Wost (?), 2d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know. [Obs.] Spenser.

wot.c: Wot Wot (?), 1st & 3d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know. See the Note under Wit, v. [Obs.]

wottest.c: Wottest Wotest { Wot"est (?), Wot"test, } 2d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know. [Obs.]

wotteth.c: Wotteth Woteth { Wot"eth (?), Wot"teth, } 3d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know. [Obs.] “He wotteth neither what he babbleth, nor what he meaneth.” Tyndale.

woul.c: Woul Woul (?), v. i. To howl. [Obs.] Wyclif.

would.c: Would Would (?), imp. of Will. [OE. & AS. wolde. See Will, v. t.] Commonly used as an auxiliary verb, either in the past tense or in the conditional or optative present. See 2d & 3d Will.

wouldbe.c: Would-be Would"-be` (?), a. Desiring or professing to be; vainly pretending to be; as, a would-be poet.

woulding.c: Woulding Would"ing, n. Emotion of desire; inclination; velleity. [Obs.] Hammond.

woulfe.c: Woulfe bottle Woulfe" bot`tle (?), n. (Chem.) A kind of wash bottle with two or three necks; -- so called after the inventor, Peter Woulfe, an English chemist.

wound.c: Wound Wound (?), imp. & p. p. of Wind to twist, and Wind to sound by blowing.

Wound Wound (?; 277), n. [OE. wounde, wunde, AS. wund; akin to OFries. wunde, OS. wunda, D. wonde, OHG. wunta, G. wunde, Icel. und, and to AS., OS., & G. wund sore, wounded, OHG. wunt, Goth. wunds, and perhaps also to Goth. winnan to suffer, E. win. √140. Cf. Zounds.]
Wound Wound (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Wounding.] [AS. wundian. √140. See Wound, n.]

woundable.c: Woundable Wound"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being wounded; vulnerable. [R.] Fuller.

wounder.c: Wounder Wound"er (?), n. One who, or that which, wounds.

woundily.c: Woundily Wound"i*ly (?), adv. In a woundy manner; excessively; woundy. [Obs.]

woundless.c: Woundless Wound"less (?), a. Free from wound or hurt; exempt from being wounded; invulnerable. “Knights whose woundless armor rusts.” Spenser.

woundwort.c: Woundwort Wound"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) Any one of certain plants whose soft, downy leaves have been used for dressing wounds, as the kidney vetch, and several species of the labiate genus Stachys.

wouwou.c: Wou-wou Wou"-wou` (?), n. [So called from its cry.] (Zool.) The agile, or silvery, gibbon; -- called also camper. See Gibbon. [Written also wow-wow.]

wove.c: Wove Wove (?), p. pr. & rare vb. n. of Weave.

wowe.c: Wowe Wowe (?), v. t. & i. To woo. [Obs.] Chaucer.

wowf.c: Wowf Wowf (?), a. Disordered or unsettled in intellect; deranged. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

wox.c: Wox Wox (?), obs. imp. of Wax. Gower.

woxen.c: Woxen Wox"en (?), obs. p. p. of Wax. Chaucer.

wrack.c: Wrack Wrack (?), n. A thin, flying cloud; a rack.
Wrack Wrack, v. t. To rack; to torment. [R.]
Wrack Wrack, n. [OE. wrak wreck. See Wreck.]
Wrack Wrack, v. t. To wreck. [Obs.] Dryden.

wraith.c: Wraith Wraith (?), n. [Scot. wraith, warth; probably originally, a guardian angel, from Icel. vörðr a warden, guardian, akin to E. ward. See Ward a guard.]

wrangle.c: Wrangle Wran"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wrangled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wrangling (?).] [OE. wranglen to wrestle. See Wrong, Wring.]
Wrangle Wran"gle, v. t. To involve in a quarrel or dispute; to embroil. [R.] Bp. Sanderson.
Wrangle Wran"gle (?), n. An angry dispute; a noisy quarrel; a squabble; an altercation.

wrangler.c: Wrangler Wran"gler (?), n. 1. An angry disputant; one who disputes with heat or peevishness. “Noisy and contentious wranglers.” I. Watts.

wranglership.c: Wranglership Wran"gler*ship, n. The honor or position of being a wrangler at the University of Cambridge, England.

wranglesome.c: Wranglesome Wran"gle*some (?), a. Contentious; quarrelsome. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

wranny.c: Wranny Wrannock { Wran"nock (?), Wran"ny (?), } n. (Zool.) The common wren. [Prov. Eng.]

wrap.c: Wrap Wrap (?), v. t. [A corrupt spelling of rap.] To snatch up; transport; -- chiefly used in the p. p. wrapt.
Wrap Wrap, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wrapped (?) or Wrapt; p. pr. & vb. n. Wrapping.] [OE. wrappen, probably akin to E. warp. √144. Cf. Warp.]
Wrap Wrap, n. A wrapper; -- often used in the plural for blankets, furs, shawls, etc., used in riding or traveling.

wrappage.c: Wrappage Wrap"page (?; 48), n. 1. The act of wrapping.

wrapper.c: Wrapper Wrap"per (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, wraps.

wraprascal.c: Wraprascal Wrap"ras`cal (?), n. A kind of coarse upper coat, or overcoat, formerly worn.

wrasse.c: Wrasse Wrasse (?), n. [W. gwrachen.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous edible, marine, spiny-finned fishes of the genus Labrus, of which several species are found in the Mediterranean and on the Atlantic coast of Europe. Many of the species are bright-colored.

wrastle.c: Wrastle Wras"tle (?), v. i. [OE. wrastlen. See Wrestle.] To wrestle. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Colloq. U. S.]

wrath.c: Wrath Wrath (?; 277), n. [OE. wrathe, wraþþe, wrethe, wræððe, AS. wrǣððo, fr. wrāð wroth; akin to Icel. reiði wrath. See Wroth, a.]
Wrath Wrath, v. t. To anger; to enrage; -- also used impersonally. [Obs.] “I will not wrathen him.” Chaucer.

wrathful.c: Wrathful Wrath"ful (?), a. 1. Full of wrath; very angry; greatly incensed; ireful; passionate; as, a wrathful man.

wrathily.c: Wrathily Wrath"i*ly (?), adv. In a wrathy manner; very angrily; wrathfully. [Colloq.]

wrathless.c: Wrathless Wrath"less, a. Free from anger or wrath. Waller.

wraw.c: Wraw Wraw (?), a. [Cf. dial. Sw. vrå willful, disobedient.] Angry; vexed; wrathful. [Obs.]

wrawl.c: Wrawl Wrawl (räl), v. i. [Cf. Dan. vraale, Sw. vråla to brawl, to roar, Dan. vraal a bawling, roaring, vræle to cry, weep, whine.] To cry, as a cat; to waul. [Obs.] Spenser.

wrawness.c: Wrawness Wraw"ness (rä"nĕs), n. Peevishness; ill temper; anger. [Obs.] Chaucer.

wray.c: Wray Wray (rā), v. t. [AS. wr?gan to accuse. See Bewray.] To reveal; to disclose. [Obs.]

wreak.c: Wreak Wreak (rēk), v. i. To reck; to care. [Obs.] Shak.

Wreak Wreak (rēk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wreaked (rēkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Wreaking.] [OE. wreken to revenge, punish, drive out, AS. wrecan; akin to OFries. wreka, OS. wrekan to punish, D. wreken to avenge, G. rächen, OHG. rehhan, Icel. reka to drive, to take vengeance, Goth. wrikan to persecute, Lith. vargas distress, vargti to suffer distress, L. urgere to drive, urge, Gr. e'i`rgein to shut, Skr. vṛj to turn away. Cf. Urge, Wreck, Wretch.]
Wreak Wreak, n. [Cf. AS. wræc exile, persecution, misery. See Wreak, v. t.] Revenge; vengeance; furious passion; resentment. [Obs.] Shak. Spenser.

wreaken.c: Wreaken Wreak"en (?), obs. p. p. of Wreak. Chaucer.

wreakful.c: Wreakful Wreak"ful (?), a. Revengeful; angry; furious. [Obs.] -- Wreak"ful*ly, adv. [Obs.]

wreath.c: Wreath Wreath (?; 277), n.; pl. Wreaths (#). [OE. wrethe, AS. wrǣð a twisted band, fr. wrīðan to twist. See Writhe.]

wreathe.c: Wreathe Wreathe (?), v. t. [imp. Wreathed (?); p. p. Wreathed; Archaic Wreathen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wreathing.] [See Wreath, n.] [Written also wreath.]
Wreathe Wreathe, v. i. To be intewoven or entwined; to twine together; as, a bower of wreathing trees. Dryden.

wreathen.c: Wreathen Wreath"en (?), a. Twisted; made into a wreath. “Wreathen work of pure gold.” Ex. xxviii. 22.

wreathless.c: Wreathless Wreath"less (?), a. Destitute of a wreath.

wreathshell.c: Wreath-shell Wreath"-shell` (?), n. (Zool.) A marine shell of the genus Turbo. See Turbo.

wreathy.c: Wreathy Wreath"y (?), a. Wreathed; twisted; curled; spiral; also, full of wreaths. “Wreathy spires, and cochleary turnings about.” Sir T. Browne.

wreck.c: Wreck Wreck (?), v. t. & n. See 2d & 3d Wreak.

Wreck Wreck, n. [OE. wrak, AS. wræc exile, persecution, misery, from wrecan to drive out, punish; akin to D. wrak, adj., damaged, brittle, n., a wreck, wraken to reject, throw off, Icel. rek a thing drifted ashore, Sw. vrak refuse, a wreck, Dan. vrag. See Wreak, v. t., and cf. Wrack a marine plant.] [Written also wrack.]
Wreck Wreck (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wrecked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wrecking.]
Wreck Wreck, v. i. 1. To suffer wreck or ruin. Milton.

wreckage.c: Wreckage Wreck"age (?; 48), n. 1. The act of wrecking, or state of being wrecked.

wrecker.c: Wrecker Wreck"er (?), n. 1. One who causes a wreck, as by false lights, and the like.

wreckfish.c: Wreckfish Wreck"fish` (?), n. [So called because it often comes in with wreckage.] (Zool.) A stone bass.

wreckful.c: Wreckful Wreck"ful (?), a. Causing wreck; involving ruin; destructive. “By wreckful wind.” Spenser.

wrecking.c: Wrecking Wreck"ing, a. & n. from Wreck, v.

wreckmaster.c: Wreck-master Wreck"-mas`ter (?), n. A person appointed by law to take charge of goods, etc., thrown on shore after a shipwreck.

wreeke.c: Wreeke Wreke { Wreke (rēk), Wreeke }, v. t. See 2d Wreak. [Obs.]

wren.c: Wren Wren (rĕn), n. [OE. wrenne, AS. wrenna, wrænna, perhaps akin to wrǣne lascivious.]

wrench.c: Wrench Wrench (rĕnch), n. [OE. wrench deceit, AS. wrenc deceit, a twisting; akin to G. rank intrigue, crookedness, renken to bend, twist, and E. wring. √144. See Wring, and cf. Ranch, v. t.]
Wrench Wrench, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wrenched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wrenching.] [OE. wrenchen, AS. wrencan to deceive, properly, to twist, from wrenc guile, deceit, a twisting.????. See Wrench, n.]

wrest.c: Wrest Wrest (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wrested; p. pr. & vb. n. Wresting.] [OE. wresten, AS. wr?stan; akin to wr?? a twisted band, and wrī?n to twist. See Writhe.]
Wrest Wrest, n. 1. The act of wresting; a wrench; a violent twist; hence, distortion; perversion. Hooker.

wrestle.c: Wrestle Wres"tle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wrestled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wrestling (?).] [OE. wrestlen, wrastlen, AS. wr?stlian, freq. of wr?stan to wrest; akin to OD. wrastelen to wrestle. See Wrest, v. t.]
Wrestle Wres"tle, v. t. To wrestle with; to seek to throw down as in wrestling.
Wrestle Wres"tle, n. A struggle between two persons to see which will throw the other down; a bout at wrestling; a wrestling match; a struggle.

wrestler.c: Wrestler Wres"tler (?), n. [AS. wrǣstlere.] One who wrestles; one who is skillful in wrestling.

wrestling.c: Wrestling Wres"tling (?), n. Act of one who wrestles; specif., the sport consisting of the hand-to-hand combat between two unarmed contestants who seek to throw each other.

wretch.c: Wretch Wretch (?), n. [OE. wrecche, AS. wrecca, wræcca, an exile, a wretch, fr. wrecan to drive out, punish; properly, an exile, one driven out, akin to AS. wræc an exile, OS. wrekkio a stranger, OHG. reccheo an exile. See Wreak, v. t.]

wretched.c: Wretched Wretch"ed, a. 1. Very miserable; sunk in, or accompanied by, deep affliction or distress, as from want, anxiety, or grief; calamitous; woeful; very afflicting. “To what wretched state reserved!” Milton.

wretchedly.c: Wretchedly Wretch"ed*ly, adv. In a wretched manner; miserably; despicable.

wretchedness.c: Wretchedness Wretch"ed*ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being wretched; utter misery. Sir W. Raleigh.

wretchless.c: Wretchless Wretch"less, a. [See Reckless.] Reckless; hence, disregarded. [Obs.] -- Wretch"less*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Wretch"less*ness, n. [Obs.] Bk. of Com. Prayer.

wrey.c: Wrey Wrey (?), v. t. See Wray. [Obs.] Chaucer.

wrie.c: Wrie Wrie (?), a. & v. See Wry. [Obs.] Chaucer.

wrig.c: Wrig Wrig (?), v. i. To wriggle. [Obs.] Skelton.

wriggle.c: Wriggle Wrig"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Wriggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wriggling (?).] [Freq. of wrig, probably from OE. wrikken to move to and fro; cf. LG. wriggeln, D. wrikken, Sw. vricka, Dan. vrikke.] To move the body to and fro with short, writhing motions, like a worm; to squirm; to twist uneasily or quickly about.
Wriggle Wrig"gle, v. t. To move with short, quick contortions; to move by twisting and squirming; like a worm.
Wriggle Wrig"gle, a. Wriggling; frisky; pliant; flexible. [Obs.] “Their wriggle tails.” Spenser.
Wriggle Wrig"gle, n. Act of wriggling; a short or quick writhing motion or contortion.

wriggler.c: Wriggler Wrig"gler (?), n. One who, or that which, wriggles. Cowper.

wright.c: Wright Wright (?), n. [OE. wrighte, writhe, AS. wyrtha, fr. wyrcean to work. √145. See Work.] One who is engaged in a mechanical or manufacturing business; an artificer; a workman; a manufacturer; a mechanic; esp., a worker in wood; -- now chiefly used in compounds, as in millwright, wheelwright, etc.

wrightine.c: Wrightine Wright"ine (?), n. (Chem.) A rare alkaloid found in the bark of an East Indian apocynaceous tree (Wrightia antidysenterica), and extracted as a bitter white crystalline substance. It was formerly used as a remedy for diarrhœa. Called also conessine, and neriine.

wring.c: Wring Wring (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wrung (?), Obs. Wringed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wringing.] [OE. wringen, AS. wringan; akin to LG. & D. wringen, OHG. ringan to struggle, G. ringen, Sw. vränga to distort, Dan. vringle to twist. Cf. Wrangle, Wrench, Wrong.]
Wring Wring, v. i. To writhe; to twist, as with anguish.
Wring Wring, n. A writhing, as in anguish; a twisting; a griping. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

wringbolt.c: Wringbolt Wring"bolt`, n. (Shipbuilding) A bolt used by shipwrights, to bend and secure the planks against the timbers till they are fastened by bolts, spikes, or treenails; -- not to be confounded with ringbolt.

wringer.c: Wringer Wring"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, wrings; hence, an extortioner.

wringing.c: Wringing Wring"ing, a. & n. from Wring, v.

wringstaff.c: Wringstaff Wring"staff` (?), n.; pl. Wringstaves (?). (Shipbuilding) A strong piece of plank used in applying wringbolts.

wrinkle.c: Wrinkle Wrin"kle (?), n. A winkle. [Local, U. S.]
Wrinkle Wrin"kle, n. [OE. wrinkil, AS. wrincle; akin to OD. wrinckel, and prob. to Dan. rynke, Sw. rynka, Icel. hrukka, OHG. runza, G. runzel, L. ruga.????.]
Wrinkle Wrin"kle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wrinkled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wrinkling (?).]
Wrinkle Wrin"kle, v. i. To shrink into furrows and ridges.

wrinkly.c: Wrinkly Wrin"kly (?), a. Full of wrinkles; having a tendency to be wrinkled; corrugated; puckered. G. Eliot.

wrist.c: Wrist Wrist (?), n. [OE. wriste, wrist, AS. wrist; akin to OFries. wriust, LG. wrist, G. rist wrist, instep, Icel. rist instep, Dan. & Sw. vrist, and perhaps to E. writhe.]

wristband.c: Wristband Wrist"band (?), n. The band of the sleeve of a shirt, or other garment, which covers the wrist.

wrister.c: Wrister Wrist"er (?), n. A covering for the wrist.

wristlet.c: Wristlet Wrist"let (?), n. An elastic band worn around the wrist, as for the purpose of securing the upper part of a glove.

writ.c: Writ Writ (?), obs. 3d pers. sing. pres. of Write, for writeth. Chaucer.
Writ Writ, archaic imp. & p. p. of Write. Dryden.
Writ Writ, n. [AS. writ, gewrit. See Write.]

writability.c: Writability Writ`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. Ability or capacity to write. [R.] Walpole.

writable.c: Writable Writ"a*ble (?), a. Capable of, or suitable for, being written down.

writative.c: Writative Writ"a*tive (?), a. Inclined to much writing; -- correlative to talkative. [R.] Pope.

write.c: Write Write (?), v. t. [imp. Wrote (?); p. p. Written (?); Archaic imp. & p. p. Writ (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Writing.] [OE. writen, AS. wrītan; originally, to scratch, to score; akin to OS. wrītan to write, to tear, to wound, D. rijten to tear, to rend, G. reissen, OHG. rīzan, Icel. rīta to write, Goth. writs a stroke, dash, letter. Cf. Race tribe, lineage.]
Write Write, v. i. 1. To form characters, letters, or figures, as representative of sounds or ideas; to express words and sentences by written signs. Chaucer.

writership.c: Writership Writ"er*ship (?), n. The office of a writer.

writhe.c: Writhe Writhe (?), v. t. [imp. Writhed (?); p. p. Writhed, Obs. or Poetic Writhen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Writhing.] [OE. writhen, AS. wrī?an to twist; akin to OHG. rīdan, Icel. rī?a, Sw. vrida, Dan. vride. Cf. Wreathe, Wrest, Wroth.]
Writhe Writhe, v. i. To twist or contort the body; to be distorted; as, to writhe with agony. Also used figuratively.

writhen.c: Writhen Writh"en (?), a. Having a twisted distorted from.

writhle.c: Writhle Wri"thle (?), v. t. [Freq. of writhe.] To wrinkle. [Obs.] Shak.

writing.c: Writing Writ"ing (?), n. 1. The act or art of forming letters and characters on paper, wood, stone, or other material, for the purpose of recording the ideas which characters and words express, or of communicating them to others by visible signs.

written.c: Written Writ"ten (?), p. p. of Write, v.

wrizzle.c: Wrizzle Wriz"zle (?), v. t. To wrinkle. [Obs.] Spenser.

wroken.c: Wroken Wro"ken (?), obs. p. p. of Wreak. Chaucer.

wrong.c: Wrong Wrong (?), obs. imp. of Wring. Wrung. Chaucer.

Wrong Wrong (?; 115), a. [OE. wrong, wrang, a. & n., AS. wrang, n.; originally, awry, wrung, fr. wringan to wring; akin to D. wrang bitter, Dan. vrang wrong, Sw. vrång, Icel. rangr awry, wrong. See Wring.]
Wrong Wrong, adv. In a wrong manner; not rightly; amiss; morally ill; erroneously; wrongly.

Wrong Wrong, n. [AS. wrang. See Wrong, a.] That which is not right. Specifically: (a) Nonconformity or disobedience to lawful authority, divine or human; deviation from duty; -- the opposite of moral right.
Wrong Wrong (?; 115), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wronged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Wronging.]

wrongdoer.c: Wrongdoer Wrong"do`er (?), n. 1. One who injures another, or who does wrong.

wrongdoing.c: Wrongdoing Wrong"do`ing, n. Evil or wicked behavior or action.

wronger.c: Wronger Wrong"er (?), n. One who wrongs or injures another. Shak. “Wrongers of the world.” Tennyson.

wrongful.c: Wrongful Wrong"ful (?), a. Full of wrong; injurious; unjust; unfair; as, a wrongful taking of property; wrongful dealing. -- Wrong"ful*ly, adv. -- Wrong"ful*ness, n.

wronghead.c: Wronghead Wrong"head` (?), n. A person of a perverse understanding or obstinate character. [R.]

wrongheaded.c: Wrongheaded Wrong"head`ed, a. Wrong in opinion or principle; having a perverse understanding; perverse. -- Wrong"head`ed*ly, adv. -- Wrong"head`ed*ness, n. Macaulay.

wrongless.c: Wrongless Wrong"less, a. Not wrong; void or free from wrong. [Obs.] -- Wrong"less*ly, adv. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

wrongly.c: Wrongly Wrong"ly, adv. In a wrong manner; unjustly; erroneously; wrong; amiss; as, he judges wrongly of my motives. “And yet wouldst wrongly win.” Shak.

wrongness.c: Wrongness Wrong"ness, n. The quality or state of being wrong; wrongfulness; error; fault.

wrongous.c: Wrongous Wron"gous (?), a. [Cf. OE. wrongwis. See Wrong, and cf. Righteous.]

wrongtimed.c: Wrong-timed Wrong"-timed` (?; 115), a. Done at an improper time; ill-timed.

wroot.c: Wroot Wroot (?), obs. imp. of Write. Wrote. Chaucer.

wrote.c: Wrote Wrote (?), v. i. [OE. wroten. See 1st Root.] To root with the snout. See 1st Root. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Wrote Wrote, imp. & archaic p. p. of Write.

wroth.c: Wroth Wroth (?), a. [OE. wroth, wrap, AS. wrāð wroth, crooked, bad; akin to wrīðan to writhe, and to OS. wrēðangry, D. wreed cruel, OHG. reid twisted, Icel. reiðr angry, Dan. & Sw. vred. See Writhe, and cf. Wrath.] Full of wrath; angry; incensed; much exasperated; wrathful. “Wroth to see his kingdom fail.” Milton.

wrought.c: Wrought Wrought (?), imp. & p. p. of Work; as, What hath God wrought?.
Wrought Wrought, a. 1. Worked; elaborated; not rough or crude.

wrung.c: Wrung Wrung (?), imp. & p. p. of Wring.

wry.c: Wry Wry (?), v. t. [AS. wreón.] To cover. [Obs.]
Wry Wry (?), a. [Compar. Wrier (?); superl. Wriest.] [Akin to OE. wrien to twist, to bend, AS. wrigian to tend towards, to drive.]
Wry Wry, v. i. 1. To twist; to writhe; to bend or wind.
Wry Wry, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Wried; p. pr. & vb. n. Wrying.] [OE. wrien. See Wry, a.] To twist; to distort; to writhe; to wrest; to vex. Sir P. Sidney.

wrymouth.c: Wrymouth Wry"mouth` (?), n. (Zool.) Any one of several species of large, elongated, marine fishes of the genus Cryptacanthodes, especially Cryptacanthodes maculatus of the American coast. A whitish variety is called ghostfish.

wrynecked.c: Wrynecked Wry"necked` (?), a. Having a distorted neck; having the deformity called wryneck{1}.

wryness.c: Wryness Wry"ness, n. The quality or state of being wry, or distorted. W. Montagu.

wrythen.c: Wrythen Wryth"en (?), obs. p. p. of Writhe. Writhen.

wulfenite.c: Wulfenite Wul"fen*ite (?), n. [So named after F. X. Wulfen, an Australian mineralogist.] (Min.) Native lead molybdate occurring in tetragonal crystals, usually tabular, and of a bright orange-yellow to red, gray, or brown color; -- also called yellow lead ore.

wull.c: Wull Wull (?), v. t. & i. See 2d Will.

wungout.c: Wung-out Wung"-out` (?), a. Having the sails set in the manner called wing-and-wing. [Sailors' slang]

wurbagool.c: Wurbagool Wur"ba*gool (?), n. (Zool.) A fruit bat (Pteropus medius) native of India. It is similar to the flying fox, but smaller.

wurraluh.c: Wurraluh Wur"ra*luh (?), n. (Zool.) The Australian white-quilled honey eater (Entomyza albipennis).

wuste.c: Wuste Wust { Wust (?), Wuste }, obs. imp. of Wit. Piers Plowman.

wyandots.c: Wyandots Wy`an*dots" (?), n. pl.; sing. Wyandot (?). (Ethnol.) Same as Hurons. [Written also Wyandottes, and Yendots.]

wychelm.c: Wych-elm Wych"-elm` (?), n. [OE. wiche a kind of elm, AS. wice a kind of tree. Cf. Wicker.] (Bot.) A species of elm (Ulmus montana) found in Northern and Western Europe; Scotch elm.

wychhazel.c: Wych-hazel Wych"-ha`zel (?), n. (Bot.) The wych-elm; -- so called because its leaves are like those of the hazel.

wycliffite.c: Wycliffite Wyclifite { Wyc"lif*ite, Wyc"liff*ite } (?), n. A follower of Wyclif, the English reformer; a Lollard.

wyla.c: Wyla Wy"la (?), n. (Zool.) A helmeted Australian cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus funereus); -- called also funeral cockatoo.

wynd.c: Wynd Wynd (?), n. [See Wind to turn.] A narrow lane or alley. [Scot.] Jamieson.

wynkernel.c: Wynkernel Wyn"ker*nel (?), n. (Zool.) The European moor hen. [Prov. Eng.]

wynn.c: Wynn Wynn (?), n. A kind of timber truck, or carriage.

wype.c: Wype Wype (?), n. The wipe, or lapwing. [Prov. Eng.]

wythe.c: Wythe Wythe (wīth), n. (Naut.). Same as Withe, n., 4.

wyten.c: Wyten Wyte { Wyte (wīt), Wy"ten (wī"t'n) }, obs. pl. pres. of Wit.
